Clonado y verificado. Repo en `mermaid-upstream/` (sparse: solo docs, sin blobs innecesarios).

**Commit:** `9ac9635` · 2026-08-14 (ayer) · mermaid **v11.16.1** — es literalmente el HEAD de upstream.

**33 archivos de sintaxis, 12.500 líneas.** Están los 31 del sidebar de mermaid.ai **más dos que la web aún no publica**:

- `usecase.md` (438 líneas) — Use Case Diagram, mergeado el 2026-08-14
- `railroad.md` (316 líneas) — Railroad/syntax diagrams

Los 31 del índice, todos presentes: flowchart, swimlanes, sequenceDiagram, classDiagram, stateDiagram, entityRelationshipDiagram, userJourney, gantt, pie, quadrantChart, requirementDiagram, gitgraph, c4, mindmap, timeline, zenuml, sankey, xyChart, block, packet, kanban, architecture, radar, eventmodeling, treemap, venn, ishikawa, wardley, cynefin, treeView, examples.

Dos notas sobre el material:

1. **`userJourney.md` son 24 líneas y `ishikawa.md` 38** — insuficientes para autocompletado serio. Para esos dos habrá que sacar la gramática real de `packages/mermaid/src/diagrams/*/parser/*.jison` (o `.langium`), que también está en el repo si amplío el sparse-checkout.
2. Hay directorios hermanos útiles que aún no traje: `docs/config/` (theming, directivas, `%%{init}%%`, accesibilidad) y `docs/diagrams/`. Para un editor con validación y config visual los vas a querer.

Antes de seguir necesito una decisión tuya, porque cambia bastante el trabajo:

**¿El editor visual (drag & drop de nodos, edición sin escribir texto) entra en el alcance ahora, o arrancamos por editor de texto + preview + export y lo visual después?** Lo pregunto porque el editor visual bidireccional (texto ↔ canvas) es el grueso del esfuerzo y solo tiene sentido para un subconjunto de diagramas (flowchart, ER, class, state, architecture); para gantt, sankey o xychart lo natural es un editor de formulario/tabla, no un canvas.

Y lo segundo: **¿dónde vive esto?** ¿Es una vertical dentro de ZapiV2 (`apps/web/features/...`, con su plan en `docs/planes/`) o un proyecto aparte? Si es dentro de ZapiV2 tengo que leer las reglas de diseño y el catálogo de primitives antes de escribir markup.

Mientras tanto, ¿amplío el sparse-checkout a `src/diagrams/` (gramáticas) y `docs/config/`?

result.output:
# ExpressJS Agent Context - Resumen del Proyecto

## Propósito

Este repositorio es un **kit de ingeniería de contexto** diseñado para que agentes de IA (Claude, Copilot, Codex) construyan aplicaciones fullstack manteniendo coherencia arquitectónica. No es código ejecutable, sino documentación Markdown que actúa como "sistema de conocimiento" para que los agentes comprendan decisiones previas antes de modificar el proyecto.

El problema que resuelve: sin contexto persistente, los agentes tienden a inventar patrones inconsistentes, duplicar componentes y omitir estados, pruebas y seguridad.

## Stack de Referencia

- **Backend**: Node.js, TypeScript, Express.js
- **Frontend**: Next.js, React, Tailwind CSS, shadcn/ui
- **Base de datos**: PostgreSQL con Prisma ORM
- **Autenticación**: Better Auth
- **Herramientas**: pnpm, Docker, React Hook Form, Zod

## Estructura de Carpetas

```
├── AGENTS.md           # Reglas para agentes
├── ARCHITECTURE.md     # Mapa técnico
├── CLAUDE.md          # Instrucciones Claude
├── .agents/skills/    # Procedimientos reutilizables
├── .github/           # Config para Copilot
├── .codex/            # Configuración
└── docs/
    ├── product/       # Especificaciones
    ├── architecture/  # Stack y patrones
    ├── plans/         # Trabajos activos
    ├── quality/       # Testing y DoD
    └── security/      # Principios y hardening
```

## Cómo Funciona

El flujo recomendado con agentes es: leer instrucciones cercanas → abrir especificación → crear plan si es complejo → implementar cambios pequeños → ejecutar verificaciones → actualizar documentación → hacer commits granulares.

Los agentes no cargan todo el repositorio; el mapa pequeño guía qué fuente de verdad consultar según la tarea específica.

3	description: Las tablas usan scroll nativo con barra propia dibujada; Radix ScrollArea no sirve acá
4	metadata: 
5	  node_type: memory

7	  originSessionId: 7beb272d-0874-4ef7-88be-b13799bfc7e7

10	
11	`packages/ui/src/components/table.tsx` usa scroll nativo (`overflow-x-auto`) con la
12	barra del sistema oculta (`no-scrollbar`) y una barra propia dibujada encima, que
13	solo lee la posición y no controla el scroll.
14	
15	Antes de llegar ahí fallaron tres enfoques, todos descartados por razones concretas:
16	
17	- **CSS sobre la barra nativa** (`::-webkit-scrollbar`, `scrollbar-width`): no se
18	  puede forzar que sea persistente, lo decide el sistema operativo.
19	- **Radix `ScrollArea`**: inyecta un `<div style="display: table">` en el viewport
20	  que rompe las medidas. El pulgar aparece descolocado y el arrastre va tosco. Bug
21	  abierto en radix-ui/primitives (issues #2722, #2964, #3129, #3646).
22	- **`scroll-fade-x`** (degradado por scroll timeline): funciona, pero es un
23	  desvanecido, no una barra. Josue quería barra.
24	
25	**Why:** el `ScrollArea` que existe en el repo se usa solo en dos diálogos con
26	scroll vertical, nunca en tablas — eso no era casualidad.
27	
28	**How to apply:** no "mejorar" la tabla migrándola a `ScrollArea`. Si hay que tocar
29	el scroll horizontal, mantener el nativo y ajustar la barra dibujada.

Quedan tres, pero **no son proyectos, son cómo trabajar contigo**: respuestas cortas, "compilar no es verificar", "no sustituir lo pedido". Los dejé porque aplican en cualquier carpeta — dime si igual los quieres fuera.

**El template ya lo tienes clonado** en `/home/giossue/Documentos/ExpressJS-agent-context/` — 48 archivos, puro Markdown (AGENTS.md, ARCHITECTURE.md, `.agents/skills/` ×5, `docs/{product,architecture,plans,quality,security}`). Adaptarlo es reescribir contenido, no estructura.

---

## Mi recomendación: shadcn, no Mantine

El argumento decisivo no es "cuál tiene más componentes", es **qué proporción de tu UI la pone la librería**. En este producto es poca:

| Superficie | Quién la construye |
|---|---|
| Editor de código (CodeMirror 6) | tú |
| Viewport SVG con pan/zoom | tú |
| Canvas drag & drop (fase 2) | tú |
| Inspector de nodos, hilos de comentarios | tú |
| Botones, dialog, tabs, popover, split panes, command palette | la librería |

Mantine gana cuando hay 40 formularios (te regala ColorPicker, Tree, Spotlight, Notifications, RichTextEditor). Aquí eso casi no aplica, y a cambio pagas su *look* reconocible: para un producto que quiere verse mejor que Mermaid Chart, pelear contra el theming de una librería es trabajo perdido.

shadcn te da lo contrario: **el código es tuyo**, Tailwind v4 + tokens. Y hay un beneficio concreto que Mantine no tiene — el tema del diagrama Mermaid y el tema de la app salen del **mismo set de tokens CSS**, así el SVG nunca desentona con la interfaz. Accesibilidad idéntica (Radix). Ya cubre `resizable`, `command` (cmdk), `context-menu`, `sonner`.

**Resto del stack que propongo** (Bun de punta a punta):

- **Runtime/PM:** Bun + workspaces
- **API:** **Hono** (no Elysia — Elysia es más rápido pero te ata a Bun y su ecosistema de plugins es más delgado; Hono es portable y maduro)
- **Front:** React 19 + Vite + TanStack Router
- **Editor:** **CodeMirror 6**, no Monaco (más liviano, funciona en móvil, y añadir 33 lenguajes propios es viable; Monaco además se empaqueta fatal con Vite)
- **Render:** mermaid 11.16.1 **en Web Worker** — esto es lo que te da el *"limitless diagram size"*: mermaid.live congela el hilo principal con diagramas grandes, tú no
- **DB:** Postgres + Drizzle (sin binario de engine como Prisma)
- **Auth:** Better Auth
- **Export:** SVG nativo, PNG/WEBP por canvas, PDF por svg2pdf — todo cliente

Un dato que cambia una decisión: **Next.js no corre sobre el runtime de Bun** (sirve como gestor de paquetes, pero el server va en Node). Si quieres Bun puro, Vite es el camino.

Tres decisiones antes de escribir la primera línea:

options.label: shadcn/ui (Recomendado)
options.description: Tailwind v4 + Radix, código propio. Máxima libertad de diseño, tokens compartidos entre app y tema del diagrama. Construyes más componentes a mano.

options.label: Mantine
options.description: 120+ componentes listos (Spotlight, ColorPicker, Tree, Notifications). Más rápido al inicio, pero look reconocible y theming menos maleable.

options.label: Base UI + Tailwind
options.description: Primitives del equipo de Radix/MUI, más nuevos y sin la capa de shadcn. Más control aún, pero menos recetas hechas y ecosistema joven.

options.label: Vite + TanStack Router (Recomendado)
options.description: Bun de punta a punta, HMR instantáneo, ideal para app canvas-heavy. Las páginas públicas de diagramas compartidos las sirve Hono con OG images.

options.label: Next.js (App Router)
options.description: SSR y SEO listos para páginas públicas/compartir/landing, un solo deployable. Pero el server corre en Node, no en Bun.

options.label: Vite ahora, Next después
options.description: Arrancar la app en Vite y añadir un Next aparte solo para landing y páginas públicas cuando toque. Dos deployables.

questions.question: ¿Qué alcance tiene la fase 1 (editor de texto + preview + export)?

options.label: Solo cliente, sin backend (Recomendado)
options.description: Editor, preview en worker, export y persistencia local (IndexedDB/OPFS). Nada de Postgres ni auth todavía. Entrega usable en días, no semanas.

options.label: Full stack desde el día 1
options.description: Ya con Hono + Postgres + Drizzle + Better Auth y almacenamiento en servidor. Más lento hasta ver algo funcionando, pero sin migración después.

options.label: Cliente + backend mínimo
options.description: Editor completo en cliente, más una API Hono sin auth solo para guardar/compartir diagramas por URL. Auth y cuentas después.

1	# ExpressJS Agent Context
2	
3	Context engineering kit para construir aplicaciones fullstack con Express.js,
4	Next.js y agentes de IA sin perder consistencia arquitectonica, calidad ni criterio de
5	interfaz.
6	
7	Este repositorio no es un starter de codigo. Contiene un sistema de conocimiento en
8	Markdown para que Codex, Claude, GitHub Copilot y otros agentes puedan entender como
9	trabajar en un proyecto antes de modificarlo.
10	
11	## Por que existe
12	
13	Un agente puede generar codigo rapidamente, pero sin contexto persistente suele:
14	
15	- inventar patrones distintos en cada modulo;
16	- mezclar reglas de negocio con infraestructura;
17	- duplicar componentes y documentacion;
18	- exponer detalles tecnicos en la interfaz;
19	- omitir estados, permisos, pruebas o migraciones;
20	- depender de conversaciones que el siguiente agente no conoce.
21	
22	Este repositorio convierte esas decisiones en instrucciones versionadas, navegables y
23	verificables dentro del propio proyecto.
24	
25	## Que obtienes
26	
27	| Area          | Contexto incluido                                              |
28	| ------------- | -------------------------------------------------------------- |
29	| Agentes       | Instrucciones para Codex, Claude y GitHub Copilot              |
30	| Arquitectura  | Express.js, Next.js, limites por capas e integraciones         |
31	| Datos         | PostgreSQL, Prisma y migraciones versionadas                   |
32	| Autenticacion | Better Auth y reglas para no reinventar sesiones               |
33	| Frontend      | shadcn/ui, Tailwind, formularios, tablas y estados compartidos |
34	| UX operativa  | Jerarquia visual, baja fatiga, responsive y accesibilidad      |
35	| Calidad       | Definition of Done, testing, code review y observabilidad      |
36	| Seguridad     | Principios, boundaries y threat model                          |
37	| Ejecucion     | Planes activos, decisiones y skills reutilizables              |
38	
39	## Stack de referencia
40	
41	- Node.js y TypeScript.
42	- Express.js para API REST.
43	- Next.js y React para frontend.
44	- Better Auth para identidad y sesiones.
45	- PostgreSQL como base de datos principal.
46	- Prisma para ORM y migraciones.
47	- Tailwind CSS y shadcn/ui para interfaz.
48	- React Hook Form y Zod para formularios.
49	- Axios para integraciones HTTP server-side.
50	- pnpm mediante Corepack.
51	- Docker para desarrollo y despliegue.
52	
53	El stack es una decision base, no una restriccion irreversible. Si un proyecto necesita
54	desviarse, debe registrar la razon y sus consecuencias en un ADR.
55	
56	## Inicio rapido
57	
58	Para iniciar un proyecto nuevo desde esta base documental:
59	
60	```bash
61	git clone --depth 1 https://github.com/Elvis-WDev/ExpressJS-agent-context.git context-template
62	rsync -av --exclude='.git' context-template/ ruta/de/tu-proyecto/
63	rm -rf context-template
64	```
65	
66	Luego completa, como minimo:
67	
68	1. Reemplaza `{{PROJECT_NAME}}` en `AGENTS.md`.
69	2. Define proposito, usuarios y workflows en [docs/product/overview.md](docs/product/overview.md).
70	3. Modela entidades y reglas en [docs/product/domain-model.md](docs/product/domain-model.md).
71	4. Revisa el stack en [docs/architecture/stack.md](docs/architecture/stack.md).
72	5. Ajusta los comandos reales de verificacion en `AGENTS.md`.
73	6. Crea las primeras especificaciones bajo `docs/product/features/`.
74	7. Registra trabajos no triviales en `docs/plans/active/`.
75	
76	Si el proyecto ya existe, copia la estructura documental y adapta cada archivo a la
77	arquitectura real antes de pedir cambios al agente.
78	
79	## Como funciona el contexto
80	
81	```text
82	AGENTS.md
83	  -> indica que leer y como trabajar
84	ARCHITECTURE.md
85	  -> muestra componentes, limites y dependencias
86	docs/product/
87	  -> explica que debe hacer el producto
88	docs/architecture/
89	  -> explica como debe construirse
90	docs/plans/
91	  -> conserva la estrategia de trabajos complejos
92	.agents/skills/
93	  -> ejecuta procedimientos repetibles
94	docs/quality/ + docs/security/
95	  -> define cuando un cambio es aceptable
96	```
97	
98	La idea no es cargar todo el repositorio en cada prompt. El agente empieza con un mapa
99	pequeno y abre solamente la fuente de verdad relevante para la tarea.
100	
101	## Flujo recomendado con agentes
102	
103	1. Leer `AGENTS.md` y las instrucciones mas cercanas al codigo afectado.
104	2. Abrir la especificacion y arquitectura relacionadas con la tarea.
105	3. Crear o actualizar un plan cuando el trabajo sea no trivial.
106	4. Implementar el cambio coherente mas pequeno.
107	5. Ejecutar formato, lint, tipos, pruebas y build.
108	6. Actualizar documentacion y referencias derivadas.
109	7. Registrar decisiones costosas o duraderas mediante ADR.
110	8. No declarar terminado mientras implementacion, pruebas y documentacion difieran.
111	
112	Ejemplo de solicitud inicial:
113	
114	```text
115	Lee AGENTS.md y la documentacion relevante para esta tarea.
116	Antes de editar, identifica la especificacion, los limites arquitectonicos y la
117	Definition of Done. Implementa, verifica y actualiza la documentacion afectada.
118	```
119	
120	## Skills incluidos
121	
122	- `implement-feature`: implementar comportamiento desde especificacion hasta verificacion.
123	- `create-migration`: cambiar modelos y datos mediante migraciones seguras.
124	- `review-code`: revisar bugs, seguridad, regresiones, arquitectura y pruebas.
125	- `update-documentation`: mantener fuentes de verdad y referencias sincronizadas.
126	- `implement-operational-frontend`: construir interfaces operativas consistentes y sin sobrecarga visual.
127	
128	Los skills viven en `.agents/skills/` y se cargan solo cuando la tarea los necesita.
129	
130	## Criterio frontend
131	
132	El contexto incluye reglas concretas para evitar que paneles administrativos y
133	aplicaciones operativas terminen como una acumulacion de cards, formularios, filtros y
134	mensajes.
135	
136	- [Arquitectura frontend](docs/architecture/frontend.md)
137	- [Sistema de componentes](docs/architecture/component-system.md)
138	- [Diseno de interfaces operativas](docs/architecture/interface-design.md)
139	- [Data tables](docs/architecture/data-tables.md)
140	- [Formularios y workflows](docs/architecture/forms-and-workflows.md)
141	- [Feedback y estados](docs/architecture/feedback-and-states.md)
142	- [Navegacion y responsive](docs/architecture/navigation-responsive.md)
143	- [Checklist frontend](docs/quality/frontend-checklist.md)
144	
145	Principios esenciales:
146	
147	- usar lenguaje de negocio y ocultar IDs o detalles internos;
148	- mantener tablas, filtros, acciones y paginacion uniformes;
149	- usar modales para CRUD breve y paginas completas para workflows complejos;
150	- comunicar acciones con feedback semantico sin llenar la pagina de banners;
151	- limitar la navegacion visible a dos niveles;
152	- reutilizar componentes antes de crear variantes por modulo;
153	- verificar desktop, mobile, teclado, light mode y dark mode;
154	- eliminar contenido redundante que no ayude a decidir o actuar.
155	
156	## Mapa del repositorio
157	
158	```text
159	.
160	├── AGENTS.md                       # Reglas permanentes para agentes
161	├── ARCHITECTURE.md                 # Mapa tecnico de alto nivel
162	├── CLAUDE.md                       # Entrada para Claude
163	├── .agents/skills/                 # Procedimientos reutilizables
164	├── .github/                        # Instrucciones para Copilot
165	├── .codex/                         # Configuracion, no conocimiento del producto
166	└── docs/
167	    ├── product/                    # Producto, dominio y features
168	    ├── architecture/               # Stack, boundaries y patrones
169	    ├── plans/                      # Trabajo activo, completado y deuda
170	    ├── quality/                    # Testing, review y Definition of Done
171	    ├── security/                   # Principios y amenazas
172	    └── generated/                  # Referencias derivadas
173	```
174	
175	## Fuentes de verdad
176	
177	- [Guia para agentes](AGENTS.md)
178	- [Mapa de arquitectura](ARCHITECTURE.md)
179	- [Indice de documentacion](docs/README.md)
180	- [Indice de arquitectura](docs/architecture/index.md)
181	- [Definition of Done](docs/quality/definition-of-done.md)
182	- [Principios de seguridad](docs/security/principles.md)
183	
184	## Que no incluye
185	
186	- Codigo de una aplicacion concreta.
187	- Requerimientos de un dominio o cliente.
188	- Dependencias instaladas o build output.
189	- Secretos, credenciales o variables de entorno reales.
190	- Una arquitectura inmutable que deba aplicarse sin evaluar contexto.
191	
192	El repositorio contiene solamente contexto Markdown reutilizable. Cada aplicacion debe
193	completar sus especificaciones de producto y mantenerlas junto al codigo.
194	
195	## Reglas que no deben romperse
196	
197	- `AGENTS.md` es un mapa corto, no una enciclopedia.
198	- `docs/` conserva el conocimiento durable del proyecto.
199	- Las instrucciones cercanas al codigo tienen prioridad sobre las globales.
200	- Los secretos permanecen fuera del repositorio y del frontend.
201	- Los cambios de base de datos usan migraciones.
202	- Las reglas criticas se convierten en tests, linters o automatizacion.
203	- Un cambio no esta terminado sin implementacion, verificacion y documentacion coherentes.
204	- Los errores repetidos del agente deben transformarse en contexto o controles ejecutables.
205

17

# Project Agent Guide

## Project

`mermaid-render` is a TypeScript application: an editor, viewer and exporter for
Mermaid diagrams that aims to cover **every** diagram type in the official syntax and
to surpass Mermaid Chart's paid tier (visual editor, unlimited storage, unlimited
diagram size, view & comment collaboration).

Stack:

- Bun as runtime, package manager and test runner.
- Bun workspaces monorepo.
- React 19 + Vite + TanStack Router for the application.
- Tailwind CSS v4 + shadcn/ui for the interface.
- CodeMirror 6 for the text editor.
- `mermaid` (upstream) executed inside a Web Worker for parsing and rendering.
- Zod for schema validation.
- Biome for format and lint.

Phase 1 is client-only: there is no server, no database and no authentication yet.
Diagrams live in the browser (IndexedDB/OPFS). Do not add a backend, an ORM or auth
without an ADR.

## Read Before Working

- Product overview: `docs/product/overview.md`
- Architecture map: `ARCHITECTURE.md`
- Architecture details: `docs/architecture/index.md`
- Stack baseline: `docs/architecture/stack.md`
- Diagram catalog: `docs/knowledge/diagram-catalog.md`
- Rendering pipeline: `docs/architecture/rendering.md`
- Text editor: `docs/architecture/editor.md`
- Frontend architecture: `docs/architecture/frontend.md`
- Interface design: `docs/architecture/interface-design.md`
- Active plans: `docs/plans/active/`
- Definition of done: `docs/quality/definition-of-done.md`
- Frontend review checklist: `docs/quality/frontend-checklist.md`
- Security principles: `docs/security/principles.md`

## Syntax Source Of Truth

Mermaid syntax is **never** written from memory or from a web summary. The upstream
repository is vendored at `mermaid-upstream/` (sparse checkout, docs only):

- Prose and examples: `mermaid-upstream/packages/mermaid/src/docs/syntax/*.md`
- Grammars, when the prose is insufficient: `mermaid-upstream/packages/mermaid/src/diagrams/*/parser/`

`mermaid-upstream/` is read-only. Do not edit it, do not commit changes into it, and
refresh it only through `bun run sync:upstream`. Every claim about a keyword, a shape
or a version gate must be traceable to a file in there.

## Workflow

1. Read this file and the nearest `AGENTS.md` for the files you will touch.
2. Open only the relevant docs for the current task.
3. For non-trivial work, create or update a plan in `docs/plans/active/`.
4. Implement the smallest coherent change.
5. Update documentation when behavior, architecture, syntax coverage, or decisions change.
6. Run the project's verification commands before calling work complete.

## Required Verification

Use Bun. Never introduce npm, yarn or pnpm.

- Install: `bun install`
- Dev: `bun run dev`
- Format: `bun run format`
- Lint: `bun run lint`
- Test: `bun test`
- Typecheck: `bun run typecheck`
- Build: `bun run build`
- Full validation: `bun run verify`
- Refresh upstream Mermaid docs: `bun run sync:upstream`

## Constraints

- Always use Bun; never use npm, yarn or pnpm for installs, scripts or lockfiles.
- Do not put product or architecture knowledge in `.codex/`.
- Do not edit anything under `mermaid-upstream/`.
- Do not describe Mermaid syntax without citing the upstream file it came from.
- Parsing and rendering run in a Web Worker. Never call `mermaid.render` on the main thread.
- Never inject rendered SVG without sanitizing it; diagram text is untrusted input.
- Keep `securityLevel` at `strict` unless an ADR documents otherwise.
- Do not add a backend, database, ORM or authentication during phase 1 without an ADR.
- Do not introduce production dependencies without documenting why.
- Do not bypass validation at storage, worker-message, import/export, or URL boundaries.
- Do not mark work complete while verification is failing.
- Keep secrets out of committed files.
- Do not expose internal IDs, storage keys or implementation details in product UI.
- Reuse the documented component, dialog, feedback and navigation patterns instead of
  inventing a different interaction model per surface.
- A diagram type is not "supported" until it renders, highlights, autocompletes and
  exports; partial support must be recorded in `docs/knowledge/diagram-catalog.md`.

## Definition Of Done

Implementation, verification, documentation, and acceptance criteria must agree.

# Architecture Map

## System Style

Default architecture:

- Client-first TypeScript application. The browser is the runtime; there is no server in phase 1.
- Bun workspaces monorepo: one application (`apps/web`) over independent packages.
- Mermaid parsing and rendering are isolated inside a Web Worker; the main thread never blocks.
- Diagram documents are persisted locally (IndexedDB for metadata, OPFS for large payloads).
- Export (SVG, PNG, WEBP, PDF) is fully client-side.
- Upstream Mermaid is vendored read-only at `mermaid-upstream/` as the syntax source of truth.

Phase 2 adds a Hono API on Bun, PostgreSQL with Drizzle, Better Auth, and Yjs-based
collaboration. Those boundaries are designed for now but not implemented yet; see
`docs/architecture/deployment.md`.

## Main Components

- `apps/web/`: React application, routes, screens, editor shell, canvas, dialogs.
- `packages/core/`: domain — diagram document model, diagram-type catalog, shared types, no DOM.
- `packages/renderer/`: Web Worker host, render pipeline, SVG sanitization, error normalization.
- `packages/editor/`: CodeMirror 6 language support, highlighting, completion, diagnostics.
- `packages/export/`: SVG/PNG/WEBP/PDF serialization.
- `packages/storage/`: storage ports plus the IndexedDB/OPFS adapter.
- `packages/ui/`: Tailwind tokens, shadcn/ui primitives, shared application components.
- `docs/product/`: product specifications and domain knowledge.
- `docs/architecture/`: technical decisions and boundaries.
- `docs/knowledge/`: distilled Mermaid syntax catalog, derived from `mermaid-upstream/`.
- `docs/plans/`: active and completed implementation plans.
- `mermaid-upstream/`: read-only vendored upstream docs. Not a workspace package.

## Dependency Direction

```text
core  ->  editor | renderer | export | storage  ->  ui  ->  apps/web
```

Rules:

- `core` depends on nothing in this repo and touches no DOM API. It must be testable under `bun test` with no browser.
- `editor`, `renderer`, `export` and `storage` may depend on `core` and on the DOM, but not on each other and not on React.
- `ui` may depend on `core` and React, never on `renderer` or `storage` directly.
- `apps/web` wires everything and is the only place allowed to know about all packages at once.
- No package imports from `apps/web`.
- Nothing imports from `mermaid-upstream/`.

## Boundaries

- **Worker boundary**: every message in and out of the render worker is a validated, structured-cloneable value. No functions, no DOM nodes, no class instances.
- **Untrusted-input boundary**: diagram text is user input. It reaches the worker as a string and comes back as SVG that must be sanitized before insertion.
- **Storage boundary**: `packages/storage` exposes ports; the IndexedDB/OPFS adapter is the only implementation that knows browser storage APIs. Schema changes are versioned migrations.
- **Import/export boundary**: files read from disk, pasted content and URL-encoded diagrams are validated before they become documents.
- **Rendering/UI boundary**: the viewport owns pan, zoom and hit-testing; the renderer owns SVG production. They exchange an SVG string and a measured viewBox, nothing else.
- **Upstream boundary**: `mermaid-upstream/` is documentation input for humans and agents, never a runtime dependency. The runtime dependency is the published `mermaid` npm package, pinned.

## Detailed Documents

- Architecture index: `docs/architecture/index.md`
- Stack baseline: `docs/architecture/stack.md`
- Bootstrap guide: `docs/architecture/bootstrap.md`
- Rendering pipeline: `docs/architecture/rendering.md`

# Stack Baseline

Technology stack for `mermaid-render`.

## Package Manager And Runtime

- Use Bun for install, scripts, tests and the lockfile (`bun.lock`).
- Do not use npm, yarn or pnpm for installs, scripts, audits or lockfile updates.
- Keep the required Bun version declared in `engines` and in `.bun-version`.

```bash
bun install
bun run dev
bun run verify
```

## Monorepo

- Bun workspaces.
- One application: `apps/web`.
- Packages: `core`, `renderer`, `editor`, `export`, `storage`, `ui`.
- Dependency direction is enforced in `ARCHITECTURE.md` and checked by lint rules.

## Frontend

- React 19 with TypeScript.
- Vite as the bundler and dev server.
- TanStack Router for type-safe routing.
- Tailwind CSS v4 with semantic theme tokens defined as CSS variables.
- shadcn/ui for reusable UI components (Radix primitives, code owned in `packages/ui`).
- lucide-react for icons.
- Zustand for editor and workspace client state.
- Zod for schema validation at every untrusted boundary.

Next.js is intentionally not used: its server does not run on the Bun runtime, and the
application is client-heavy enough that SSR adds no value. Public shareable pages will
be served by the phase-2 Hono API. Recorded in `adr/0001-vite-over-nextjs.md`.

## Text Editor

- CodeMirror 6.
- One language mode per Mermaid diagram type, sharing a common tokenizer core.
- Completion, diagnostics and folding come from `packages/editor`.

Monaco is intentionally not used: heavier, worse mobile behavior, and painful to bundle
with Vite. Recorded in `adr/0002-codemirror-over-monaco.md`.

## Rendering

- The published `mermaid` npm package, pinned to an exact version.
- Executed inside a dedicated Web Worker. The main thread never calls `mermaid.render`.
- `securityLevel: 'strict'`; SVG output is sanitized before insertion.
- The pinned version must match the version vendored at `mermaid-upstream/`.

## Persistence

Phase 1 is client-only:

- IndexedDB holds documents, metadata and revision history.
- OPFS holds large payloads and export artifacts when they exceed the IndexedDB budget.
- Storage schema changes use versioned migrations, same as a database.

Phase 2 adds PostgreSQL with Drizzle as the server-side source of truth. Prisma is not
used: it ships an engine binary and adds weight Bun does not need.

## Backend (Phase 2, Not Implemented)

- Hono on Bun for the HTTP API.
- Better Auth for identity and sessions.
- PostgreSQL and Drizzle for persistence and migrations.
- Yjs for collaborative editing and anchored comment threads.

Elysia was considered and rejected: faster, but Bun-locked with a thinner plugin
ecosystem. Recorded in `adr/0003-hono-over-elysia.md`.

## Export

- SVG: direct serialization of the sanitized output.
- PNG and WEBP: rasterized through `OffscreenCanvas` at a selectable scale.
- PDF: vector output, not a rasterized image.
- All export runs client-side; no server round trip.

## Tooling

- Biome for format and lint, replacing ESLint and Prettier.
- `bun test` for unit tests.

# Rendering Pipeline

Owner package: `packages/renderer`.

## Why Not A Web Worker

Mermaid lays out diagrams by measuring real text: it calls `getBBox` and
`getComputedTextLength` on SVG nodes that the browser has actually laid out. A Web
Worker has no DOM and no layout engine, so `mermaid.render` cannot run there. Upstream
states the same constraint for its own test suite:

> The layout cannot work in `jsdomIt` tests because JSDOM has no rendering engine.
> — `mermaid-upstream/packages/mermaid/src/docs/community/contributing.md:340`

Any proposal to "move rendering to a worker" is wrong and must be rejected in review.
DOM shims (JSDOM, linkedom) do not solve it, because the missing piece is layout, not
the DOM API surface.

## The Render Frame

Rendering happens inside a dedicated hidden `<iframe>` — the **render frame** — created
once and reused.

What the iframe buys:

- **Layout isolation.** A 5,000-node diagram triggers style recalculation and layout in
  its own document. The application's document is untouched, so the editor keeps
  responding while a large diagram lays out. This is the single biggest difference from
  mermaid.live, where a large diagram freezes the whole page.
- **CSS isolation.** Mermaid injects global styles and relies on inherited font metrics.
  In the main document those styles leak into the application; in the frame they cannot.
- **Deterministic measurement.** The frame loads a fixed stylesheet and a fixed, locally
  hosted font set. The same diagram measures the same way regardless of the user's
  application theme or a late-loading webfont.
- **A security layer.** The frame carries `sandbox="allow-scripts"` without
  `allow-same-origin`, so scripts smuggled through diagram text cannot reach the
  application origin, its storage, or its cookies.

What the iframe does **not** buy: a separate thread. A same-origin iframe shares the
event loop with its parent. Serving the frame from a distinct origin makes browsers with
site isolation give it its own renderer process, which does yield true parallelism; this
is an optimization to evaluate, not an assumption to build on. Perceived responsiveness
comes from scheduling and cancellation, described below.

## Contract

The frame and the host exchange structured-cloneable messages only. Every message is
validated with Zod on both sides.

```text
host  -> frame :  { type: 'render', jobId, text, config, theme }
host  -> frame :  { type: 'cancel', jobId }
frame -> host  :  { type: 'ok',    jobId, svg, viewBox, elements }
frame -> host  :  { type: 'error', jobId, error: { kind, message, line?, column?, excerpt? } }
```

Rules:

- SVG crosses the boundary as a **string**, never as a node.
- `elements` is a flat list of `{ id, kind, box }` used by the viewport for hit-testing
  and, later, by the visual editor. It is derived in the frame, where the layout exists.
- `bindFunctions` from `mermaid.render` is never transferred. Interactivity is
  reattached on the host side from `elements`, under our own event handling.
- A `jobId` that the host has already cancelled is discarded on arrival.

## Scheduling And Cancellation

The editor emits on every keystroke; the renderer must not.

1. **Debounce** input, with a shorter delay for small documents and a longer one for
   large ones.
2. **Parse before render.** `mermaid.parse` is much cheaper than a full render. A
   document that fails to parse produces diagnostics for the editor and never reaches
   the render step, so a half-typed diagram costs almost nothing.
3. **One job in flight.** A new job cancels the previous one. Cancellation is
   cooperative: the frame checks the cancel flag between phases.
4. **Keep the last good frame.** While a new render is in flight, the viewport keeps
   showing the previous successful SVG, dimmed rather than blanked. Errors annotate the
   editor gutter; they never clear the canvas. Losing your diagram because you typed a
   stray character is the failure mode this exists to prevent.

## Sanitization

Diagram text is untrusted input. Two layers, both required:

1. Mermaid runs with `securityLevel: 'strict'`, which escapes HTML in labels.
2. The SVG string is sanitized on the host with DOMPurify configured for SVG plus MathML
   before it is inserted into the application document.

`securityLevel: 'loose'` and `antiscript` are forbidden. Mermaid's own `sandbox` level is
not used, because our render frame already provides the isolation and `sandbox` would
strip the interactivity we want to keep — see
`mermaid-upstream/packages/mermaid/src/docs/config/usage.md:111-122`.

## Theming

The application theme and the diagram theme are generated from **one** token set.

- `packages/ui` owns the semantic tokens as CSS variables.
- `packages/renderer` maps those tokens to Mermaid `themeVariables` and passes them in
  the render config.
- Theme reference: `mermaid-upstream/packages/mermaid/src/docs/config/theming.md`.

A diagram must never look pasted in from another product. When the user switches to dark
mode, the diagram switches with it, from the same source values.

## Large Diagrams

"Limitless diagram size" is a rendering-pipeline requirement, not a marketing line:

- Never re-render on every keystroke; see scheduling above.
- Never serialize the SVG to a data URL for display. Insert the sanitized node.
- The viewport pans and zooms with a CSS transform on a single container, so panning
  costs no re-layout.
- Above a node-count threshold, the preview downgrades to a coarse mode (labels hidden,
  simplified edges) until interaction stops, then renders in full.
- Raster export at high scale runs in a real Web Worker over `OffscreenCanvas` — that
  step is DOM-free and genuinely parallelizable.

## Verification

- Golden-file tests: every diagram type in `docs/knowledge/diagram-catalog.md` renders
  from its canonical example, under `bun test`.
- Playwright visual regression across light and dark themes.
- A cancellation test proving an in-flight job for stale text never reaches the viewport.
- A sanitization test with a diagram that attempts script injection through a label,
  a link and a `click` directive.

# Text Editor

Owner package: `packages/editor`. Built on CodeMirror 6.

## Why CodeMirror, Not Monaco

- Bundles cleanly with Vite; Monaco needs worker plumbing and ships far more code.
- Works on touch devices, which Monaco effectively does not.
- Its language support is composable, which matters here: this project needs **33**
  language modes, not one.
- Its decoration and extension model is what the phase-2 features need — inline comment
  anchors, collaborative cursors, error underlines.

Recorded in `adr/0002-codemirror-over-monaco.md`.

## Language Architecture

Mermaid is not one language. It is a family of grammars sharing a preamble. The editor
mirrors that shape:

```text
packages/editor/
├── core/          # preamble: frontmatter, directives, comments, common tokens
├── dialects/      # one module per diagram type
└── registry.ts    # header pattern -> dialect
```

- **Detection.** The first non-comment, non-frontmatter line selects the dialect
  (`flowchart`, `sequenceDiagram`, `gantt`, …). Detection is a pure function over the
  document head, shared with `packages/core` so the app, the editor and the renderer all
  agree on the diagram type.
- **Shared preamble.** YAML frontmatter (`---`), init directives (`%%{init: ...}%%`) and
  comments (`%%`) are highlighted identically in every dialect. Written once.
- **Per-dialect layer.** Keywords, operators, node shapes and structural blocks. Sourced
  strictly from `docs/knowledge/diagrams/<type>.md`, which is itself derived from
  `mermaid-upstream/`.

Start each dialect as a CodeMirror `StreamLanguage`, which is cheap to write and enough
for highlighting and completion. Promote a dialect to a Lezer grammar only when it needs
a real syntax tree — folding by block, structural selection, or bidirectional visual
editing. Flowchart, class, state, ER and architecture are the ones expected to graduate.

## Completion

Completion is context-aware, not a flat keyword dump:

- At the start of an empty document: the diagram-type picker.
- At the start of a line: statements valid for the current dialect.
- After a node identifier: shapes, then edge operators.
- Inside a shape delimiter: nothing — it is a label, stay out of the way.
- After `class`/`style`/`classDef`: classes already defined in the document.
- After an edge operator: identifiers already defined in the document, then a new-node affordance.

Every completion entry carries the minimum Mermaid version that supports it, taken from
the catalog. Entries above the pinned runtime version are shown but marked, never
offered silently.

## Diagnostics

- `mermaid.parse` is the source of truth for validity. The editor does not maintain a
  second, divergent notion of "valid".
- Parse errors are normalized in `packages/renderer` into `{ kind, message, line, column, excerpt }`
  and surfaced as CodeMirror diagnostics on the offending line.
- Mermaid's raw error text is often unhelpful. The normalizer maps known error shapes to
  actionable messages, and keeps the raw text available behind a disclosure.
- A parse failure never clears the preview; see `rendering.md`.

## Editor Affordances

- Fold by block: `subgraph`, `loop`/`alt`/`opt`, `class`, `section`, `namespace`.
- Bracket and quote closing aware of Mermaid's shape delimiters (`[]`, `()`, `{}`, `[[]]`, `([])`, `[()]`, `{{}}`).
- Selection-aware comment toggle using `%%`.
- Rename symbol across a document, scoped to node identifiers.
- Jump to definition for node identifiers and class definitions.
- A command palette exposing every diagram type with a canonical starter snippet.

## Boundaries

- `packages/editor` must not import `packages/renderer`, `packages/storage` or React.
  It exposes CodeMirror extensions; `apps/web` wires them.
- Dialect data is generated from the catalog, not hand-maintained in two places. If a
  keyword exists in a dialect but not in `docs/knowledge/diagrams/<type>.md`, the catalog
  is wrong and gets fixed — not the other way around.

## Verification

- Every dialect has a highlighting test over the canonical example from the catalog.
- Completion tests assert context: the same cursor position in two dialects offers
  different entries.
- A test asserts that every diagram type listed in the catalog has a registered dialect,
  so adding a type to the catalog without an editor mode fails the build.

# Product Overview

## Purpose

`mermaid-render` is an editor, viewer and exporter for Mermaid diagrams that covers
**every** diagram type in the official syntax — 33 of them, including the ones the public
documentation site has not published yet — and does it better than Mermaid Chart's paid
tier.

The bet is narrow and testable: the official playground is good at small diagrams and
falls apart at everything else. It blocks the page on large diagrams, blanks the canvas
on a typo, offers no real autocomplete, and gates storage and collaboration behind a
subscription. Each of those is a fixable engineering problem, not a pricing problem.

## Users

- **Primary user**: a developer or architect who writes Mermaid by hand, in a repo or in
  documentation, and needs a fast loop between text and picture.
- **Secondary user**: a teammate who does not write Mermaid — a PM, a designer, an
  analyst — who needs to read a diagram, edit it without learning syntax, and comment on it.
- **Admin/operator**: not applicable in phase 1; the product is single-user and local.

## Problems Solved

1. **Coverage.** Most editors support flowcharts well and everything else poorly. This
   one treats Radar, Wardley, Cynefin, TreeView and Event Modeling as first-class.
2. **Scale.** Large diagrams freeze existing editors. Layout isolation, cancellation and
   coarse-mode preview keep the editor responsive regardless of diagram size.
3. **Authoring friction.** Mermaid's syntax is wide and its errors are cryptic.
   Context-aware completion and normalized diagnostics remove most of the guesswork.
4. **Fragile feedback.** Existing editors clear the preview on a parse error, so the
   diagram disappears mid-thought. The last good render always stays on screen.
5. **Access to non-authors.** A person who cannot write Mermaid still needs to change a
   label or leave a note. That is what the visual editor and comments are for.
6. **Lock-in.** Diagrams are text. Storage, export and history stay under the user's
   control and leave in open formats.

## Feature Parity Target

The paid tier being matched or beaten:

| Their feature | Our position |
| --- | --- |
| Visual editor | Phase 3. Bidirectional text ↔ canvas, not a one-way generator. |
| 300 AI credits | Phase 4. Bring-your-own-key, so there is no credit meter. |
| Unlimited diagram storage | Phase 1, locally. Phase 2 on the server. |
| Limitless diagram size | Phase 1, as an architectural property. See `docs/architecture/rendering.md`. |
| View & comment collaboration | Phase 2. Comments anchored to node IDs, not to line numbers. |

Beyond parity: full 33-type coverage, offline-first, vector PDF export, diagram diffing,
and a local-first storage model.

## Core Workflows

1. **Write and see.** Type Mermaid, get a live preview that never blanks, with
   completion and diagnostics from the real parser.
2. **Start from a type.** Pick any of the 33 diagram types and get a canonical starter
   snippet that renders immediately.
3. **Navigate.** Pan, zoom, fit, and focus a node in a diagram far larger than the viewport.
4. **Export.** SVG, PNG, WEBP at a chosen scale, and vector PDF — all client-side.
5. **Keep.** Diagrams and their revision history persist locally, with no account.
6. **Edit visually** (phase 3). Drag nodes, draw edges, rename labels; the text updates.
7. **Review** (phase 2). Share a link, let someone comment on a node without editing it.

## Phasing

- **Phase 1 (current)**: client-only. Editor, preview, export, local storage. No server, no account.
- **Phase 2**: Hono API on Bun, PostgreSQL, Better Auth, sharing, comments.
- **Phase 3**: bidirectional visual editor.
- **Phase 4**: AI assistance with the user's own key.

## Non-Goals

- Not a general drawing tool. Everything is a Mermaid document; if it cannot round-trip
  to text, it does not belong here.
- Not a fork of Mermaid. Upstream is a pinned dependency; syntax gaps get reported
  upstream rather than patched locally.
- No account, server or telemetry in phase 1.
- No AI-generated diagrams before the manual editor is genuinely good.
- Not a real-time multi-cursor editor in phase 2; view and comment first.

## Source Of Truth

- Domain model: `docs/product/domain-model.md`
- Glossary: `docs/product/glossary.md`
- Diagram catalog: `docs/knowledge/diagram-catalog.md`
- Features: `docs/product/features/`
- Architecture: `ARCHITECTURE.md`

# Frontend Architecture

## Runtime

- Framework: React 19 with Vite. No Next.js — see `adr/0001-vite-over-nextjs.md`.
- Routing: TanStack Router, file-based, fully typed.
- Language: TypeScript in strict mode.
- Styling: Tailwind CSS v4 with semantic theme tokens as CSS variables.
- Component system: shadcn/ui, with the generated code owned in `packages/ui`.
- Icons: lucide-react.
- Client state: Zustand.
- Validation: Zod at every untrusted boundary.
- Text editor: CodeMirror 6 via `packages/editor`.
- Feedback: one shared semantic toast system.

## Product UI Principle

The product is a tool, not a dashboard. Its center is a document and a picture of that
document; everything else is chrome and should behave like chrome — present when
reached for, silent otherwise.

Concretely: the editor and the canvas own the screen. Toolbars stay thin, panels stay
collapsed by default, and no surface competes with the diagram for attention. If a
control is used once per session, it belongs in the command palette, not on the toolbar.

Do not treat every option as a settings panel, every list as a card grid, or every action
as a permanent button. Choose the smallest surface that supports the workflow.

## Screen Shape

The primary screen is a resizable split: source on one side, canvas on the other, with a
thin toolbar above and a status strip below.

- The split ratio, orientation and collapsed state persist per user.
- On narrow viewports the split becomes a tab switch, not a stack — a squeezed editor
  above a squeezed canvas is useless on both counts.
- The canvas is the surface that grows. When in doubt, give it the pixels.

## State Ownership

- **Document state**: the Mermaid text plus its metadata. Owned by the workspace store,
  persisted through `packages/storage`. Single source of truth.
- **Editor state**: cursor, selection, folding. Owned by CodeMirror. Do not mirror it.
- **Render state**: last good SVG, in-flight job, diagnostics. Owned by the renderer
  store. Never derived twice.
- **Viewport state**: pan, zoom, focused node. Local to the canvas, serialized into the
  URL so a view can be linked.
- **URL state**: active document, viewport, and shareable options.
- **Local UI state**: transient interaction only, such as an open dialog.

Do not mirror the same state across URL, store, component and storage without a single
declared owner.

## Component Policy

1. Reuse an existing product component.
2. Compose shadcn/ui primitives from `packages/ui`.
3. Add a shared application component when at least two surfaces need the same contract.
4. Create a surface-specific component only when its behavior is genuinely specific.

shadcn is a source of code, not a dependency: installed components are read, stripped of
demo assumptions, mapped to project tokens, checked for accessibility, and aligned with
the existing contract before use. Do not accumulate near-duplicate primitives.

## Theme Tokens

`packages/ui` owns one semantic token set. Both the application chrome and the Mermaid
`themeVariables` are generated from it — see `rendering.md`. A change to a token must
move the interface and the diagram together. A diagram that does not match the
surrounding interface is a bug, not a preference.

## Technical Information Boundary

Storage keys, document UUIDs, worker job IDs, sanitizer decisions and Mermaid's internal
error strings do not appear in product UI. The user sees diagram names, a line and column,
and an actionable message.

A developer panel may expose raw parser output and render timings, but it stays behind an
explicit toggle and looks visibly distinct from the product.

## Verification Baseline

Before completion, exercise the screen with:

- an empty document, a one-line document, and a diagram large enough to exceed the viewport;
- a document that fails to parse, and one that parses but fails to render;
- every diagram type touched by the change;
- long labels, unicode labels, right-to-left text, and the smallest supported viewport;
- keyboard-only navigation and visible focus;
- light and dark themes, checking the diagram and the chrome together;
- rapid typing, to confirm cancellation works and the canvas never blanks;
- the shared frontend checklist.

A clean build proves nothing about how this looks. Open it.

# Storage

Owner package: `packages/storage`.

In phase 1 there is no database and no server. The browser is the store. It is still
treated with database discipline: an explicit schema, versioned migrations, and a port
that hides the implementation.

## Model

- **IndexedDB** holds documents, metadata, revision history and workspace preferences.
- **OPFS** holds large payloads: export artifacts, embedded images, and document bodies
  past the size where keeping them in IndexedDB hurts read latency.
- Nothing depends on `localStorage`. It is synchronous, small, and string-only.

## Object Stores

| Store | Key | Contents |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `documents` | `id` (UUID v7) | name, diagram type, body or OPFS pointer, timestamps, tags |
| `revisions` | `[documentId, seq]` | prior bodies for history and diffing |
| `folders` | `id` | tree of user-defined folders |
| `preferences` | `key` | split ratio, theme, editor options |
| `blobs` | `id` | OPFS pointers with size and content type |

Indexes: `documents.by-updated`, `documents.by-type`, `documents.by-folder`,
`revisions.by-document`.

UUID v7 rather than v4, so keys sort by creation time and listing does not need a
secondary index.

## Ports

`packages/storage` exposes ports, not an IndexedDB client:

```text
DocumentRepository   list, get, create, update, delete, restore
RevisionRepository   append, list, get, prune
BlobStore            put, get, delete, size
PreferenceStore      get, set
```

The IndexedDB/OPFS adapter is the only module that imports a browser storage API. When
phase 2 adds a server, it implements the same ports; nothing above the port changes.
That is the whole reason the indirection exists — do not bypass it "just this once".

## Migrations

Storage schema changes are migrations, exactly as they would be against Postgres:

- One numbered migration per change, in `packages/storage/migrations/`.
- Migrations run in IndexedDB's `upgradeneeded` and must be idempotent and forward-only.
- Never rename or repurpose an existing store in place; add and backfill.
- Every migration has a test that opens a fixture database at the previous version and
  asserts the resulting shape.
- A user's data is not disposable because it is local. A migration that can lose a
  diagram is a defect.

## Quotas

Browser storage can be evicted. The product must not pretend otherwise:

- Request persistent storage via `navigator.storage.persist()` on first save.
- Surface usage against quota in settings, in human terms.
- Warn before the quota is reached, not after a write fails.
- A failed write is a visible, recoverable error with the content still in the editor —
  never a silent loss.

## Export And Portability

- The full workspace exports as a single archive of plain `.mmd` files plus a manifest.
- Import accepts that archive, a folder of `.mmd` files, or a single file.
- Everything imported is validated with Zod before becoming a document.
- Diagrams are text and leave in text. There is no proprietary format.

## Phase 2

PostgreSQL with Drizzle becomes the server-side source of truth, and the local store
becomes an offline-first cache with sync. Prisma is not used: it ships an engine binary
and adds weight Bun does not need. Local-first stays the model — the product works with
no network.

# mermaid-render

An editor, viewer and exporter for **every** Mermaid diagram type — 33 of them,
including the ones the official documentation site has not published yet — built to beat
Mermaid Chart's paid tier on the things that actually hurt: large diagrams, authoring
friction, and lock-in.

Built with Bun, React 19, Vite, TanStack Router, Tailwind v4, shadcn/ui and CodeMirror 6.

> Phase 1 is client-only. No server, no account, no telemetry. Your diagrams stay in your
> browser and leave as plain text.

## Why

The official playground is good at small flowcharts and poor at everything else. It
blocks the page on large diagrams, blanks the canvas the moment you mistype, has no real
autocomplete, and puts storage and collaboration behind a subscription.

None of that is a pricing problem. It is an architecture problem:

| Problem | What we do instead |
| --- | --- |
| Large diagrams freeze the page | Layout runs in an isolated render frame; jobs are cancellable |
| A typo blanks the preview | The last good render stays on screen; errors go to the gutter |
| No meaningful autocomplete | Context-aware completion per dialect, from the real grammar |
| Cryptic parser errors | Normalized diagnostics with line, column and an actionable message |
| Only flowcharts are well supported | All 33 types are first-class, tracked in a catalog |
| Your diagrams live in their account | Local-first storage, open export, no proprietary format |

## Feature Target

| Mermaid Chart paid | Here |
| --- | --- |
| Visual editor | Phase 3 — bidirectional text ↔ canvas, not a one-way generator |
| 300 AI credits | Phase 4 — bring your own key, no credit meter |
| Unlimited diagram storage | Phase 1 locally, phase 2 on the server |
| Limitless diagram size | Phase 1, as an architectural property |
| View & comment collaboration | Phase 2 — comments anchored to node IDs, not line numbers |

Plus: full 33-type coverage, offline-first, vector PDF export, and diagram diffing.

## Quick Start

```bash
bun install
bun run dev
```

Bun only. Do not use npm, yarn or pnpm.

## Commands

| Command | Purpose |
| --- | --- |
| `bun run dev` | Dev server |
| `bun run build` | Production build |
| `bun run typecheck` | TypeScript, strict |
| `bun run lint` | Biome |
| `bun run format` | Biome |
| `bun test` | Unit tests |
| `bun run verify` | Everything above |
| `bun run sync:upstream` | Refresh the vendored Mermaid docs |

## Repository Map

```text
.
├── AGENTS.md                       # Permanent rules for agents
├── ARCHITECTURE.md                 # High-level technical map
├── CLAUDE.md                       # Entry point for Claude
├── apps/web/                       # React application
├── packages/
│   ├── core/                       # Domain: document model, diagram catalog
│   ├── renderer/                   # Render frame, pipeline, sanitization
│   ├── editor/                     # CodeMirror language support, 33 dialects
│   ├── export/                     # SVG, PNG, WEBP, PDF
│   ├── storage/                    # Ports plus the IndexedDB/OPFS adapter
│   └── ui/                         # Tokens, shadcn primitives, shared components
├── docs/
│   ├── product/                    # Product, domain and features
│   ├── architecture/               # Stack, boundaries and subsystems
│   ├── knowledge/                  # Distilled Mermaid syntax catalog
│   ├── plans/                      # Active work, completed work, debt
│   ├── quality/                    # Testing, review, Definition of Done
│   └── security/                   # Principles and threats
├── .agents/skills/                 # Reusable procedures
└── mermaid-upstream/               # Vendored upstream docs — READ ONLY
```

## Syntax Source Of Truth

Mermaid syntax is never written from memory or from a web summary. Upstream is vendored
read-only at `mermaid-upstream/` (sparse checkout, docs only), and
`docs/knowledge/diagram-catalog.md` is distilled from it. Every claim about a keyword, a
shape or a version gate cites the upstream file it came from.

Refresh with `bun run sync:upstream`. Never edit anything inside `mermaid-upstream/`.

## Two Things That Are Easy To Get Wrong

**Mermaid cannot render in a Web Worker.** It measures text with `getBBox` and
`getComputedTextLength`, which need a real layout engine. Rendering runs in a dedicated
sandboxed iframe instead. Workers are used only for DOM-free work. Details and the
upstream citation are in [docs/architecture/rendering.md](docs/architecture/rendering.md).

**Diagram text is untrusted input.** Mermaid runs at `securityLevel: 'strict'` and the
resulting SVG is sanitized again before it enters the application document. `loose` and
`antiscript` are forbidden.

## Sources Of Truth

- [Agent guide](AGENTS.md)
- [Architecture map](ARCHITECTURE.md)
- [Documentation index](docs/README.md)
- [Architecture index](docs/architecture/index.md)
- [Diagram catalog](docs/knowledge/diagram-catalog.md)
- [Definition of Done](docs/quality/definition-of-done.md)
- [Security principles](docs/security/principles.md)

## Credits

The context-engineering structure in `AGENTS.md`, `.agents/skills/` and `docs/` is
adapted from [ExpressJS-agent-context](https://github.com/Elvis-WDev/ExpressJS-agent-context)
by Elvis-WDev, re-targeted from Express/Next/Prisma to this stack.

[Mermaid](https://github.com/mermaid-js/mermaid) is MIT licensed and is a pinned
dependency here, not a fork.

# Bootstrap Guide

How to bring the repository up from a clean clone.

## Prerequisites

- Bun, at the version pinned in `.bun-version`.
- Git.
- A Chromium-based browser for Playwright.

No Node, no npm, no Docker in phase 1.

## Steps

```bash
git clone <repo> mermaid-render
cd mermaid-render
bun install
bun run sync:upstream     # vendors mermaid-upstream/ (sparse, docs only)
bun run verify            # format, lint, typecheck, test, build
bun run dev
```

## Vendored Upstream

`mermaid-upstream/` is a sparse, blobless checkout of `mermaid-js/mermaid` limited to
`packages/mermaid/src/docs`. It is documentation input, never a runtime dependency:

```bash
git clone --depth 1 --filter=blob:none --sparse \
  https://github.com/mermaid-js/mermaid.git mermaid-upstream
cd mermaid-upstream && git sparse-checkout set packages/mermaid/src/docs
```

`sync:upstream` wraps this. It is gitignored — each clone fetches its own.

The pinned `mermaid` npm version and the vendored checkout must describe the same
release. When they drift, the catalog is regenerated and the mismatch is resolved before
anything else lands.

## Workspace Layout

Bun workspaces, declared in the root `package.json`:

```json
{ "workspaces": ["apps/*", "packages/*"] }
```

`mermaid-upstream/` is deliberately outside both globs. It is not a package.

## Environment

Phase 1 needs no environment variables and has no `.env`. If a variable ever becomes
necessary, it is validated with Zod at startup and documented here — never read
ad hoc from `import.meta.env` deep in a component.

## First Verification

A clean bootstrap is correct when:

- `bun run verify` passes;
- `bun run dev` serves the app;
- every diagram type in `docs/knowledge/diagram-catalog.md` renders its canonical
  example in the golden-file test;
- `mermaid-upstream/packages/mermaid/src/docs/syntax/` contains 33 `.md` files.

# Backend Architecture

> **Phase 2. Not implemented.** Phase 1 is client-only. Do not build any of this without
> an ADR promoting the project to phase 2. This document exists so phase-1 boundaries are
> drawn in the right places, not as a to-do list.

## Runtime

- Language: TypeScript.
- Runtime: Bun.
- Framework: Hono. Not Express — see `adr/0003-hono-over-elysia.md` for why Hono and not
  Elysia; Express is simply not a candidate on Bun.
- Database access: Drizzle.
- Database: PostgreSQL.
- Authentication: Better Auth.
- Validation: Zod, shared with the client through `packages/core`.

## Layers

### Domain

Entities, value objects, domain errors, invariants. Already exists as `packages/core`
and is shared with the client — the diagram document model is the same object on both
sides. Must not depend on HTTP frameworks, database clients or external SDKs.

### Application / Use Cases

Workflows, ports, DTOs, transaction boundaries. Must not depend on concrete
infrastructure or on HTTP request/response objects.

### Infrastructure

Hono routes, Drizzle repositories, external clients, jobs, runtime configuration.

## API Conventions

- Success envelope: `{ data, meta? }`.
- Error envelope: `{ error: { code, message, details? } }`.
- Pagination metadata on every collection.
- Sessions come from Better Auth middleware; routes never parse cookies by hand.
- Validate params, query, body, environment and external payloads with Zod.

## Storage Boundary

The server implements the same ports `packages/storage` already defines for IndexedDB.
That is the point of the port: adding a server must not change anything above it. Local
storage becomes an offline-first cache, not a legacy path to delete.

## Rendering Boundary

Rendering stays on the client. The server never runs Mermaid, with one exception:
generating OG preview images for public share links, which runs headless Chromium in a
job — because, as `rendering.md` explains, Mermaid needs a real layout engine and there
is no server-side shortcut around that.

## Collaboration Boundary

- Comments anchor to node IDs from the render `elements` list, never to line numbers.
  Line numbers move when the text is edited; a node ID survives.
- Yjs owns document convergence when real-time editing arrives. View-and-comment ships
  first and does not need it.

## Background Jobs

Persisted, for work that must survive a refresh: OG image generation, workspace export,
bulk import. Each job records ownership, retry policy, cancellation and progress.

# Authentication

> **Phase 2. Not implemented.** Phase 1 has no accounts, no sessions and no identity.
> Adding auth requires an ADR.

## Phase 1 Position

There is deliberately no login. The product is fully usable with no account: diagrams are
local, export is local, nothing leaves the browser. "Sign in to continue" is the exact
friction this product exists to avoid, so an account must never become a prerequisite for
the core loop — only for the features that genuinely need a server (sharing, comments, sync).

## Phase 2 Design

- Better Auth owns sign-in, sign-out, sessions, cookies, password hashing and auth tables.
- Do not implement custom password hashing or session tables unless an ADR replaces Better Auth.
- Better Auth mounts at `/api/auth/*` and is registered before body-parsing middleware.
- Application use cases receive the authenticated identity as plain data, never as a
  framework object.
- Anonymous use stays first-class: an unauthenticated visitor can open, edit and export.
  Signing in adopts the local workspace rather than replacing it.

## Sharing Without Accounts

A share link must be readable without an account. Access is carried by an unguessable
link token, checked server-side, with an explicit visibility setting per diagram
(`private`, `link`, `public`). Commenting may require identity; viewing must not.

## Boundaries

- Tokens and secrets stay server-side.
- The client never receives a credential it does not need.
- Session checks happen in middleware, not per route by hand.

# Deployment

## Phase 1

The application is a static bundle. `bun run build` produces `apps/web/dist`, which is
served by any static host or CDN. There is no server, no database and no container.

Requirements:

- Serve over HTTPS. `navigator.storage.persist()` and OPFS need a secure context.
- Set a strict Content Security Policy. The render frame is the only place that executes
  diagram-derived content, and it is sandboxed without `allow-same-origin`.
- Serve the render frame document from its own path, with its own CSP.
- Fonts are self-hosted. Text measurement must not depend on a third-party CDN being up
  or fast — a late font swap changes diagram layout.
- Ship a service worker so the editor works offline. Local-first is a product promise.
- Cache-bust the Mermaid chunk on version change; a stale renderer against a fresh
  catalog produces confusing "unsupported syntax" errors.

## Render Frame Origin

The render frame may optionally be served from a distinct origin so browsers with site
isolation give it its own renderer process. This is a performance optimization for very
large diagrams, not a correctness requirement — the sandbox already provides the security
boundary. If adopted, the second origin is part of the deployment contract and must be
documented here.

## Phase 2

- Bun container for the Hono API.
- PostgreSQL, managed or self-hosted, never destroyed on redeploy.
- Drizzle migrations run as a separate, explicit step before the new version serves traffic.
- Health checks on the API container.
- The static frontend and the API can share one public domain routed by path (`/` and `/api`).
- Headless Chromium for OG image generation runs as a job worker, not in the API process.

## Not Deployed

`mermaid-upstream/` is gitignored and never shipped. It is a local documentation
checkout for humans and agents.

# Integrations

## Phase 1

The only external dependency at runtime is the pinned `mermaid` npm package, bundled.
Phase 1 makes no network requests. That is a feature, and a regression test asserts it:
loading the app and rendering every diagram type must produce zero outbound requests.

Integrations that run entirely in the browser and are therefore allowed:

- **Clipboard**: paste Mermaid text or an image of a diagram; copy SVG or PNG.
- **File system**: open and save `.mmd` files through the File System Access API, with a
  download fallback.
- **URL encoding**: a diagram compressed into a link, compatible with the encoding used
  by mermaid.live so existing links open here. Decoding is validated with Zod — a URL is
  untrusted input.

## Mermaid As A Dependency

- Pinned to an exact version, never a range. A minor bump can change layout output and
  invalidate every visual snapshot.
- Upgrades are their own change: bump, re-vendor `mermaid-upstream/`, regenerate the
  catalog, review the visual diffs, then land.
- This project does not fork Mermaid. Missing syntax is reported upstream, not patched
  locally.

## Phase 2 Candidates

Each needs its own spec before it exists:

- GitHub and GitLab: read `.mmd` files from a repository, open a PR with a change.
- Confluence, Notion, Slack: render a share link into an image preview.
- CLI: render a file from a terminal, sharing `packages/renderer`.

## Rules

- External clients live in infrastructure, behind typed ports, never called from UI code.
- Provider tokens come from validated server-side configuration. Phase 1 has none, and
  no integration may introduce a client-side secret.
- Provider errors are normalized before reaching UI code.
- Any AI provider (phase 4) uses the user's own key, held server-side for their session
  only, and is never a required dependency of the editor.

# Domain Model

Owned by `packages/core`. No DOM, no React, no storage APIs — testable under `bun test`
with no browser.

## Entities

### Document

The unit the product exists to manage.

| Field | Notes |
| --- | --- |
| `id` | UUID v7, sorts by creation time |
| `name` | User-facing. Falls back to the diagram's own title when unnamed |
| `type` | `DiagramType`, detected from the body, overridable only by editing the body |
| `body` | The Mermaid source. The single source of truth for everything visual |
| `folderId` | Optional |
| `tags` | Free-form |
| `createdAt` / `updatedAt` | |
| `schemaVersion` | For storage migrations |

Invariants:

- `body` is authoritative. Nothing derived from it — type, node list, thumbnail — is ever
  stored as a competing truth. Derived data is cache, and cache may be dropped.
- A document with an unparseable body is still a valid document. Invalid text is a normal
  state during editing, not a corruption.

### Revision

An earlier `body` for a `Document`, keyed by `[documentId, seq]`, with a timestamp and an
optional label. Revisions are append-only and prunable by policy, never rewritten.

### DiagramType

A closed enum of the 33 types in `docs/knowledge/diagram-catalog.md`. Each carries:

- its detection pattern (the header that identifies it);
- its minimum Mermaid version;
- its canonical starter example;
- its editor dialect;
- its support status.

This is generated from the catalog, not hand-written. Adding a type to the enum without a
catalog entry fails the build.

### Folder

A user-defined tree node: `id`, `name`, `parentId`, `position`. Depth is not limited by
the model; the interface collapses deep paths rather than forbidding them.

## Value Objects

- `MermaidSource` — the diagram text, with detection and normalization helpers.
- `DiagramElement` — `{ id, kind, box }`, produced by the renderer from real layout. The
  bridge to the phase-3 visual editor.
- `RenderError` — `{ kind, message, line?, column?, excerpt? }`, normalized from Mermaid's
  raw parser output.
- `Viewport` — `{ x, y, zoom }`, serializable into a URL.

## Rules

- Text is the source of truth. Every feature, including the visual editor, is a
  transformation of `body`. If a feature cannot round-trip to text, it does not ship.
- Detection is one pure function, shared by app, editor and renderer. Three different
  answers about "what kind of diagram is this" is a defect class we refuse to have.
- Deletion is soft first: a deleted document is recoverable until it is purged.

## Source Of Truth

- Diagram catalog: `docs/knowledge/diagram-catalog.md`
- Storage schema: `docs/architecture/database.md`
- Glossary: `docs/product/glossary.md`

# Glossary

| Term | Meaning |
| --- | --- |
| Document | A saved Mermaid diagram: its source text plus metadata. The unit the product manages. |
| Body | The Mermaid source text of a document. Always the source of truth. |
| Diagram type | One of the 33 types in the catalog: flowchart, sequence, gantt, radar, wardley… |
| Dialect | The editor's language mode for one diagram type. One per type. |
| Catalog | `docs/knowledge/diagram-catalog.md`: the distilled, citable record of what syntax exists. |
| Upstream | `mermaid-upstream/`, the vendored read-only Mermaid docs. The only citable syntax source. |
| Render frame | The sandboxed iframe where Mermaid runs. Not a Web Worker — Mermaid needs layout. |
| Render job | One cancellable attempt to turn a body into SVG, identified by a `jobId`. |
| Last good render | The most recent successful SVG. Stays on screen while a new job runs or fails. |
| Element | `{ id, kind, box }` derived from real layout. Used for hit-testing, comments and visual editing. |
| Viewport | Pan and zoom state over the canvas. Serializable into a URL. |
| Coarse mode | Degraded preview for very large diagrams during interaction. |
| Diagnostic | A normalized parse error placed on a line in the editor. |
| Workspace | Everything stored locally: documents, folders, revisions, preferences. |
| Revision | A prior body of a document, append-only. |
| Phase | Delivery stage. 1 client-only, 2 server and comments, 3 visual editor, 4 AI. |

## Naming Rules

- Use product language in UI copy: "diagram", not "document record"; "version", not "revision row".

# Add Diagram Type

The core repeated procedure of this project. There are 33 diagram types; this skill is
how each one goes from "renders by accident" to "supported".

## Context To Load

Read, in order:

- `AGENTS.md`
- `docs/knowledge/diagram-catalog.md`
- `mermaid-upstream/packages/mermaid/src/docs/syntax/<type>.md` — **completely**, not skimmed
- `docs/architecture/editor.md`
- `docs/architecture/rendering.md`
- An existing dialect in `packages/editor/dialects/` as a reference

If the prose is ambiguous about a token, open the grammar at
`mermaid-upstream/packages/mermaid/src/diagrams/<type>/parser/`. Never resolve ambiguity
by guessing or by searching the web.

## Definition Of Supported

A type is supported when all five hold. Anything less is recorded as partial in the
catalog, with the specific gap named:

1. **Renders** — the canonical example produces SVG, covered by a golden-file test.
2. **Highlights** — a registered dialect, covering every keyword in the catalog entry.
3. **Completes** — context-aware completion, not a flat keyword list.
4. **Diagnoses** — parse errors normalized to line, column and an actionable message.
5. **Exports** — SVG, PNG and PDF, verified against this type's own quirks.

## Workflow

1. Read the upstream syntax page in full. List every keyword, operator, shape,
   direction, block structure and configuration option it documents.
2. Note the version gate. Many types and many features carry a minimum version
   (`v11.3.0+`, `v11.16.0+`). Record it per feature, not just per type.
3. Write or update `docs/knowledge/diagrams/<type>.md`, citing the upstream file and line
   for anything non-obvious. This entry is the source the code generates from.
4. Add the detection pattern to `packages/core`, with a test that it does not collide
   with any other type's pattern.
5. Add the canonical starter example. It must render and it must be genuinely useful as a
   starting point, not a two-node stub.
6. Implement the dialect in `packages/editor/dialects/`. Start as a `StreamLanguage`;
   promote to Lezer only if the type needs a real syntax tree.
7. Add completion sources, scoped to context.
8. Add golden-file and visual-regression tests.
9. Update the status row in `docs/knowledge/diagram-catalog.md`.
10. Run `bun run verify`.

## Guardrails

- Never write Mermaid syntax from memory. Cite `mermaid-upstream/`.
- Never edit anything inside `mermaid-upstream/`.
- Do not mark a type supported when one of the five criteria fails. Record the gap and
  move on; a false "supported" row is worse than an honest partial one.
- Keywords live in the catalog and are generated into the dialect. If the two disagree,
  the catalog is fixed first.
- Version-gated features are shown and marked, never silently offered.
- Types marked experimental upstream (`-beta` suffixes, 🔥 or ⚠️ markers) keep that
  marking in our catalog and in the UI.
- Do not fork or patch Mermaid to make a type work. Report it upstream and record the
  limitation.

# Create Storage Migration

There is no database in phase 1, but the browser store is treated with the same
discipline. A user's diagrams are not disposable because they happen to be local.

## Context To Load

Read:

- `docs/architecture/database.md`
- `docs/architecture/stack.md`
- `docs/product/domain-model.md`
- `docs/security/principles.md`
- Existing migrations in `packages/storage/migrations/`
- Relevant feature spec.

## Workflow

1. Understand the model change and which workflows read the affected stores.
2. Decide whether the migration is additive, destructive, or data-transforming.
3. Add one numbered migration in `packages/storage/migrations/`. Never edit a migration
   that has already shipped.
4. Bump `schemaVersion` on affected records.
5. Update the ports and DTOs in `packages/storage`, then the adapter.
6. Update the store table in `docs/architecture/database.md`.
7. Add a test that opens a fixture database at the previous version and asserts the
   resulting shape.
8. Run `bun run verify`.

## Guardrails

- Migrations run in `upgradeneeded`, are idempotent, and are forward-only.
- Never rename or repurpose a store in place. Add, backfill, then retire in a later
  release once the backfill has shipped.
- Destructive changes require an explicit data plan written into the migration file.
- A migration that can lose a diagram is a defect, not a trade-off.
- Handle quota failures explicitly. A failed write surfaces as a recoverable error with
  the content still in the editor.
- Phase 2 will implement the same ports against Postgres and Drizzle. Do not leak
  IndexedDB specifics above the port.
- Prisma is not used in this project.

# Implement App Surface

The editor and the canvas are the product. This skill covers everything around them: the
library of saved diagrams, folders, the export dialog, settings, the command palette,
navigation and responsive behavior.

  - `docs/architecture/feedback-and-states.md`.
  - `docs/architecture/navigation-responsive.md`.
- `docs/quality/frontend-checklist.md`.

## Workflow

1. Inspect the existing surface, shared components in `packages/ui`, the storage ports it
   will call, and neighboring surfaces.
2. State the primary user task and choose the smallest suitable surface: inline control,
   command-palette entry, popover, dialog, or full page.
3. Remove duplicated headings, summaries, cards, helper text and persistent feedback that
   do not help the task.
4. Reuse shared primitives before adding components. Extend the shared contract when
   behavior belongs across surfaces.
5. Implement every relevant state: loading, empty, filtered-empty, partial, pending,
   success, validation, quota-exceeded, conflict, and unexpected failure.
6. Keep internal identifiers in values only. Render diagram names and human references.
7. Exercise keyboard, touch, responsive layouts, long content, light and dark themes,
   repeated actions, and slow storage.
8. Run `bun run verify` and complete the frontend checklist.
9. Update architecture or feature docs when the workflow or a shared contract changes.

## Component Decisions

- Use the shared TanStack-based table for the diagram library.
- Use Zod schemas from `packages/core` for form validation.
- Use shadcn/ui primitives from `packages/ui` and Lucide icons.
- Use a semantic toast for routine action results.
- Use inline field errors for correctable input.
- Use a dialog for short records such as rename or new folder.
- Use a full page for long, high-risk, multi-section workflows such as workspace import.
- Put anything used once per session in the command palette, not on the toolbar.
- Reads and writes go through `packages/storage` ports, never a direct IndexedDB call.

## Guardrails

- Do not let chrome compete with the canvas. When in doubt, give the canvas the pixels.
- Do not expose storage keys, document UUIDs, job IDs, sanitizer decisions or raw
  Mermaid error text without a documented operational need.
- Do not create a third navigation level.
- Do not invent surface-specific pagination, toast, tooltip, dialog or table behavior.

  project tokens, accessibility and shared contracts.
- Do not mark complete with overlap, clipped controls, missing states, or a diagram whose
  colors no longer match the chrome.
