# ADR 0001: Vite and TanStack Router instead of Next.js

## Status

Accepted

## Context

The reference context kit this project is adapted from assumes Next.js. This project
targets Bun end to end, and the application is an editor: a long-lived client session
around a CodeMirror instance, a render frame and a pan/zoom canvas.

Three facts drove the decision:

- Next.js does not run its server on the Bun runtime. Bun works as the package manager,
  but the server process is Node. Choosing Next.js means the "Bun everywhere" premise is
  false from day one.
- Server rendering contributes nothing to the primary screen. The editor cannot be
  rendered on the server in any useful way, and phase 1 has no server at all.
- Vite's dev server and HMR are materially faster for a client-heavy application, which
  matters when the inner loop is "change a dialect, look at the highlighting".

The genuine argument for Next.js is public shareable diagram pages: SEO and Open Graph
previews. That is a phase-2 concern and it is a small, well-bounded surface.

## Decision

Use React 19 with Vite and TanStack Router for the application. Do not use Next.js.

When phase 2 needs public share pages with OG previews, the Hono API serves them,
generating preview images in a job. That keeps one runtime and one deployable rather than
adopting a second framework for a handful of routes.

## Consequences

- Positive: one runtime, Bun, from install through test through serve.
- Positive: faster dev loop, simpler bundling for CodeMirror and the render frame.
- Positive: the phase-1 build is a static bundle deployable to any CDN.
- Negative: no built-in SSR, file-system API routes, or image optimization. Each must be
  chosen deliberately if it turns out to be needed.
- Negative: public share pages need explicit work in phase 2 instead of coming free.
- Follow-up: revisit if public, indexable diagram pages become a primary acquisition
  channel rather than a convenience.

# ADR 0002: CodeMirror 6 instead of Monaco

## Status

Accepted

## Context

The product needs a real code editor with syntax highlighting, context-aware completion,
diagnostics, folding and, later, collaborative cursors and inline comment anchors.

The two candidates are Monaco, which powers VS Code, and CodeMirror 6.

The deciding constraint is that Mermaid is not one language. It is 33 grammars sharing a
preamble. Whatever is chosen will be extended 33 times, so the cost of adding one
language mode dominates the decision — not the feature list of the editor itself.

## Decision

Use CodeMirror 6.

Reasons, in order of weight:

- Language support is composable. A `StreamLanguage` dialect is small enough to write and
  review 33 times, and can be promoted to a Lezer grammar per type when a real syntax
  tree is needed. Monaco's Monarch is workable but its language services are heavier.
- Monaco does not work usably on touch devices. CodeMirror 6 does.
- Monaco requires worker plumbing and awkward bundling with Vite; CodeMirror is a plain
  ES-module dependency.
- Bundle size differs by roughly an order of magnitude, on the primary screen.
- The decoration and extension model is the natural fit for phase-2 comment anchors and
  collaborative cursors.

## Consequences

- Positive: adding a diagram type is a small, reviewable change.
- Positive: the editor is usable on tablets and phones.
- Positive: smaller bundle on the screen that matters most.
- Negative: no IntelliSense-grade tooling for free; completion and diagnostics are built
  deliberately, per dialect.
- Negative: fewer engineers have prior CodeMirror 6 experience, and its API changed
  significantly from version 5, so older material online is misleading.
- Follow-up: define which dialects graduate to Lezer. Flowchart, class, state, ER and
  architecture are expected to, because the visual editor needs their syntax trees.

# ADR 0003: Render in a sandboxed iframe, not a Web Worker

## Status

Accepted

## Context

A defining goal is that large diagrams must not freeze the application, which the
official playground does. The obvious answer is to move rendering off the main thread
into a Web Worker.

That answer is wrong, and it is wrong in a way that looks right until it is implemented.
Mermaid lays out diagrams by measuring real text: it calls `getBBox` and
`getComputedTextLength` on SVG elements the browser has actually laid out. A Web Worker
has no DOM and, more importantly, no layout engine. Upstream states the same constraint
about its own test suite:

> The layout cannot work in `jsdomIt` tests because JSDOM has no rendering engine.
> — `mermaid-upstream/packages/mermaid/src/docs/community/contributing.md:340`

DOM shims do not help. JSDOM and linkedom provide API surface, not layout; `getBBox`
returns zeros and every diagram collapses.

This decision was initially recorded incorrectly in this repository as "render in a Web
Worker" and was corrected before any code existed. The ADR is written partly so the
mistake is not made a second time.

## Decision

Run Mermaid inside a dedicated, reused, hidden `<iframe>` — the render frame — carrying
`sandbox="allow-scripts"` without `allow-same-origin`. SVG crosses back to the host as a
sanitized string.

Web Workers are still used, but only for work that is genuinely DOM-free: raster export
over `OffscreenCanvas`, document serialization, and diffing.

Responsiveness comes from the frame's layout isolation plus debouncing,
parse-before-render, single-job-in-flight cancellation, and coarse mode for very large
diagrams. Details in `docs/architecture/rendering.md`.

## Consequences

- Positive: heavy style recalculation and layout happen in a separate document, so the
  editor keeps responding.
- Positive: Mermaid's global CSS injection cannot leak into the application.
- Positive: measurement is deterministic — fixed stylesheet, self-hosted fonts, no
  dependence on the user's theme or a late font swap.
- Positive: a sandbox without `allow-same-origin` is a real security boundary against
  script smuggled through diagram text.
- Negative: a same-origin iframe shares the event loop with its parent, so this is not
  true parallelism. Cancellation and scheduling do the real work.
- Negative: an extra document to build, style and cache-bust, and an asynchronous message
  contract to validate on both sides.
- Follow-up: evaluate serving the render frame from a distinct origin, so site isolation
  gives it its own renderer process. Treat as an optimization, never as an assumption.
- Follow-up: reject any future proposal to "just move rendering to a worker" with a link
  to this ADR.

# ADR 0004: Hono for the phase-2 API, not Elysia or Express

## Status

Proposed — applies when the project enters phase 2. No server exists yet.

## Context

Phase 2 adds an HTTP API on Bun for sharing, comments and sync. Express is not a
candidate: it is a Node-shaped framework and using it on Bun forfeits the reason for
choosing Bun. That leaves Hono and Elysia.

Elysia is Bun-native and benchmarks faster, with strong end-to-end type inference through
Eden. Hono is portable across Bun, Node, Deno and edge runtimes, with a larger middleware
ecosystem and broader production use.

Raw throughput is not the constraint here. This API serves diagram documents and comment
threads for an application whose expensive work — parsing, layout, export — happens in
the browser. Request volume per user is low.

## Decision

Use Hono.

- Portability is worth more than throughput for this workload. If the render frame ever
  moves to its own origin, or preview generation moves to an edge function, Hono runs
  there unchanged.
- Better Auth integrates with Hono along a well-travelled path.
- A thinner plugin ecosystem is a real cost when the need is ordinary: CORS, sessions,
  rate limiting, validation.

## Consequences

- Positive: one framework across every deployment target under consideration.
- Positive: mature middleware for the unglamorous requirements.
- Negative: measurably slower than Elysia in synthetic benchmarks. Accepted, because the
  bottleneck is not the HTTP layer.
- Negative: type inference between server and client is good but not Eden-grade. Zod
  schemas shared through `packages/core` close most of that gap.
- Follow-up: revisit if a workload appears where HTTP throughput actually is the
  bottleneck. Diagram documents are not that workload.

# GitHub Copilot Instructions

Read `AGENTS.md` first.

Use `docs/` as the source of truth for product, architecture, quality, and security context.

For path-specific guidance, use files in `.github/instructions/`.

# Package Instructions

Apply to files under `packages/`.

- Respect the dependency direction in `ARCHITECTURE.md`:
  `core` → `editor` | `renderer` | `export` | `storage` → `ui` → `apps/web`.
- `packages/core` touches no DOM API and no React. It must pass `bun test` with no browser.
- `packages/editor` exposes CodeMirror extensions. It does not import React, the renderer,
  or storage.
- `packages/renderer` owns the render frame. Never call `mermaid.render` anywhere else,
  and never propose moving it to a Web Worker.
- Validate every render-frame message with Zod on both sides. Only structured-cloneable
  values cross: no functions, DOM nodes or class instances.
- Sanitize SVG before it enters the application document.
- `packages/storage` exposes ports. The IndexedDB/OPFS adapter is the only module that
  imports a browser storage API. Schema changes ship a numbered migration with a test.
- No package imports from `apps/web`. Nothing imports from `mermaid-upstream/`.
- Validate all external input at the boundary: files, pasted content, URL-encoded
  diagrams, stored records.

Apply to files under `apps/web/` and `packages/ui/`.

  match the interface is a bug.
- Never let a parse error clear the preview.
- Use virtualization for large collections; the diagram library can grow without bound.
- Verify light and dark themes, desktop and mobile, and keyboard-only navigation before
  completion. A clean build proves nothing about how it looks — open it.

# Diagram Catalog

The citable record of what Mermaid syntax exists and how far this project supports it.

**Source**: `mermaid-upstream/packages/mermaid/src/docs/syntax/`, at upstream commit
`9ac9635` (2026-08-14), Mermaid **v11.16.1**.

Every row below is derived from a file in that directory. Nothing here is written from
memory. Per-type detail lives in `docs/knowledge/diagrams/<file>.md` and cites upstream
by file and line.

## Status Legend

A type is **supported** only when all five hold: renders, highlights, completes,
diagnoses, exports. Anything less is `partial`, with the gap named. See the
`add-diagram-type` skill.

- `—` not started
- `partial` some criteria met; gap named in the per-type page
- `supported` all five criteria met, with tests

## The 33 Types

| # | Type | Upstream file | Header keyword | Min version | Status |

## Notes On The List

- The official documentation site publishes **31** entries. `usecase` and `railroad`
  exist upstream but are not yet on the site. `usecase.md` was merged 2026-08-14 and its
  version gate is still the literal placeholder `<MERMAID_RELEASE_VERSION>`, so its

  test fixtures.

- Header keywords above were extracted from the first example in each upstream page.

`mermaid-upstream/packages/mermaid/src/diagrams/<type>/parser/`, which requires widening
the sparse checkout.

- This file changes in the same commit as the code whose support status it describes.
- Re-run `bun run sync:upstream` before trusting the version column after an upstream bump.
- The pinned `mermaid` npm version and this file's source commit must describe the same

#!/usr/bin/env bash
# Vendors the Mermaid upstream documentation as a read-only syntax reference.
#
# This is NOT a runtime dependency. The runtime dependency is the pinned `mermaid`
# npm package. This checkout exists so humans and agents can cite syntax instead of
# recalling it. See AGENTS.md, "Syntax Source Of Truth".
set -euo pipefail

REPO="https://github.com/mermaid-js/mermaid.git"
DIR="mermaid-upstream"
SPARSE="packages/mermaid/src/docs"

cd "$(dirname "$0")/.."

if [ -d "$DIR/.git" ]; then
  echo "Updating $DIR..."
  git -C "$DIR" fetch --depth 1 origin HEAD
  git -C "$DIR" reset --hard FETCH_HEAD
else
  echo "Cloning $DIR (sparse, docs only)..."
  rm -rf "$DIR"
  git clone --depth 1 --filter=blob:none --sparse "$REPO" "$DIR"
  git -C "$DIR" sparse-checkout set "$SPARSE"
fi

COMMIT=$(git -C "$DIR" rev-parse --short HEAD)
DATE=$(git -C "$DIR" log -1 --format=%ad --date=short)
COUNT=$(find "$DIR/$SPARSE/syntax" -maxdepth 1 -name '*.md' | wc -l | tr -d ' ')

echo
echo "Upstream at $COMMIT ($DATE), $COUNT syntax pages."
echo "Verify docs/knowledge/diagram-catalog.md still cites this commit."
echo "Verify the pinned 'mermaid' npm version matches this release."

# Testing Strategy

Runner: `bun test` for unit and integration. Playwright for end-to-end and visual regression.

## Test Pyramid

- Unit tests for pure logic in `packages/core` — no browser required.
- Package tests for `editor`, `renderer`, `export` and `storage` against their contracts.
- Integration tests across boundaries: render frame, storage, import/export.
- End-to-end tests for critical user workflows.
- Visual regression across every supported diagram type, in light and dark themes.

## What Must Be Tested

Syntax and rendering:

- A golden-file render per diagram type, from its canonical catalog example.
- Every catalog type has a registered editor dialect. Adding a catalog entry without a
  dialect fails the build.
- Diagram-type detection is unambiguous: no two header patterns collide.
- Version-gated features are marked rather than silently offered.
- Highlighting and context-aware completion per dialect.

Render pipeline:

- Cancellation: a stale job never reaches the viewport.
- A parse error leaves the last good render on screen.
- Sanitization: diagram text attempting script injection through a label, a link and a
  `click` directive.
- Render-frame message validation rejects malformed payloads on both sides.
- Coarse mode engages above the node-count threshold and recovers after interaction.

Storage:

- Migrations: open a fixture database at the previous version, assert the resulting shape.
- Quota exhaustion surfaces a recoverable error with content still in the editor.
- Round-trip: workspace export then import produces identical documents.

Boundaries and product:

- Validation of files, pasted content, URL-encoded diagrams and stored records.
- Phase 1 makes zero outbound network requests.
- Export output for SVG, PNG and PDF, including types with known quirks.
- Table search, filters, sorting, pagination, column visibility and row actions.
- Dialog focus management, dismissal, scroll containment and submission states.
- Toast semantics and retry behavior for successful and failed actions.
- Responsive layout, long text, unicode labels, empty and large collections, dark mode.

## Test Data

- Use deterministic fixtures. `mermaid-upstream/.../syntax/examples.md` is a useful
  source of cross-type fixtures.
- Pin the Mermaid version. A minor bump can change layout output and invalidate every
  visual snapshot; that is a deliberate, reviewed change, never an incidental one.
- Avoid real secrets.
- Avoid relying on unstable external services in CI.

/**

  readonly id: string
  /** Human label, in product language. */

import { z } from 'zod'

/**
 * The document model. `body` is authoritative: everything visual derives from it, and
 * nothing derived is ever stored as a competing truth. See docs/product/domain-model.md.
 */

export const documentSchema = z.object({
  id: z.uuid(),
  name: z.string().max(200),
  /** Diagram type id, cached from detection. Derived data — `body` still wins. */
  typeId: z.string().nullable(),
  body: z.string(),
  folderId: z.uuid().nullable(),
  tags: z.array(z.string().max(50)).max(50),
  createdAt: z.number().int(),
  updatedAt: z.number().int(),
  deletedAt: z.number().int().nullable(),
  schemaVersion: z.number().int().nonnegative(),
})

export type DiagramDocument = z.infer<typeof documentSchema>

export const revisionSchema = z.object({
  documentId: z.uuid(),
  seq: z.number().int().nonnegative(),
  body: z.string(),
  label: z.string().max(200).nullable(),
  createdAt: z.number().int(),
})

export type Revision = z.infer<typeof revisionSchema>

export const folderSchema = z.object({
  id: z.uuid(),
  name: z.string().max(200),
  parentId: z.uuid().nullable(),
  position: z.number().int(),
})

export type Folder = z.infer<typeof folderSchema>

export const viewportSchema = z.object({
  x: z.number(),
  y: z.number(),
  zoom: z.number().positive(),
})

export type Viewport = z.infer<typeof viewportSchema>

/** A laid-out element, derived in the render frame where real geometry exists. */
export const diagramElementSchema = z.object({
  id: z.string(),
  kind: z.string(),
  box: z.object({
    x: z.number(),
    y: z.number(),
    width: z.number(),
    height: z.number(),
  }),
})

export type DiagramElement = z.infer<typeof diagramElementSchema>

export const CURRENT_SCHEMA_VERSION = 1

import DOMPurify from 'dompurify'

/**
 * Second sanitization layer.
 *
 * The first is mermaid running at `securityLevel: 'strict'` inside the render frame.
 * This one runs on the host, immediately before the SVG enters the application document.
 * Both are required: the frame is sandboxed, but the string it returns is still derived
 * from untrusted user text and is about to be parsed by the application's own document.
 */
export function sanitizeSvg(svg: string): string {
  return DOMPurify.sanitize(svg, {
    USE_PROFILES: { svg: true, svgFilters: true, mathMl: true },
    ADD_ATTR: ['transform', 'marker-end', 'marker-start', 'xmlns:xlink'],
    FORBID_TAGS: ['script', 'foreignObject'],
    FORBID_ATTR: ['onload', 'onerror', 'onclick', 'onmouseover'],
  })
}

**Lo que quedó funcionando de verdad:**

- `packages/core` — registro de los 33 tipos con las **regex de detección transcritas de los detectores de upstream**, no inventadas. 59 tests verifican que cada tipo se detecta por su keyword canónica y que no hay colisiones, incluidas las variantes (`graph`/`flowchart`/`flowchart-elk`, `classDiagram-v2`, `stateDiagram-v2`, `sankey-beta`, las 4 de railroad, `C4Container`) y el preámbulo (frontmatter + `%%{init}%%` + comentarios).
- `packages/renderer` — contrato de mensajes con Zod en ambos lados y sanitización DOMPurify.
- `apps/web` — frame de render aislado (`sandbox="allow-scripts"` sin `allow-same-origin`), host con cancelación y timeout, CodeMirror, canvas con pan/zoom por transform, y el último render bueno atenuado en vez de borrado cuando hay error.

**Tres correcciones sobre la marcha**, todas por verificar en vez de asumir:

1. `bun test` recogía los ~300 specs de `mermaid-upstream` → script acotado a `./packages ./apps`.
2. `tsc --build` emitía JS a `dist/`, así que los tests corrían dos veces (118 en vez de 59) → `emitDeclarationOnly`.
3. Versiones que no existían (`idb@^8.0.5`, `@types/react-dom@^19.2.5`) → ajustadas a las reales.

**Hallazgos que cambian el conteo de "33":**

- **Railroad son 4 notaciones** con detector propio cada una: `railroad-beta`, `-abnf-`, `-ebnf-`, `-peg-`. Una sola página de docs.
- **ZenUML no tiene detector** en el paquete `mermaid`: se distribuye como `@mermaid-js/mermaid-zenuml` y hay que registrarlo con `registerExternalDiagrams`. Marcado `external: true` en el registro.
- **`info` existe y no está documentado** — tiene detector y renderiza. Lo incluí para que la detección sea exhaustiva.
- Cuenta real: **32 tipos documentados** (`examples.md` no es un tipo) **+ `info` = 33**. Coincidencia con tu lista, por casualidad: el sitio publica 31 y le faltan `usecase` y `railroad`.

5	# Flowcharts - Basic Syntax
6	
7	Flowcharts are composed of **nodes** (geometric shapes) and **edges** (arrows or lines). The Mermaid code defines how nodes and edges are made and accommodates different arrow types, multi-directional arrows, and any linking to and from subgraphs.
8	
9	```warning
10	If you are using the word "end" in a Flowchart node, capitalize the entire word or any of the letters (e.g., "End" or "END"), or apply this [workaround](https://github.com/mermaid-js/mermaid/issues/1444#issuecomment-639528897). Typing "end" in all lowercase letters will break the Flowchart.
11	```
12	
13	```warning
14	If you are using the letter "o" or "x" as the first letter in a connecting Flowchart node, add a space before the letter or capitalize the letter (e.g., "dev--- ops", "dev---Ops").
15	
16	Typing "A---oB" will create a [circle edge](#circle-edge-example).
17	
18	Typing "A---xB" will create a [cross edge](#cross-edge-example).
19	```
20	
21	### A node (default)
22	
23	```mermaid-example
24	---
25	title: Node
26	---
27	flowchart LR
28	    id
29	```
30	
31	```note
32	The id is what is displayed in the box.
33	```
34	
35	```tip
36	Instead of `flowchart` one can also use `graph`.
37	```
38	
39	### A node with text
40	
41	It is also possible to set text in the box that differs from the id. If this is done several times, it is the last text
42	found for the node that will be used. Also if you define edges for the node later on, you can omit text definitions. The
43	one previously defined will be used when rendering the box.
44	
45	```mermaid-example
46	---
47	title: Node with text
48	---
49	flowchart LR
50	    id1[This is the text in the box]
51	```
52	
53	#### Unicode text
54	
55	Use `"` to enclose the unicode text.
56	
57	```mermaid-example
58	flowchart LR
59	    id["This ❤ Unicode"]
60	```
61	
62	#### Markdown formatting
63	
64	Use double quotes and backticks "\` text \`" to enclose the markdown text.
65	
66	```mermaid-example
67	---
68	config:
69	  htmlLabels: false
70	---
71	flowchart LR
72	    markdown["`This **is** _Markdown_`"]
73	    newLines["`Line1
74	    Line 2
75	    Line 3`"]
76	    markdown --> newLines
77	```

79	### Direction
80	
81	This statement declares the direction of the Flowchart.
82	
83	This declares the flowchart is oriented from top to bottom (`TD` or `TB`).

88	```
89	
90	This declares the flowchart is oriented from left to right (`LR`).
91	
92	```mermaid-example

94	    Start --> Stop
95	```

97	Possible FlowChart orientations are:
98	
99	- TB - Top to bottom
100	- TD - Top-down/ same as top to bottom
101	- BT - Bottom to top
102	- RL - Right to left
103	- LR - Left to right

200	## Expanded Node Shapes in Mermaid Flowcharts (v11.3.0+)
201	
202	Mermaid introduces 30 new shapes to enhance the flexibility and precision of flowchart creation. These new shapes provide more options to represent processes, decisions, events, data storage visually, and other elements within your flowcharts, improving clarity and semantic meaning.
203	
204	New Syntax for Shape Definition
205	
206	Mermaid now supports a general syntax for defining shape types to accommodate the growing number of shapes. This syntax allows you to assign specific shapes to nodes using a clear and flexible format:
207	
208	```
209	A@{ shape: rect }
210	```
211	
212	This syntax creates a node A as a rectangle. It renders in the same way as `A["A"]`, or `A`.

555	## Special shapes in Mermaid Flowcharts (v11.3.0+)
556	
557	Mermaid also introduces 2 special shapes to enhance your flowcharts: **icon** and **image**. These shapes allow you to include icons and images directly within your flowcharts, providing more visual context and clarity.
558	
559	### Icon Shape
560	
561	You can use the `icon` shape to include an icon in your flowchart. To use icons, you need to register the icon pack first. Follow the instructions to [add custom icons](../config/icons.md). The syntax for defining an icon shape is as follows:
562	
563	```mermaid-example
564	flowchart TD
565	    A@{ icon: "fa:user", form: "square", label: "User Icon", pos: "t", h: 60 }
566	```
567	
568	#### Parameters
569	
570	- **icon**: The name of the icon from the registered icon pack.
571	- **form**: Specifies the background shape of the icon. If not defined there will be no background to icon. Options include:
572	  - `square`
573	  - `circle`
574	  - `rounded`
575	- **label**: The text label associated with the icon. This can be any string. If not defined, no label will be displayed.
576	- **pos**: The position of the label. If not defined label will default to bottom of icon. Possible values are:
577	  - `t`
578	  - `b`
579	- **h**: The height of the icon. If not defined this will default to 48 which is minimum.
580	
581	### Image Shape
582	
583	You can use the `image` shape to include an image in your flowchart. The syntax for defining an image shape is as follows:
584	
585	```
586	flowchart TD
587	    A@{ img: "https://example.com/image.png", label: "Image Label", pos: "t", w: 60, h: 60, constraint: "off" }
588	```
589	
590	#### Parameters
591	
592	- **img**: The URL of the image to be displayed.
593	- **label**: The text label associated with the image. This can be any string. If not defined, no label will be displayed.
594	- **pos**: The position of the label. If not defined, the label will default to the bottom of the image. Possible values are:
595	  - `t`
596	  - `b`
597	- **w**: The width of the image. If not defined, this will default to the natural width of the image.
598	- **h**: The height of the image. If not defined, this will default to the natural height of the image.
599	- **constraint**: Determines if the image should constrain the node size. This setting also ensures the image maintains its original aspect ratio, adjusting the width (`w`) accordingly to the height (`h`). If not defined, this will default to `off` Possible values are:
600	  - `on`
601	  - `off`
602	
603	If you want to resize an image, but keep the same aspect ratio, set `h`, and set `constraint: on` to constrain the aspect ratio. E.g.
604	
605	```mermaid
606	flowchart TD
607	  %% My image with a constrained aspect ratio
608	  A@{ img: "https://mermaid.js.org/favicon.svg", label: "My example image label", pos: "t", h: 60, constraint: "on" }
609	```

730	### Attaching an ID to Edges
731	
732	Mermaid now supports assigning IDs to edges, similar to how IDs and metadata can be attached to nodes. This feature lays the groundwork for more advanced styling, classes, and animation capabilities on edges.
733	
734	**Syntax:**
735	
736	To give an edge an ID, prepend the edge syntax with the ID followed by an `@` character. For example:
737	
738	```mermaid
739	flowchart LR
740	  A e1@--> B
741	```
742	
743	In this example, `e1` is the ID of the edge connecting `A` to `B`. You can then use this ID in later definitions or style statements, just like with nodes.
744	
745	### Turning an Animation On
746	
747	Once you have assigned an ID to an edge, you can turn on animations for that edge by defining the edge’s properties:
748	
749	```mermaid
750	flowchart LR
751	  A e1@==> B
752	  e1@{ animate: true }
753	```
754	
755	This tells Mermaid that the edge `e1` should be animated.
756	
757	### Selecting Type of Animation
758	
759	In the initial version, two animation speeds are supported: `fast` and `slow`. Selecting a specific animation type is a shorthand for enabling animation and setting the animation speed in one go.
760	
761	**Examples:**
762	
763	```mermaid
764	flowchart LR
765	  A e1@--> B
766	  e1@{ animation: fast }
767	```
768	
769	This is equivalent to `{ animate: true, animation: fast }`.
770	
771	### Using classDef Statements for Animations
772	
773	You can also animate edges by assigning a class to them and then defining animation properties in a `classDef` statement. For example:
774	
775	```mermaid
776	flowchart LR
777	  A e1@--> B
778	  classDef animate stroke-dasharray: 9,5,stroke-dashoffset: 900,animation: dash 25s linear infinite;
779	  class e1 animate
780	```
781	
782	In this snippet:
783	
784	- `e1@-->` creates an edge with ID `e1`.
785	- `classDef animate` defines a class named `animate` with styling and animation properties.
786	- `class e1 animate` applies the `animate` class to the edge `e1`.
787	
788	**Note on Escaping Commas:**
789	When setting the `stroke-dasharray` property, remember to escape commas as `\,` since commas are used as delimiters in Mermaid’s style definitions.
790

823	### Minimum length of a link
824	
825	Each node in the flowchart is ultimately assigned to a rank in the rendered
826	graph, i.e. to a vertical or horizontal level (depending on the flowchart
827	orientation), based on the nodes to which it is linked. By default, links
828	can span any number of ranks, but you can ask for any link to be longer
829	than the others by adding extra dashes in the link definition.
830	
831	In the following example, two extra dashes are added in the link from node _B_
832	to node _E_, so that it spans two more ranks than regular links:
833	
834	```mermaid-example
835	flowchart TD
836	    A[Start] --> B{Is it?}
837	    B -->|Yes| C[OK]
838	    C --> D[Rethink]
839	    D --> B
840	    B ---->|No| E[End]
841	```
842	
843	> **Note** Links may still be made longer than the requested number of ranks
844	> by the rendering engine to accommodate other requests.
845	
846	When the link label is written in the middle of the link, the extra dashes must
847	be added on the right side of the link. The following example is equivalent to
848	the previous one:
849	
850	```mermaid-example
851	flowchart TD
852	    A[Start] --> B{Is it?}
853	    B -- Yes --> C[OK]
854	    C --> D[Rethink]
855	    D --> B
856	    B -- No ----> E[End]
857	```
858	
859	For dotted or thick links, the characters to add are equals signs or dots,
860	as summed up in the following table:
861	
862	| Length            |   1    |    2    |    3     |
863	| ----------------- | :----: | :-----: | :------: |
864	| Normal            | `---`  | `----`  | `-----`  |
865	| Normal with arrow | `-->`  | `--->`  | `---->`  |
866	| Thick             | `===`  | `====`  | `=====`  |
867	| Thick with arrow  | `==>`  | `===>`  | `====>`  |
868	| Dotted            | `-.-`  | `-..-`  | `-...-`  |
869	| Dotted with arrow | `-.->` | `-..->` | `-...->` |
870

896	end
897	```
898	
899	An example below:
900	
901	```mermaid-example
902	flowchart TB
903	    c1-->a2
904	    subgraph one
905	    a1-->a2
906	    end
907	    subgraph two
908	    b1-->b2
909	    end
910	    subgraph three
911	    c1-->c2
912	    end
913	```
914	
915	You can also set an explicit id for the subgraph.
916	
917	```mermaid-example

920	    subgraph ide1 [one]
921	    a1-->a2
922	    end
923	```
924	
925	### flowcharts
926	
927	With the graphtype flowchart it is also possible to set edges to and from subgraphs as in the flowchart below.
928	
929	```mermaid-example
930	flowchart TB
931	    c1-->a2
932	    subgraph one
933	    a1-->a2
934	    end
935	    subgraph two
936	    b1-->b2
937	    end
938	    subgraph three
939	    c1-->c2
940	    end
941	    one --> two
942	    three --> two
943	    two --> c2
944	```
945	
946	### Direction in subgraphs
947	
948	With the graphtype flowcharts you can use the direction statement to set the direction which the subgraph will render like in this example.
949	
950	```mermaid-example
951	flowchart LR
952	  subgraph TOP
953	    direction TB
954	    subgraph B1
955	        direction RL
956	        i1 -->f1
957	    end
958	    subgraph B2
959	        direction BT
960	        i2 -->f2
961	    end
962	  end
963	  A --> TOP --> B
964	  B1 --> B2
965	```
966	
967	#### Limitation
968	
969	If any of a subgraph's nodes are linked to the outside, subgraph direction will be ignored. Instead the subgraph will inherit the direction of the parent graph:
970	
971	```mermaid-example
972	flowchart LR
973	    subgraph subgraph1
974	        direction TB
975	        top1[top] --> bottom1[bottom]
976	    end
977	    subgraph subgraph2
978	        direction TB
979	        top2[top] --> bottom2[bottom]
980	    end
981	    %% ^ These subgraphs are identical, except for the links to them:
982	
983	    %% Link *to* subgraph1: subgraph1 direction is maintained
984	    outside --> subgraph1
985	    %% Link *within* subgraph2:
986	    %% subgraph2 inherits the direction of the top-level graph (LR)
987	    outside ---> top2
988	```
989	
990	### Collapsible subgraphs (v<MERMAID_RELEASE_VERSION>+)
991	
992	A subgraph can be collapsed into a single compact node by attaching the metadata
993	`@{ view: collapsed }` to its id. This is useful for hiding the internals of a
994	group while still showing how it connects to the rest of the diagram.
995	
996	```mermaid-example
997	flowchart TD
998	    Start --> one
999	    subgraph one [My Group]
1000	        A --> B
1001	        B --> C
1002	    end
1003	    one --> End
1004	    one@{ view: collapsed }
1005	```
1006	
1007	The metadata is attached with the existing `id@{ ... }` statement syntax, where
1008	`id` is the subgraph id (use `subgraph id [Title]` to give a subgraph an explicit
1009	id). When a subgraph is collapsed:
1010	
1011	- Its internal nodes are hidden and it is drawn as a single node carrying the
1012	  subgraph's title.
1013	- Edges that cross the subgraph boundary are **redirected to the collapsed node**.
1014	- Edges that are entirely internal to the collapsed subgraph are dropped (they
1015	  would otherwise become self-loops on the collapsed node).
1016	- For nested subgraphs, a collapse resolves to the **outermost** collapsed
1017	  ancestor, so an edge pointing at a deeply nested node lands on the outermost
1018	  collapsed group.
1019	
1020	`view: expanded` is the default and renders the subgraph normally, so omitting the
1021	metadata (or setting `view: expanded`) keeps the existing behavior.

1023	## Markdown Strings
1024	
1025	The "Markdown Strings" feature enhances flowcharts and mind maps by offering a more versatile string type, which supports text formatting options such as bold and italics, and automatically wraps text within labels.
1026	
1027	```mermaid-example
1028	---
1029	config:
1030	  htmlLabels: false
1031	---
1032	flowchart LR
1033	subgraph "One"
1034	  a("`The **cat**
1035	  in the hat`") -- "edge label" --> b{{"`The **dog** in the hog`"}}
1036	end
1037	subgraph "`**Two**`"
1038	  c("`The **cat**
1039	  in the hat`") -- "`Bold **edge label**`" --> d("The dog in the hog")
1040	end
1041	```
1042	
1043	Formatting:
1044	
1045	- For bold text, use double asterisks (`**`) before and after the text.
1046	- For italics, use single asterisks (`*`) before and after the text.
1047	- With traditional strings, you needed to add `<br>` tags for text to wrap in nodes. However, markdown strings automatically wrap text when it becomes too long and allows you to start a new line by simply using a newline character instead of a `<br>` tag.
1048	
1049	This feature is applicable to node labels, edge labels, and subgraph labels.
1050	
1051	The auto wrapping can be disabled by using
1052	
1053	```
1054	---
1055	config:
1056	  markdownAutoWrap: false
1057	---
1058	graph LR
1059	```
1060	
1061	## Interaction
1062	
1063	It is possible to bind a click event to a node, the click can lead to either a javascript callback or to a link which will be opened in a new browser tab.
1064	
1065	```note
1066	This functionality is disabled when using `securityLevel='strict'` and enabled when using `securityLevel='loose'`.
1067	```
1068	
1069	```
1070	click nodeId callback
1071	click nodeId call callback()
1072	```
1073	
1074	- nodeId is the id of the node
1075	- callback is the name of a javascript function defined on the page displaying the graph, the function will be called with the nodeId as parameter.
1076	
1077	Examples of tooltip usage below:
1078	
1079	```html
1080	<script>
1081	  window.callback = function () {
1082	    alert('A callback was triggered');
1083	  };
1084	</script>
1085	```
1086	
1087	The tooltip text is surrounded in double quotes. The styles of the tooltip are set by the class `.mermaidTooltip`.
1088	
1089	```mermaid-example
1090	flowchart LR
1091	    A-->B
1092	    B-->C
1093	    C-->D
1094	    click A callback "Tooltip for a callback"
1095	    click B "https://www.github.com" "This is a tooltip for a link"
1096	    click C call callback() "Tooltip for a callback"
1097	    click D href "https://www.github.com" "This is a tooltip for a link"
1098	```
1099	
1100	> **Success** The tooltip functionality and the ability to link to urls are available from version 0.5.2.
1101	
1102	?> Due to limitations with how Docsify handles JavaScript callback functions, an alternate working demo for the above code can be viewed at [this jsfiddle](https://jsfiddle.net/yk4h7qou/2/).
1103	
1104	Links are opened in the same browser tab/window by default. It is possible to change this by adding a link target to the click definition (`_self`, `_blank`, `_parent` and `_top` are supported):
1105	
1106	```mermaid-example
1107	flowchart LR
1108	    A-->B
1109	    B-->C
1110	    C-->D
1111	    D-->E
1112	    click A "https://www.github.com" _blank
1113	    click B "https://www.github.com" "Open this in a new tab" _blank
1114	    click C href "https://www.github.com" _blank
1115	    click D href "https://www.github.com" "Open this in a new tab" _blank
1116	```
1117	
1118	Beginner's tip—a full example using interactive links in a html context:
1119	
1120	```html
1121	<body>
1122	  <pre class="mermaid">
1123	    flowchart LR
1124	        A-->B
1125	        B-->C
1126	        C-->D
1127	        click A callback "Tooltip"
1128	        click B "https://www.github.com" "This is a link"
1129	        click C call callback() "Tooltip"
1130	        click D href "https://www.github.com" "This is a link"
1131	  </pre>
1132	
1133	  <script>
1134	    window.callback = function () {
1135	      alert('A callback was triggered');
1136	    };
1137	    const config = {
1138	      startOnLoad: true,
1139	      htmlLabels: true,
1140	      flowchart: { useMaxWidth: true, curve: 'cardinal' },
1141	      securityLevel: 'loose',
1142	    };
1143	    mermaid.initialize(config);
1144	  </script>
1145	</body>
1146	```

1148	### Comments
1149	
1150	Comments can be entered within a flow diagram, which will be ignored by the parser. Comments need to be on their own line, and must be prefaced with `%%` (double percent signs). Any text after the start of the comment to the next newline will be treated as a comment, including any flow syntax
1151	
1152	```mermaid
1153	flowchart LR
1154	%% this is a comment A -- text --> B{node}
1155	   A -- text --> B -- text2 --> C
1156	```
1157	
1158	## Styling and classes
1159	
1160	### Styling links
1161	
1162	It is possible to style links. For instance, you might want to style a link that is going backwards in the flow. As links
1163	have no ids in the same way as nodes, some other way of deciding what style the links should be attached to is required.
1164	Instead of ids, the order number of when the link was defined in the graph is used, or use default to apply to all links.
1165	In the example below the style defined in the linkStyle statement will belong to the fourth link in the graph:
1166	
1167	```
1168	linkStyle 3 stroke:#ff3,stroke-width:4px,color:red;
1169	```
1170	
1171	It is also possible to add style to multiple links in a single statement, by separating link numbers with commas:
1172	
1173	```
1174	linkStyle 1,2,7 color:blue;
1175	```
1176	
1177	### Styling line curves
1178	
1179	It is possible to style the type of curve used for lines between items, if the default method does not meet your needs.
1180	Available curve styles include `basis`, `bumpX`, `bumpY`, `cardinal`, `catmullRom`, `linear`, `monotoneX`, `monotoneY`,
1181	`natural`, `step`, `stepAfter`, and `stepBefore`.
1182	
1183	For a full list of available curves, including an explanation of custom curves, refer to
1184	the [Shapes](https://d3js.org/d3-shape/curve) documentation in the [d3-shape](https://github.com/d3/d3-shape/) project.
1185	
1186	Line styling can be achieved in two ways:
1187	
1188	1. Change the curve style of all the lines
1189	2. Change the curve style of a particular line
1190	
1191	#### Diagram level curve style
1192	
1193	In this example, a left-to-right graph uses the `stepBefore` curve style:
1194	
1195	```
1196	---
1197	config:
1198	  flowchart:
1199	    curve: stepBefore
1200	---
1201	graph LR
1202	```
1203	
1204	#### Edge level curve style using Edge IDs (v11.10.0+)
1205	
1206	You can assign IDs to [edges](#attaching-an-id-to-edges). After assigning an ID you can modify the line style by modifying the edge's `curve` property using the following syntax:
1207	
1208	```mermaid
1209	flowchart LR
1210	    A e1@==> B
1211	    A e2@--> C
1212	    e1@{ curve: linear }
1213	    e2@{ curve: natural }
1214	```
1215	
1216	```info
1217	Any edge curve style modified at the edge level overrides the diagram level style.
1218	```
1219	
1220	```info
1221	If the same edge is modified multiple times the last modification will be rendered.
1222	```
1223	
1224	### Styling a node
1225	
1226	It is possible to apply specific styles such as a thicker border or a different background color to a node.
1227	
1228	```mermaid-example
1229	flowchart LR
1230	    id1(Start)-->id2(Stop)
1231	    style id1 fill:#f9f,stroke:#333,stroke-width:4px
1232	    style id2 fill:#bbf,stroke:#f66,stroke-width:2px,color:#fff,stroke-dasharray: 5 5
1233	```
1234	
1235	#### Classes
1236	
1237	More convenient than defining the style every time is to define a class of styles and attach this class to the nodes that
1238	should have a different look.
1239	
1240	A class definition looks like the example below:
1241	
1242	```
1243	    classDef className fill:#f9f,stroke:#333,stroke-width:4px;
1244	```
1245	
1246	Also, it is possible to define style to multiple classes in one statement:
1247	
1248	```
1249	    classDef firstClassName,secondClassName font-size:12pt;
1250	```
1251	
1252	Attachment of a class to a node is done as per below:
1253	
1254	```
1255	    class nodeId1 className;
1256	```
1257	
1258	It is also possible to attach a class to a list of nodes in one statement:
1259	
1260	```
1261	    class nodeId1,nodeId2 className;
1262	```
1263	
1264	A shorter form of adding a class is to attach the classname to the node using the `:::`operator as per below:
1265	
1266	```mermaid-example
1267	flowchart LR
1268	    A:::someclass --> B
1269	    classDef someclass fill:#f96
1270	```
1271	
1272	This form can be used when declaring multiple links between nodes:
1273	
1274	```mermaid-example
1275	flowchart LR
1276	    A:::foo & B:::bar --> C:::foobar
1277	    classDef foo stroke:#f00
1278	    classDef bar stroke:#0f0
1279	    classDef foobar stroke:#00f
1280	```
1281	
1282	### CSS classes
1283	
1284	> **Note:** Applying styles to Mermaid nodes via external CSS (e.g., `.cssClass > rect { fill: ... }`) does **not** work reliably. Mermaid's internal styles are injected with `!important` and scoped to the SVG element ID, giving them higher specificity than external CSS rules. External CSS will be silently overridden.
1285	>
1286	> The recommended approach is to use the `classDef` syntax shown in the [Classes](#classes) section above, which works correctly and is the intended styling mechanism.
1287	>
1288	> If external CSS is strictly required, every property must use `!important` to override Mermaid's styles — but this is not recommended.
1289	
1290	**Working approach — use `classDef` instead:**
1291	
1292	```mermaid-example
1293	flowchart LR
1294	    A:::myStyle --> B
1295	    classDef myStyle fill:#ff0000,stroke:#ffff00,stroke-width:4px
1296	```
1297	
1298	### Default class
1299	
1300	If a class is named default it will be assigned to all classes without specific class definitions.
1301	
1302	```
1303	    classDef default fill:#f9f,stroke:#333,stroke-width:4px;
1304	```
1305	
1306	## Basic support for fontawesome
1307	
1308	It is possible to add icons from fontawesome.
1309	
1310	The icons are accessed via the syntax fa:#icon class name#.
1311	
1312	```mermaid-example
1313	flowchart TD
1314	    B["fa:fa-twitter for peace"]
1315	    B-->C[fa:fa-ban forbidden]
1316	    B-->D(fa:fa-spinner)
1317	    B-->E(A fa:fa-camera-retro perhaps?)
1318	```
1319	
1320	There are two ways to display these FontAwesome icons:
1321	
1322	### Register FontAwesome icon packs (v11.7.0+)
1323	
1324	You can register your own FontAwesome icon pack following the ["Registering icon packs" instructions](../config/icons.md).
1325	
1326	Supported prefixes: `fa`, `fab`, `fas`, `far`, `fal`, `fad`.
1327	
1328	```note
1329	Note that it will fall back to FontAwesome CSS if FontAwesome packs are not registered.
1330	```
1331	
1332	### Register FontAwesome CSS
1333	
1334	Mermaid supports Font Awesome if the CSS is included on the website.
1335	Mermaid does not have any restriction on the version of Font Awesome that can be used.
1336	
1337	Please refer the [Official Font Awesome Documentation](https://fontawesome.com/start) on how to include it in your website.
1338	
1339	Adding this snippet in the `<head>` would add support for Font Awesome v6.5.1
1340	
1341	```html
1342	<link
1343	  href="https://cdnjs.cloudflare.com/ajax/libs/font-awesome/6.5.1/css/all.min.css"
1344	  rel="stylesheet"
1345	/>
1346	```
1347	
1348	### Custom icons
1349	
1350	It is possible to use custom icons served from Font Awesome as long as the website imports the corresponding kit.
1351	
1352	Note that this is currently a paid feature from Font Awesome.
1353	
1354	For custom icons, you need to use the `fak` prefix.
1355	
1356	**Example**
1357	
1358	```
1359	flowchart TD
1360	    B[fa:fa-twitter] %% standard icon
1361	    B-->E(fak:fa-custom-icon-name) %% custom icon
1362	```
1363	
1364	And trying to render it
1365	
1366	```mermaid-example
1367	flowchart TD
1368	    B["fa:fa-twitter for peace"]
1369	    B-->C["fab:fa-truck-bold a custom icon"]
1370	```
1371	
1372	## Graph declarations with spaces between vertices and link and without semicolon
1373	
1374	- In graph declarations, the statements also can now end without a semicolon. After release 0.2.16, ending a graph statement with semicolon is just optional. So the below graph declaration is also valid along with the old declarations of the graph.
1375	
1376	- A single space is allowed between vertices and the link. However there should not be any space between a vertex and its text and a link and its text. The old syntax of graph declaration will also work and hence this new feature is optional and is introduced to improve readability.
1377	
1378	Below is the new declaration of the graph edges which is also valid along with the old declaration of the graph edges.
1379	
1380	```mermaid-example
1381	flowchart LR
1382	    A[Hard edge] -->|Link text| B(Round edge)
1383	    B --> C{Decision}
1384	    C -->|One| D[Result one]
1385	    C -->|Two| E[Result two]
1386	```
1387	
1388	## Configuration
1389	
1390	### Renderer
1391	
1392	The layout of the diagram is done with the renderer. The default renderer is dagre.
1393	
1394	Starting with Mermaid version 9.4, you can use an alternate renderer named elk. The elk renderer is better for larger and/or more complex diagrams.
1395	
1396	The _elk_ renderer is an experimental feature.
1397	You can change the renderer to elk by adding this directive:
1398	
1399	```
1400	config:
1401	  flowchart:
1402	    defaultRenderer: "elk"
1403	```
1404	
1405	```note
1406	Note that the site needs to use mermaid version 9.4+ for this to work and have this featured enabled in the lazy-loading configuration.
1407	```
1408	
1409	### Width
1410	
1411	It is possible to adjust the width of the rendered flowchart.
1412	
1413	This is done by defining **mermaid.flowchartConfig** or by the CLI to use a JSON file with the configuration. How to use the CLI is described in the mermaidCLI page.
1414	mermaid.flowchartConfig can be set to a JSON string with config parameters or the corresponding object.
1415	
1416	```javascript
1417	mermaid.flowchartConfig = {
1418	    width: 100%
1419	}
1420	```
1421	
1422	<!--- cspell:ignore lagom --->

1 # Sequence diagrams 2 3 > A Sequence diagram is an interaction diagram that shows how processes operate with one another and in what order. 4 5 Mermaid can render sequence diagrams. 6 7 ```mermaid-example 8 sequenceDiagram 9 Alice->>John: Hello John, how are you? 10 John-->>Alice: Great! 11 Alice-)John: See you later! 12 ``` 13 14 ```note 15 A note on nodes, the word "end" could potentially break the diagram, due to the way that the mermaid language is scripted. 16 17 If unavoidable, one must use parentheses(), quotation marks "", or brackets {},[], to enclose the word "end". i.e : (end), [end], {end}. 18 ``` 19 20 ## Syntax 21 22 ### Participants 23 24 The participants can be defined implicitly as in the first example on this page. The participants or actors are 25 rendered in order of appearance in the diagram source text. Sometimes you might want to show the participants in a 26 different order than how they appear in the first message. It is possible to specify the actor's order of 27 appearance by doing the following: 28 29 ```mermaid-example 30 sequenceDiagram 31 participant Alice 32 participant Bob 33 Bob->>Alice: Hi Alice 34 Alice->>Bob: Hi Bob 35 ``` 36 37 ### Actors 38 39 If you specifically want to use the actor symbol instead of a rectangle with text you can do so by using actor statements as per below. 40 41 ```mermaid-example 42 sequenceDiagram 43 actor Alice 44 actor Bob 45 Alice->>Bob: Hi Bob 46 Bob->>Alice: Hi Alice 47 ``` 48 49 ### Boundary 50 51 If you want to use the boundary symbol for a participant, use the JSON configuration syntax as shown below. 52 53 ```mermaid-example 54 sequenceDiagram 55 participant Alice@{ "type" : "boundary" } 56 participant Bob 57 Alice->>Bob: Request from boundary 58 Bob->>Alice: Response to boundary 59 ``` 60 61 ### Control 62 63 If you want to use the control symbol for a participant, use the JSON configuration syntax as shown below. 64 65 ```mermaid-example 66 sequenceDiagram 67 participant Alice@{ "type" : "control" } 68 participant Bob 69 Alice->>Bob: Control request 70 Bob->>Alice: Control response 71 ``` 72 73 ### Entity 74 75 If you want to use the entity symbol for a participant, use the JSON configuration syntax as shown below. 76 77 ```mermaid-example 78 sequenceDiagram 79 participant Alice@{ "type" : "entity" } 80 participant Bob 81 Alice->>Bob: Entity request 82 Bob->>Alice: Entity response 83 ``` 84 85 ### Database 86 87 If you want to use the database symbol for a participant, use the JSON configuration syntax as shown below. 88 89 ```mermaid-example 90 sequenceDiagram 91 participant Alice@{ "type" : "database" } 92 participant Bob 93 Alice->>Bob: DB query 94 Bob->>Alice: DB result 95 ``` 96 97 ### Collections 98 99 If you want to use the collections symbol for a participant, use the JSON configuration syntax as shown below. 100 101 ```mermaid-example 102 sequenceDiagram 103 participant Alice@{ "type" : "collections" } 104 participant Bob 105 Alice->>Bob: Collections request 106 Bob->>Alice: Collections response 107 ``` 108 109 ### Queue 110 111 If you want to use the queue symbol for a participant, use the JSON configuration syntax as shown below. 112 113 ```mermaid-example 114 sequenceDiagram 115 participant Alice@{ "type" : "queue" } 116 participant Bob 117 Alice->>Bob: Queue message 118 Bob->>Alice: Queue response 119 ``` 120 121 ### Aliases 122 123 The actor can have a convenient identifier and a descriptive label. Aliases can be defined in two ways: using external syntax with the `as` keyword, or inline within the configuration object. 124 125 #### External Alias Syntax 126 127 You can define an alias using the `as` keyword after the participant declaration: 128 129 ```mermaid-example 130 sequenceDiagram 131 participant A as Alice 132 participant J as John 133 A->>J: Hello John, how are you? 134 J->>A: Great! 135 ``` 136 137 The external alias syntax also works with participant stereotype configurations, allowing you to combine type specification with aliases: 138 139 ```mermaid-example 140 sequenceDiagram 141 participant API@{ "type": "boundary" } as Public API 142 actor DB@{ "type": "database" } as User Database 143 participant Svc@{ "type": "control" } as Auth Service 144 API->>Svc: Authenticate 145 Svc->>DB: Query user 146 DB-->>Svc: User data 147 Svc-->>API: Token 148 ``` 149 150 #### Inline Alias Syntax 151 152 Alternatively, you can define an alias directly inside the configuration object using the `"alias"` field. This works with both `participant` and `actor` keywords: 153 154 ```mermaid-example 155 sequenceDiagram 156 participant API@{ "type": "boundary", "alias": "Public API" } 157 participant Auth@{ "type": "control", "alias": "Auth Service" } 158 participant DB@{ "type": "database", "alias": "User Database" } 159 API->>Auth: Login request 160 Auth->>DB: Query user 161 DB-->>Auth: User data 162 Auth-->>API: Access token 163 ``` 164 165 #### Alias Precedence 166 167 When both inline alias (in the configuration object) and external alias (using `as` keyword) are provided, the **external alias takes precedence**: 168 169 ```mermaid-example 170 sequenceDiagram 171 participant API@{ "type": "boundary", "alias": "Internal Name" } as External Name 172 participant DB@{ "type": "database", "alias": "Internal DB" } as External DB 173 API->>DB: Query 174 DB-->>API: Result 175 ``` 176 177 In the example above, "External Name" and "External DB" will be displayed, not "Internal Name" and "Internal DB". 178 179 ### Actor Creation and Destruction (v10.3.0+) 180 181 It is possible to create and destroy actors by messages. To do so, add a create or destroy directive before the message. 182 183 ``` 184 create participant B 185 A --> B: Hello 186 ``` 187 188 Create directives support actor/participant distinction and aliases. The sender or the recipient of a message can be destroyed but only the recipient can be created. 189 190 ```mermaid-example 191 sequenceDiagram 192 Alice->>Bob: Hello Bob, how are you ? 193 Bob->>Alice: Fine, thank you. And you? 194 create participant Carl 195 Alice->>Carl: Hi Carl! 196 create actor D as Donald 197 Carl->>D: Hi! 198 destroy Carl 199 Alice-xCarl: We are too many 200 destroy Bob 201 Bob->>Alice: I agree 202 ``` 203 204 #### Unfixable actor/participant creation/deletion error 205 206 If an error of the following type occurs when creating or deleting an actor/participant: 207 208 > The destroyed participant **participant-name** does not have an associated destroying message after its declaration. Please check the sequence diagram. 209 210 And fixing diagram code does not get rid of this error and rendering of all other diagrams results in the same error, then you need to update the mermaid version to (v10.7.0+). 211 212 ### Grouping / Box 213 214 The actor(s) can be grouped in vertical boxes. You can define a color (if not, it will be transparent) and/or a descriptive label using the following notation: 215 216 ```note 217 For colored boxes, the color value must be placed **before** the optional description. 218 ``` 219 220 ``` 221 box Aqua Group Description 222 ... actors ... 223 end 224 box Group without description 225 ... actors ... 226 end 227 box rgb(33,66,99) 228 ... actors ... 229 end 230 box rgba(33,66,99,0.5) 231 ... actors ... 232 end 233 box hsl(10, 40%, 90%) 234 ... actors ... 235 end 236 box hsla(10, 40%, 90%, 0.5) 237 ... actors ... 238 end 239 ``` 240 241 ```warning 242 **Hex colors** (e.g., `#ff0000`) are currently **not supported** as the `#` character is interpreted as comment syntax. 243 ``` 244 245 ```note 246 If your group name is a color you can force the color to be transparent: 247 ``` 248 249 ``` 250 box transparent Aqua 251 ... actors ... 252 end 253 ``` 254 255 ```mermaid-example 256 sequenceDiagram 257 box Purple Alice & John 258 participant A 259 participant J 260 end 261 box Another Group 262 participant B 263 participant C 264 end 265 A->>J: Hello John, how are you? 266 J->>A: Great! 267 A->>B: Hello Bob, how is Charley? 268 B->>C: Hello Charley, how are you? 269 ``` 270 271 ## Messages 272 273 Messages can be of two displayed either solid or with a dotted line. 274 275 ``` 276 [Actor][Arrow][Actor]:Message text 277 ``` 278 279 Lines can be solid or dotted, and can end with various types of arrowheads, crosses, or open arrows. 280 281 #### Supported Arrow Types 282 283 **Standard Arrow Types** 284 285 | Type | Description | 286 | -------- | ---------------------------------------------------- | 287 | `->` | Solid line without arrow | 288 | `-->` | Dotted line without arrow | 289 | `->>` | Solid line with arrowhead | 290 | `-->>` | Dotted line with arrowhead | 291 | `<<->>` | Solid line with bidirectional arrowheads (v11.0.0+) | 292 | `<<-->>` | Dotted line with bidirectional arrowheads (v11.0.0+) | 293 | `-x` | Solid line with a cross at the end | 294 | `--x` | Dotted line with a cross at the end | 295 | `-)` | Solid line with an open arrow at the end (async) | 296 | `--)` | Dotted line with a open arrow at the end (async) | 297 298 **Half-Arrows (v11.12.3+)** 299 300 The following half-arrow types are supported for more expressive sequence diagrams. Both solid and dotted variants are available by increasing the number of dashes (`-` → `--`). 301 302 --- 303 304 | Type | Description | 305 | ------- | ---------------------------------------------------- | 306 | `-\|\` | Solid line with top half arrowhead | 307 | `--\|\` | Dotted line with top half arrowhead | 308 | `-\|/` | Solid line with bottom half arrowhead | 309 | `--\|/` | Dotted line with bottom half arrowhead | 310 | `/\|-` | Solid line with reverse top half arrowhead | 311 | `/\|--` | Dotted line with reverse top half arrowhead | 312 | `\\-` | Solid line with reverse bottom half arrowhead | 313 | `\\--` | Dotted line with reverse bottom half arrowhead | 314 | `-\\` | Solid line with top stick half arrowhead | 315 | `--\\` | Dotted line with top stick half arrowhead | 316 | `-//` | Solid line with bottom stick half arrowhead | 317 | `--//` | Dotted line with bottom stick half arrowhead | 318 | `//-` | Solid line with reverse top stick half arrowhead | 319 | `//--` | Dotted line with reverse top stick half arrowhead | 320 | `\\-` | Solid line with reverse bottom stick half arrowhead | 321 | `\\--` | Dotted line with reverse bottom stick half arrowhead | 322 323 ## Central Connections (v11.12.3+) 324 325 Mermaid sequence diagrams support **central lifeline connections** using a `()`. 326 This is useful to represent messages or signals that connect to a central point, rather than from one actor directly to another. 327 328 To indicate a central connection, append `()` to the arrow syntax. 329 330 #### Basic Syntax 331 332 ```mermaid-example 333 sequenceDiagram 334 participant Alice 335 participant John 336 Alice->>()John: Hello John 337 Alice()->>John: How are you? 338 John()->>()Alice: Great! 339 ``` 340 341 ## Activations 342 343 It is possible to activate and deactivate an actor. (de)activation can be dedicated declarations: 344 345 ```mermaid-example 346 sequenceDiagram 347 Alice->>John: Hello John, how are you? 348 activate John 349 John-->>Alice: Great! 350 deactivate John 351 ``` 352 353 There is also a shortcut notation by appending `+`/`-` suffix to the message arrow: 354 355 ```mermaid-example 356 sequenceDiagram 357 Alice->>+John: Hello John, how are you? 358 John-->>-Alice: Great! 359 ``` 360 361 Activations can be stacked for same actor: 362 363 ```mermaid-example 364 sequenceDiagram 365 Alice->>+John: Hello John, how are you? 366 Alice->>+John: John, can you hear me? 367 John-->>-Alice: Hi Alice, I can hear you! 368 John-->>-Alice: I feel great! 369 ``` 370 371 ## Notes 372 373 It is possible to add notes to a sequence diagram. This is done by the notation 374 Note [ right of | left of | over ] [Actor]: Text in note content 375 376 See the example below: 377 378 ```mermaid-example 379 sequenceDiagram 380 participant John 381 Note right of John: Text in note 382 ``` 383 384 It is also possible to create notes spanning two participants: 385 386 ```mermaid-example 387 sequenceDiagram 388 Alice->John: Hello John, how are you? 389 Note over Alice,John: A typical interaction 390 ``` 391 392 ## Line breaks 393 394 Line break can be added to Note and Message: 395 396 ```mermaid-example 397 sequenceDiagram 398 Alice->John: Hello John,
how are you? 399 Note over Alice,John: A typical interaction
But now in two lines 400 ``` 401 402 Line breaks in Actor names requires aliases: 403 404 ```mermaid-example 405 sequenceDiagram 406 participant Alice as Alice
Johnson 407 Alice->John: Hello John,
how are you? 408 Note over Alice,John: A typical interaction
But now in two lines 409 ``` 410 411 ## Loops 412 413 It is possible to express loops in a sequence diagram. This is done by the notation 414 415 ``` 416 loop Loop text 417 ... statements ... 418 end 419 ``` 420 421 See the example below: 422 423 ```mermaid-example 424 sequenceDiagram 425 Alice->John: Hello John, how are you? 426 loop Every minute 427 John-->Alice: Great! 428 end 429 ``` 430 431 ## Alt 432 433 It is possible to express alternative paths in a sequence diagram. This is done by the notation 434 435 ``` 436 alt Describing text 437 ... statements ... 438 else 439 ... statements ... 440 end 441 ``` 442 443 or if there is sequence that is optional (if without else). 444 445 ``` 446 opt Describing text 447 ... statements ... 448 end 449 ``` 450 451 See the example below: 452 453 ```mermaid-example 454 sequenceDiagram 455 Alice->>Bob: Hello Bob, how are you? 456 alt is sick 457 Bob->>Alice: Not so good :( 458 else is well 459 Bob->>Alice: Feeling fresh like a daisy 460 end 461 opt Extra response 462 Bob->>Alice: Thanks for asking 463 end 464 ``` 465 466 ## Parallel 467 468 It is possible to show actions that are happening in parallel. 469 470 This is done by the notation 471 472 ``` 473 par [Action 1] 474 ... statements ... 475 and [Action 2] 476 ... statements ... 477 and [Action N] 478 ... statements ... 479 end 480 ``` 481 482 See the example below: 483 484 ```mermaid-example 485 sequenceDiagram 486 par Alice to Bob 487 Alice->>Bob: Hello guys! 488 and Alice to John 489 Alice->>John: Hello guys! 490 end 491 Bob-->>Alice: Hi Alice! 492 John-->>Alice: Hi Alice! 493 ``` 494 495 It is also possible to nest parallel blocks. 496 497 ```mermaid-example 498 sequenceDiagram 499 par Alice to Bob 500 Alice->>Bob: Go help John 501 and Alice to John 502 Alice->>John: I want this done today 503 par John to Charlie 504 John->>Charlie: Can we do this today? 505 and John to Diana 506 John->>Diana: Can you help us today? 507 end 508 end 509 ``` 510 511 ## Critical Region 512 513 It is possible to show actions that must happen automatically with conditional handling of circumstances. 514 515 This is done by the notation 516 517 ``` 518 critical [Action that must be performed] 519 ... statements ... 520 option [Circumstance A] 521 ... statements ... 522 option [Circumstance B] 523 ... statements ... 524 end 525 ``` 526 527 See the example below: 528 529 ```mermaid-example 530 sequenceDiagram 531 critical Establish a connection to the DB 532 Service-->DB: connect 533 option Network timeout 534 Service-->Service: Log error 535 option Credentials rejected 536 Service-->Service: Log different error 537 end 538 ``` 539 540 It is also possible to have no options at all 541 542 ```mermaid-example 543 sequenceDiagram 544 critical Establish a connection to the DB 545 Service-->DB: connect 546 end 547 ``` 548 549 This critical block can also be nested, equivalently to the `par` statement as seen above. 550 551 ## Break 552 553 It is possible to indicate a stop of the sequence within the flow (usually used to model exceptions). 554 555 This is done by the notation 556 557 ``` 558 break [something happened] 559 ... statements ... 560 end 561 ``` 562 563 See the example below: 564 565 ```mermaid-example 566 sequenceDiagram 567 Consumer-->API: Book something 568 API-->BookingService: Start booking process 569 break when the booking process fails 570 API-->Consumer: show failure 571 end 572 API-->BillingService: Start billing process 573 ``` 574 575 ## Background Highlighting 576 577 It is possible to highlight flows by providing colored background rects. This is done by the notation 578 579 ``` 580 rect COLOR 581 ... content ... 582 end 583 ``` 584 585 The colors are defined using rgb and rgba syntax. 586 587 ``` 588 rect rgb(0, 255, 0) 589 ... content ... 590 end 591 ``` 592 593 ``` 594 rect rgba(0, 0, 255, .1) 595 ... content ... 596 end 597 ``` 598 599 See the examples below: 600 601 ```mermaid-example 602 sequenceDiagram 603 participant Alice 604 participant John 605 606 rect rgb(191, 223, 255) 607 note right of Alice: Alice calls John. 608 Alice->>+John: Hello John, how are you? 609 rect rgb(200, 150, 255) 610 Alice->>+John: John, can you hear me? 611 John-->>-Alice: Hi Alice, I can hear you! 612 end 613 John-->>-Alice: I feel great! 614 end 615 Alice ->>+ John: Did you want to go to the game tonight? 616 John -->>- Alice: Yeah! See you there. 617 618 ``` 619 620 ## Comments 621 622 Comments can be entered within a sequence diagram, which will be ignored by the parser. Comments need to be on their own line, and must be prefaced with `%%` (double percent signs). Any text after the start of the comment to the next newline will be treated as a comment, including any diagram syntax 623 624 ```mermaid-example 625 sequenceDiagram 626 Alice->>John: Hello John, how are you? 627 %% this is a comment 628 John-->>Alice: Great! 629 ``` 630 631 ## Entity codes to escape characters 632 633 It is possible to escape characters using the syntax exemplified here. 634 635 ```mermaid-example 636 sequenceDiagram 637 A->>B: I #9829; you! 638 B->>A: I #9829; you #infin; times more! 639 ``` 640 641 Numbers given are base 10, so `#` can be encoded as `#35;`. It is also supported to use HTML character names. 642 643 Because semicolons can be used instead of line breaks to define the markup, you need to use `#59;` to include a semicolon in message text. 644 645 ## sequenceNumbers 646 647 It is possible to get a sequence number attached to each arrow in a sequence diagram. This can be configured when adding mermaid to the website as shown below: 648 649 ```html 650 653 ``` 654 655 It can also be turned on via the diagram code as in the diagram: 656 657 ```mermaid-example 658 sequenceDiagram 659 autonumber 660 Alice->>John: Hello John, how are you? 661 loop HealthCheck 662 John->>John: Fight against hypochondria 663 end 664 Note right of John: Rational thoughts! 665 John-->>Alice: Great! 666 John->>Bob: How about you? 667 Bob-->>John: Jolly good! 668 ``` 669 670 ### Start and Increment values (v11.15.0+) 671 672 It is possible to specify a starting value and an increment value for automatic numbering. Both the starting value and increment value can include decimals up to the hundredths place. 673 674 Use the following syntax in your diagram definition: 675 676 ``` 677 autonumber 678 ``` 679 680 ## Actor Menus 681 682 Actors can have popup-menus containing individualized links to external pages. For example, if an actor represented a web service, useful links might include a link to the service health dashboard, repo containing the code for the service, or a wiki page describing the service. 683 684 This can be configured by adding one or more link lines with the format: 685 686 ``` 687 link : @ 688 ``` 689 690 ```mermaid 691 sequenceDiagram 692 participant Alice 693 participant John 694 link Alice: Dashboard @ https://dashboard.contoso.com/alice 695 link Alice: Wiki @ https://wiki.contoso.com/alice 696 link John: Dashboard @ https://dashboard.contoso.com/john 697 link John: Wiki @ https://wiki.contoso.com/john 698 Alice->>John: Hello John, how are you? 699 John-->>Alice: Great! 700 Alice-)John: See you later! 701 ``` 702 703 #### Advanced Menu Syntax 704 705 There is an advanced syntax that relies on JSON formatting. If you are comfortable with JSON format, then this exists as well. 706 707 This can be configured by adding the links lines with the format: 708 709 ``` 710 links : 711 ``` 712 713 An example is below: 714 715 ```mermaid-example 716 sequenceDiagram 717 participant Alice 718 participant John 719 links Alice: {"Dashboard": "https://dashboard.contoso.com/alice", "Wiki": "https://wiki.contoso.com/alice"} 720 links John: {"Dashboard": "https://dashboard.contoso.com/john", "Wiki": "https://wiki.contoso.com/john"} 721 Alice->>John: Hello John, how are you? 722 John-->>Alice: Great! 723 Alice-)John: See you later! 724 ``` 725 726 ## Styling 727 728 Styling of a sequence diagram is done by defining a number of css classes. During rendering these classes are extracted from the file located at src/themes/sequence.scss 729 730 ### Classes used 731 732 | Class | Description | 733 | -------------- | -------------------------------------------------------------- | 734 | actor | Styles for the actor box. | 735 | actor-top | Styles for the actor figure/ box at the top of the diagram. | 736 | actor-bottom | Styles for the actor figure/ box at the bottom of the diagram. | 737 | text.actor | Styles for text of all of the actors. | 738 | text.actor-box | Styles for text of the actor box. | 739 | text.actor-man | Styles for text of the actor figure. | 740 | actor-line | The vertical line for an actor. | 741 | messageLine0 | Styles for the solid message line. | 742 | messageLine1 | Styles for the dotted message line. | 743 | messageText | Defines styles for the text on the message arrows. | 744 | labelBox | Defines styles label to left in a loop. | 745 | labelText | Styles for the text in label for loops. | 746 | loopText | Styles for the text in the loop box. | 747 | loopLine | Defines styles for the lines in the loop box. | 748 | note | Styles for the note box. | 749 | noteText | Styles for the text on in the note boxes. | 750 751 ### Sample stylesheet 752 753 ```css 754 body { 755 background: white; 756 } 757 758 .actor { 759 stroke: #ccccff; 760 fill: #ececff; 761 } 762 text.actor { 763 fill: black; 764 stroke: none; 765 font-family: Helvetica; 766 } 767 768 .actor-line { 769 stroke: grey; 770 } 771 772 .messageLine0 { 773 stroke-width: 1.5; 774 stroke-dasharray: '2 2'; 775 marker-end: 'url(#arrowhead)'; 776 stroke: black; 777 } 778 779 .messageLine1 { 780 stroke-width: 1.5; 781 stroke-dasharray: '2 2'; 782 stroke: black; 783 } 784 785 #arrowhead { 786 fill: black; 787 } 788 789 .messageText { 790 fill: black; 791 stroke: none; 792 font-family: 'trebuchet ms', verdana, arial; 793 font-size: 14px; 794 } 795 796 .labelBox { 797 stroke: #ccccff; 798 fill: #ececff; 799 } 800 801 .labelText { 802 fill: black; 803 stroke: none; 804 font-family: 'trebuchet ms', verdana, arial; 805 } 806 807 .loopText { 808 fill: black; 809 stroke: none; 810 font-family: 'trebuchet ms', verdana, arial; 827 stroke: none; 828 font-family: 'trebuchet ms', verdana, arial; 829 font-size: 14px; 830 } 831 ``` 832 833 ## Configuration 834 835 It is possible to adjust the margins for rendering the sequence diagram. 836 837 This is done by defining `mermaid.sequenceConfig` or by the CLI to use a json file with the configuration. 838 How to use the CLI is described in the [mermaidCLI](../config/mermaidCLI.md) page. 839 `mermaid.sequenceConfig` can be set to a JSON string with config parameters or the corresponding object. 840 841 ```javascript 842 mermaid.sequenceConfig = { 843 diagramMarginX: 50, 844 diagramMarginY: 10, 845 boxTextMargin: 5, 846 noteMargin: 10, 847 messageMargin: 35, 848 mirrorActors: true, 849 }; 850 ``` 851 852 ### Possible configuration parameters: 853 854 | Parameter | Description | Default value | 855 | ----------------- | ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------ | ------------------------------ | 856 | mirrorActors | Turns on/off the rendering of actors below the diagram as well as above it | false | 857 | bottomMarginAdj | Adjusts how far down the graph ended.
