1 # Class diagrams 2 3 > "In software engineering, a class diagram in the Unified Modeling Language (UML) is a type of static structure diagram that describes the structure of a system by showing the system's classes, their attributes, operations (or methods), and the relationships among objects." 4 > 5 > -Wikipedia 6 7 The class diagram is the main building block of object-oriented modeling. It is used for general conceptual modeling of the structure of the application, and for detailed modeling to translate the models into programming code. Class diagrams can also be used for data modeling. The classes in a class diagram represent both the main elements, interactions in the application, and the classes to be programmed. 8 9 Mermaid can render class diagrams. 10 11 ```mermaid-example 12 --- 13 title: Animal example 14 --- 15 classDiagram 16 note "From Duck till Zebra" 17 Animal <|-- Duck 18 note for Duck "can fly
can swim
can dive
can help in debugging" 19 Animal <|-- Fish 20 Animal <|-- Zebra 21 Animal : +int age 22 Animal : +String gender 23 Animal: +isMammal() 24 Animal: +mate() 25 class Duck{ 26 +String beakColor 27 +swim() 28 +quack() 29 } 30 class Fish{ 31 -int sizeInFeet 32 -canEat() 33 } 34 class Zebra{ 35 +bool is_wild 36 +run() 37 } 38 ``` 39 40 ## Syntax 41 42 ### Class 43 44 UML provides mechanisms to represent class members, such as attributes and methods, and additional information about them. 45 A single instance of a class in the diagram contains three compartments: 46 47 - The top compartment contains the name of the class. It is printed in bold and centered, and the first letter is capitalized. It may also contain optional annotation text describing the nature of the class. 48 - The middle compartment contains the attributes of the class. They are left-aligned and the first letter is lowercase. 49 - The bottom compartment contains the operations the class can execute. They are also left-aligned and the first letter is lowercase. 50 51 ```mermaid-example 52 --- 53 title: Bank example 54 --- 55 classDiagram 56 class BankAccount 57 BankAccount : +String owner 58 BankAccount : +Bigdecimal balance 59 BankAccount : +deposit(amount) 60 BankAccount : +withdrawal(amount) 61 62 ``` 63 64 ## Define a class 65 66 There are two ways to define a class: 67 68 - Explicitly using keyword **class** like `class Animal` which would define the Animal class. 69 - Via a **relationship** which defines two classes at a time along with their relationship. For instance, `Vehicle <|-- Car`. 70 71 ```mermaid-example 72 classDiagram 73 class Animal 74 Vehicle <|-- Car 75 ``` 76 77 Naming convention: a class name should be composed only of alphanumeric characters (including unicode), underscores, and dashes (-). 78 79 ### Class labels 80 81 In case you need to provide a label for a class, you can use the following syntax: 82 83 ```mermaid-example 84 classDiagram 85 class Animal["Animal with a label"] 86 class Car["Car with *! symbols"] 87 Animal --> Car 88 ``` 89 90 You can also use backticks to escape special characters in the label: 91 92 ```mermaid-example 93 classDiagram 94 class `Animal Class!` 95 class `Car Class` 96 `Animal Class!` --> `Car Class` 97 ``` 98 99 ## Defining Members of a class 100 101 UML provides mechanisms to represent class members such as attributes and methods, as well as additional information about them. 102 103 Mermaid distinguishes between attributes and functions/methods based on if the **parenthesis** `()` are present or not. The ones with `()` are treated as functions/methods, and all others as attributes. 104 105 There are two ways to define the members of a class, and regardless of whichever syntax is used to define the members, the output will still be same. The two different ways are : 106 107 - Associate a member of a class using **:** (colon) followed by member name, useful to define one member at a time. For example: 108 109 ```mermaid-example 110 classDiagram 111 class BankAccount 112 BankAccount : +String owner 113 BankAccount : +BigDecimal balance 114 BankAccount : +deposit(amount) 115 BankAccount : +withdrawal(amount) 116 ``` 117 118 - Associate members of a class using **{}** brackets, where members are grouped within curly brackets. Suitable for defining multiple members at once. For example: 119 120 ```mermaid-example 121 classDiagram 122 class BankAccount{ 123 +String owner 124 +BigDecimal balance 125 +deposit(amount) 126 +withdrawal(amount) 127 } 128 ``` 129 130 #### Return Type 131 132 Optionally you can end a method/function definition with the data type that will be returned (note: there must be a space between the final `)` and the return type). An example: 133 134 ```mermaid-example 135 classDiagram 136 class BankAccount{ 137 +String owner 138 +BigDecimal balance 139 +deposit(amount) bool 140 +withdrawal(amount) int 141 } 142 ``` 143 144 #### Generic Types 145 146 Generics can be represented as part of a class definition, and for class members/return types. In order to denote an item as generic, you enclose that type within `~` (**tilde**). **Nested** type declarations such as `List>` are supported, though generics that include a comma are currently not supported. (such as `List>`) 147 148 > _note_ when a generic is used within a class definition, the generic type is NOT considered part of the class name. i.e.: for any syntax which required you to reference the class name, you need to drop the type part of the definition. This also means that mermaid does not currently support having two classes with the same name, but different generic types. 149 150 ```mermaid-example 151 classDiagram 152 class Square~Shape~{ 153 int id 154 List~int~ position 155 setPoints(List~int~ points) 156 getPoints() List~int~ 157 } 158 159 Square : -List~string~ messages 160 Square : +setMessages(List~string~ messages) 161 Square : +getMessages() List~string~ 162 Square : +getDistanceMatrix() List~List~int~~ 163 ``` 164 165 #### Visibility 166 167 To describe the visibility (or encapsulation) of an attribute or method/function that is a part of a class (i.e. a class member), optional notation may be placed before that members' name: 168 169 - `+` Public 170 - `-` Private 171 - `#` Protected 172 - `~` Package/Internal 173 174 > _note_ you can also include additional _classifiers_ to a method definition by adding the following notation to the _end_ of the method, i.e.: after the `()` or after the return type: 175 > 176 > - `*` Abstract e.g.: `someAbstractMethod()*` or `someAbstractMethod() int*` 177 > - `$` Static e.g.: `someStaticMethod()$` or `someStaticMethod() String$` 178 179 > _note_ you can also include additional _classifiers_ to a field definition by adding the following notation to the very end: 180 > 181 > - `$` Static e.g.: `String someField$` 182 183 ## Defining Relationship 184 185 A relationship is a general term covering the specific types of logical connections found on class and object diagrams. 186 187 ``` 188 [classA][Arrow][ClassB] 189 ``` 190 191 There are eight different types of relations defined for classes under UML which are currently supported: 192 193 | Type | Description | 194 | ------- | ------------- | 195 | `<\|--` | Inheritance | 196 | `*--` | Composition | 197 | `o--` | Aggregation | 198 | `-->` | Association | 199 | `--` | Link (Solid) | 200 | `..>` | Dependency | 201 | `..\|>` | Realization | 202 | `..` | Link (Dashed) | 203 204 ```mermaid-example 205 classDiagram 206 classA <|-- classB 207 classC *-- classD 208 classE o-- classF 209 classG <-- classH 210 classI -- classJ 211 classK <.. classL 212 classM <|.. classN 213 classO .. classP 214 215 ``` 216 217 We can use the labels to describe the nature of the relation between two classes. Also, arrowheads can be used in the opposite direction as well: 218 219 ```mermaid-example 220 classDiagram 221 classA --|> classB : Inheritance 222 classC --* classD : Composition 223 classE --o classF : Aggregation 224 classG --> classH : Association 225 classI -- classJ : Link(Solid) 226 classK ..> classL : Dependency 227 classM ..|> classN : Realization 228 classO .. classP : Link(Dashed) 229 230 ``` 231 232 ### Labels on Relations 233 234 It is possible to add label text to a relation: 235 236 ``` 237 [classA][Arrow][ClassB]:LabelText 238 ``` 239 240 ```mermaid-example 241 classDiagram 242 classA <|-- classB : implements 243 classC *-- classD : composition 244 classE o-- classF : aggregation 245 ``` 246 247 ### Two-way relations 248 249 Relations can logically represent an N:M association: 250 251 ```mermaid-example 252 classDiagram 253 Animal <|--|> Zebra 254 ``` 255 256 Here is the syntax: 257 258 ``` 259 [Relation Type][Link][Relation Type] 260 ``` 261 262 Where `Relation Type` can be one of: 263 264 | Type | Description | 265 | ----- | ----------- | 266 | `<\|` | Inheritance | 267 | `\*` | Composition | 268 | `o` | Aggregation | 269 | `>` | Association | 270 | `<` | Association | 271 | `\|>` | Realization | 272 273 And `Link` can be one of: 274 275 | Type | Description | 276 | ---- | ----------- | 277 | -- | Solid | 278 | .. | Dashed | 279 280 ### Lollipop Interfaces 281 282 Classes can also be given a special relation type that defines a lollipop interface on the class. A lollipop interface is defined using the following syntax: 283 284 - `bar ()-- foo` 285 - `foo --() bar` 286 287 The interface (bar) with the lollipop connects to the class (foo). 288 289 Note: Each interface that is defined is unique and is meant to not be shared between classes / have multiple edges connecting to it. 290 291 ```mermaid-example 292 classDiagram 293 bar ()-- foo 294 ``` 295 296 ```mermaid-example 297 classDiagram 298 class Class01 { 299 int amount 300 draw() 301 } 302 Class01 --() bar 303 Class02 --() bar 304 305 foo ()-- Class01 306 ``` 307 308 ## Define Namespace 309 310 A namespace groups classes. 311 312 ```mermaid-example 313 classDiagram 314 namespace BaseShapes { 315 class Triangle 316 class Rectangle { 317 double width 318 double height 319 } 320 } 321 ``` 322 323 ### Namespace Labels (v11.15.0+) 324 325 A namespace can be given a display label using square bracket syntax, similar to class labels: 326 327 ```mermaid-example 328 classDiagram 329 namespace Auth["Authentication Service"] { 330 class UserService { 331 +login() 332 +logout() 333 } 334 } 335 ``` 336 337 The label replaces the namespace name in the rendered diagram, while the name is still used internally for relationships and nesting. 338 339 ### Nested Namespaces (v11.15.0+) 340 341 Namespaces can be nested to represent hierarchical groupings. There are two ways to define nested namespaces: 342 343 **Dot notation** creates intermediate namespaces automatically: 344 345 ```mermaid-example 346 classDiagram 347 namespace Company.Engineering.Backend { 348 class Developer { 349 +writeCode() 350 } 351 } 352 namespace Company.Engineering.Frontend { 353 class Designer { 354 +createMockup() 355 } 356 } 357 namespace Company.Engineering { 358 class TechLead { 359 +planSprint() 360 } 361 } 362 TechLead --> Developer : leads 363 TechLead --> Designer : leads 364 ``` 365 366 **Syntactic nesting** places namespace blocks inside other namespace blocks: 367 368 ```mermaid-example 369 classDiagram 370 namespace Platform { 371 namespace Auth { 372 class UserService { 373 +login() 374 +logout() 375 } 376 } 377 namespace Data { 378 class Repository { 379 +find() 380 +save() 381 } 382 } 383 class Gateway { 384 +route() 385 } 386 } 387 Gateway --> UserService : delegates 388 Gateway --> Repository : delegates 389 ``` 390 391 Both approaches can be combined. Dot notation like `namespace A.B.C` will automatically create namespaces `A` and `A.B` as parents if they don't already exist. 392 393 #### Compact rendering (`hierarchicalNamespaces: false`) 394 395 By default (`hierarchicalNamespaces: true`), each segment of a dotted or syntactically-nested namespace name renders as its own cluster, producing a nested layout. 396 397 Setting `hierarchicalNamespaces: false` in the class diagram config switches to **compact mode**: only namespaces the user explicitly declares are drawn — each as a single flat box labelled with its fully-qualified name. Auto-created intermediate ancestors are skipped, and classes inside them are moved to their nearest declared namespace. 398 399 ```mermaid-example 400 --- 401 config: 402 class: 403 hierarchicalNamespaces: false 404 --- 405 classDiagram 406 namespace Company.Engineering.Backend { 407 class Developer { 408 +writeCode() 409 } 410 } 411 namespace Company.Engineering.Frontend { 412 class Designer { 413 +createMockup() 414 } 415 } 416 namespace Company { 417 class CEO { 418 +makeDecisions() 419 } 420 } 421 CEO --> Developer : oversees 422 CEO --> Designer : oversees 423 ``` 424 425 ## Cardinality / Multiplicity on relations 426 427 Multiplicity or cardinality in class diagrams indicates the number of instances of one class that can be linked to an instance of the other class. For example, each company will have one or more employees (not zero), and each employee currently works for zero or one companies. 428 429 Multiplicity notations are placed near the end of an association. 430 431 The different cardinality options are : 432 433 - `1` Only 1 434 - `0..1` Zero or One 435 - `1..*` One or more 436 - `*` Many 437 - `n` n (where n>1) 438 - `0..n` zero to n (where n>1) 439 - `1..n` one to n (where n>1) 440 441 Cardinality can be easily defined by placing the text option within quotes `"` before or after a given arrow. For example: 442 443 ``` 444 [classA] "cardinality1" [Arrow] "cardinality2" [ClassB]:LabelText 445 ``` 446 447 ```mermaid-example 448 classDiagram 449 Customer "1" --> "*" Ticket 450 Student "1" --> "1..*" Course 451 Galaxy --> "many" Star : Contains 452 ``` 453 454 ## Annotations on classes 455 456 It is possible to annotate classes with markers to provide additional metadata about the class. This can give a clearer indication about its nature. Some common annotations include: 457 458 - `<>` To represent an Interface class 459 - `<>` To represent an abstract class 460 - `<>` To represent a service class 461 - `<>` To represent an enum 462 463 Annotations are defined within the opening `<<` and closing `>>`. There are three ways to add an annotation to a class, and in all cases the output will be the same: 464 465 - **Inline** with the class definition: 466 467 ```mermaid-example 468 classDiagram 469 class Shape <> 470 ``` 471 472 - In a **_separate line_** after a class is defined: 473 474 ```mermaid-example 475 classDiagram 476 class Shape 477 <> Shape 478 Shape : noOfVertices 479 Shape : draw() 480 ``` 481 482 - In a **_nested structure_** along with the class definition: 483 484 ```mermaid-example 485 classDiagram 486 class Shape{ 487 <> 488 noOfVertices 489 draw() 490 } 491 class Color{ 492 <> 493 RED 494 BLUE 495 GREEN 496 WHITE 497 BLACK 498 } 499 500 ``` 501 502 ## Comments 503 504 Comments can be entered within a class diagram, which will be ignored by the parser. Comments need to be on their own line, and must be prefaced with `%%` (double percent signs). Any text until the next newline will be treated as a comment, including any class diagram syntax. 505 506 ```mermaid 507 classDiagram 508 %% This whole line is a comment classDiagram class Shape <> 509 class Shape{ 510 <> 511 noOfVertices 512 draw() 513 } 514 ``` 515 516 ## Setting the direction of the diagram 517 518 With class diagrams you can use the direction statement to set the direction in which the diagram will render: 519 520 ```mermaid-example 521 classDiagram 522 direction RL 523 class Student { 524 -idCard : IdCard 525 } 526 class IdCard{ 527 -id : int 528 -name : string 529 } 530 class Bike{ 531 -id : int 532 -name : string 533 } 534 Student "1" --o "1" IdCard : carries 535 Student "1" --o "1" Bike : rides 536 ``` 537 538 ## Interaction 539 540 It is possible to bind a click event to a node. The click can lead to either a javascript callback or to a link which will be opened in a new browser tab. **Note**: This functionality is disabled when using `securityLevel='strict'` and enabled when using `securityLevel='loose'`. 541 542 You would define these actions on a separate line after all classes have been declared. 543 544 ``` 545 action className "reference" "tooltip" 546 click className call callback() "tooltip" 547 click className href "url" "tooltip" 548 ``` 549 550 - _action_ is either `link` or `callback`, depending on which type of interaction you want to have called 551 - _className_ is the id of the node that the action will be associated with 552 - _reference_ is either the url link, or the function name for callback. 553 - (_optional_) tooltip is a string to be displayed when hovering over element (note: The styles of the tooltip are set by the class .mermaidTooltip.) 554 - note: callback function will be called with the nodeId as parameter. 555 556 ## Notes 557 558 It is possible to add notes on the diagram using `note "line1\nline2"`. A note can be added for a specific class using `note for "line1\nline2"`. 559 560 ### Examples 561 562 ```mermaid 563 classDiagram 564 note "This is a general note" 565 note for MyClass "This is a note for a class" 566 class MyClass{ 567 } 568 ``` 569 570 _URL Link:_ 571 572 ```mermaid 573 classDiagram 574 class Shape 575 link Shape "https://www.github.com" "This is a tooltip for a link" 576 class Shape2 577 click Shape2 href "https://www.github.com" "This is a tooltip for a link" 578 ``` 579 580 _Callback:_ 581 582 ```mermaid 583 classDiagram 584 class Shape 585 callback Shape "callbackFunction" "This is a tooltip for a callback" 586 class Shape2 587 click Shape2 call callbackFunction() "This is a tooltip for a callback" 588 ``` 589 590 ```html 591 596 ``` 597 598 ```mermaid 599 classDiagram 600 class Class01 601 class Class02 602 callback Class01 "callbackFunction" "Callback tooltip" 603 link Class02 "https://www.github.com" "This is a link" 604 class Class03 605 class Class04 606 click Class03 call callbackFunction() "Callback tooltip" 607 click Class04 href "https://www.github.com" "This is a link" 608 ``` 609 610 > **Success** The tooltip functionality and the ability to link to urls are available from version 0.5.2. 611 612 Beginner's tip—a full example using interactive links in an HTML page: 613 614 ```html 615 616 
617	    classDiagram
618	    Animal <|-- Duck
619	    Animal <|-- Fish
620	    Animal <|-- Zebra
621	    Animal : +int age
622	    Animal : +String gender
623	    Animal: +isMammal()
624	    Animal: +mate()
625	    class Duck{
626	      +String beakColor
627	      +swim()
628	      +quack()
629	      }
630	    class Fish{
631	      -int sizeInFeet
632	      -canEat()
633	      }
634	    class Zebra{
635	      +bool is_wild
636	      +run()
637	      }
638	
639	      callback Duck "callback" "Tooltip"
640	      link Zebra "https://www.github.com" "This is a link"
641
642 643 653 654 ``` 655 656 ## Styling 657 658 ### Styling a node 659 660 It is possible to apply specific styles such as a thicker border or a different background color to an individual node using the `style` keyword. 661 662 Note that notes and namespaces cannot be styled individually but do support themes. 663 664 ```mermaid-example 665 classDiagram 666 class Animal 667 class Mineral 668 style Animal fill:#f9f,stroke:#333,stroke-width:4px 669 style Mineral fill:#bbf,stroke:#f66,stroke-width:2px,color:#fff,stroke-dasharray: 5 5 670 ``` 671 672 #### Classes 673 674 More convenient than defining the style every time is to define a class of styles and attach this class to the nodes that 675 should have a different look. 676 677 A class definition looks like the example below: 678 679 ``` 680 classDef className fill:#f9f,stroke:#333,stroke-width:4px; 681 ``` 682 683 Also, it is possible to define style to multiple classes in one statement: 684 685 ``` 686 classDef firstClassName,secondClassName font-size:12pt; 687 ``` 688 689 Attachment of a class to a node is done as per below: 690 691 ``` 692 cssClass "nodeId1" className; 693 ``` 694 695 It is also possible to attach a class to a list of nodes in one statement: 696 697 ``` 698 cssClass "nodeId1,nodeId2" className; 699 ``` 700 701 A shorter form of adding a class is to attach the classname to the node using the `:::` operator: 702 703 ```mermaid-example 704 classDiagram 705 class Animal:::someclass 706 classDef someclass fill:#f96 707 ``` 708 709 Or: 710 711 ```mermaid-example 712 classDiagram 713 class Animal:::someclass { 714 -int sizeInFeet 715 -canEat() 716 } 717 classDef someclass fill:#f96 718 ``` 719 720 ### Default class 721 722 If a class is named default it will be applied to all nodes. Specific styles and classes should be defined afterwards to override the applied default styling. 723 724 ``` 725 classDef default fill:#f9f,stroke:#333,stroke-width:4px; 726 ``` 727 728 ```mermaid-example 729 classDiagram 730 class Animal:::pink 731 class Mineral 732 733 classDef default fill:#f96,color:red 734 classDef pink color:#f9f 735 ``` 736 737 ### CSS Classes 738 739 It is also possible to predefine classes in CSS styles that can be applied from the graph definition as in the example 740 below: 741 742 **Example style** 743 744 ```html 745 752 ``` 753 754 **Example definition** 755 756 ```mermaid-example 757 classDiagram 758 class Animal:::styleClass 759 ``` 760 761 > cssClasses cannot be added using this shorthand method at the same time as a relation statement. 762 763 ## Configuration 764 765 ### Members Box 766 767 It is possible to hide the empty members box of a class node. 768 769 This is done by changing the **hideEmptyMembersBox** value of the class diagram configuration. For more information on how to edit the Mermaid configuration see the [configuration page.](https://mermaid.js.org/config/configuration.html) 770 771 ### Possible configuration parameters: 772 773 | Parameter | Description | Default value | 774 | ------------------- | ------------------------------------------------------------ | ------------- | 775 | hideEmptyMembersBox | Hides the empty members box of a class node when set to true | false | 776 777 ```mermaid-example 778 --- 779 config: 780 class: 781 hideEmptyMembersBox: true 782 --- 783 classDiagram 784 class Duck 785 ``` 786

# Class Diagram

**Source**: `mermaid-upstream/packages/mermaid/src/docs/syntax/classDiagram.md` (785 lines)
**Detector**: `src/diagrams/class/classDetector-V2.ts` — `/^\s*classDiagram-v2/`, `/^\s*classDiagram/`
**Registry id**: `class`

## Statements

| Keyword | Form |
| --- | --- |
| `class` | `class Animal`, `class Animal["label"]`, `class Animal { … }`, `class Animal:::someclass` |
| `namespace` | `namespace Name { … }`, `namespace Name["label"] { … }` (label v11.15.0+) |
| `direction` | `direction RL` (also TB/TD/BT/LR) |
| `note` | `note "text"`, `note for <CLASS> "text"` |
| `style` | `style Animal fill:#f9f,…` |
| `classDef` | `classDef className fill:…`, multiple names comma-separated |
| `cssClass` | `cssClass "nodeId1,nodeId2" className;` — note the **quotes**, unlike flowchart's `class` |
| `link` / `callback` / `click` | interaction, see below |
| `<<annotation>>` | `<<Interface>>`, `<<Abstract>>`, `<<Service>>`, `<<Enumeration>>` |

Class names: alphanumeric (incl. unicode), underscores and dashes only (`:77`). Backticks
escape special characters: `` class `Animal Class!` `` (`:90-97`).

## Members (`:99-182`)

Two equivalent forms: `BankAccount : +String owner`, or a `{ … }` block.

**Attribute vs method is decided by the presence of `()`** (`:103`).

- Return type: `+deposit(amount) bool` — **a space is required** between `)` and the type (`:132`).
- Generics with `~`: `List~int~`, nested `List~List~int~~`. **Generics containing a comma
  are not supported** (`List~K, V~`) (`:146`).
- A generic in a class definition is **not** part of the class name, so two classes
  differing only by generic type are not supported (`:148`).

Visibility prefixes (`:169-172`): `+` public, `-` private, `#` protected, `~` package.

Classifiers, placed at the very end (after `()` or after the return type) (`:174-181`):
`*` abstract, `$` static. Fields accept `$` only.

## Relations (`:183-215`)

| Arrow | Meaning |
| --- | --- |
| `<\|--` | Inheritance |
| `*--` | Composition |
| `o--` | Aggregation |
| `-->` | Association |
| `--` | Link (solid) |
| `..>` | Dependency |
| `..\|>` | Realization |
| `..` | Link (dashed) |

Arrowheads may be reversed (`--|>`, `--*`, `--o`, …). Label: `classA <|-- classB : implements`.

**Two-way** (`:247-279`): `[Relation Type][Link][Relation Type]`, e.g. `Animal <|--|> Zebra`.
Relation types: `<|`, `*`, `o`, `>`, `<`, `|>`. Links: `--` solid, `..` dashed.

**Lollipop interfaces** (`:280-306`): `bar ()-- foo` or `foo --() bar`. Each interface is
unique and is not meant to be shared across classes.

**Cardinality** (`:425-452`): quoted, before and/or after the arrow —
`Customer "1" --> "*" Ticket`. Options: `1`, `0..1`, `1..*`, `*`, `n`, `0..n`, `1..n`, and
free text such as `"many"`.

## Namespaces (`:308-423`)

- Flat: `namespace BaseShapes { class Triangle }`
- Labels (v11.15.0+): `namespace Auth["Authentication Service"] { … }` — the name is still
  used internally for relations and nesting.
- Nested (v11.15.0+), two ways, combinable:
  - Dot notation: `namespace Company.Engineering.Backend` auto-creates `Company` and
    `Company.Engineering`.
  - Syntactic nesting: `namespace` blocks inside `namespace` blocks.
- `config.class.hierarchicalNamespaces` (default `true`): each segment becomes its own
  cluster. Set `false` for compact mode — only explicitly declared namespaces are drawn,
  each as one flat box with its fully-qualified name; auto-created ancestors are skipped
  and their classes move to the nearest declared namespace.

## Annotations (`:454-500`)

Three equivalent placements: inline (`class Shape <<interface>>`), on a separate line
(`<<interface>> Shape`), or as the first entry inside the `{ }` block.

## Interaction (`:538-554`)

```
link className "url" "tooltip"
callback className "functionName" "tooltip"
click className call callback() "tooltip"
click className href "url" "tooltip"
```

Defined after all classes are declared. **Disabled under `securityLevel: 'strict'`**,
which this project pins.

## Styling (`:656-761`)

Same vocabulary as flowchart with two differences worth a diagnostic:

1. Attachment uses `cssClass "nodeId" className;` with **quoted** ids, not flowchart's
   `class nodeId className;`.
2. `:::` shorthand works on `class Animal:::someclass`, with or without a `{ }` block, but
   **cannot be combined with a relation statement** (`:761`).

`classDef default` applies to all nodes. Notes and namespaces cannot be styled
individually, though they follow the theme (`:662`).

## Configuration

| Parameter | Default |
| --- | --- |
| `class.hideEmptyMembersBox` | `false` |
| `class.hierarchicalNamespaces` | `true` |

## Editor Notes

- A Lezer grammar is justified here: the visual editor needs the member/relation tree.
- Fold `class X { … }` and `namespace X { … }`.
- Completion contexts differ sharply: inside `{ }` offer visibility prefixes and
  classifiers; at line start offer statements; after a class name offer relation arrows.
- `~` is generic delimiter **and** package visibility. Disambiguate by position: leading
  `~` on a member is visibility, paired `~…~` is a generic.
- Diagnostic: a method return type written without the space before it (`deposit()bool`)
  is a silent misparse.
- Diagnostic: a generic containing a comma is unsupported and should be flagged, not
  passed through.

1	# State diagrams
2	
3	> "A state diagram is a type of diagram used in computer science and related fields to describe the behavior of systems.
4	> State diagrams require that the system described is composed of a finite number of states; sometimes, this is indeed the
5	> case, while at other times this is a reasonable abstraction." Wikipedia
6	
7	Mermaid can render state diagrams. The syntax tries to be compliant with the syntax used in plantUml as this will make
8	it easier for users to share diagrams between mermaid and plantUml.
9	
10	```mermaid-example
11	---
12	title: Simple sample
13	---
14	stateDiagram-v2
15	    [*] --> Still
16	    Still --> [*]
17	
18	    Still --> Moving
19	    Moving --> Still
20	    Moving --> Crash
21	    Crash --> [*]
22	```
23	
24	Older renderer:
25	
26	```mermaid-example
27	stateDiagram
28	    [*] --> Still
29	    Still --> [*]
30	
31	    Still --> Moving
32	    Moving --> Still
33	    Moving --> Crash
34	    Crash --> [*]
35	```
36	
37	In state diagrams systems are described in terms of _states_ and how one _state_ can change to another _state_ via
38	a _transition._ The example diagram above shows three states: **Still**, **Moving** and **Crash**. You start in the
39	**Still** state. From **Still** you can change to the **Moving** state. From **Moving** you can change either back to the **Still** state or to
40	the **Crash** state. There is no transition from **Still** to **Crash**. (You can't crash if you're still.)
41	
42	## States
43	
44	A state can be declared in multiple ways. The simplest way is to define a state with just an id:
45	
46	```mermaid-example
47	stateDiagram-v2
48	    stateId
49	```
50	
51	Another way is by using the state keyword with a description as per below:
52	
53	```mermaid-example
54	stateDiagram-v2
55	    state "This is a state description" as s2
56	```
57	
58	Another way to define a state with a description is to define the state id followed by a colon and the description:
59	
60	```mermaid-example
61	stateDiagram-v2
62	    s2 : This is a state description
63	```
64	
65	## Transitions
66	
67	Transitions are path/edges when one state passes into another. This is represented using text arrow, "\-\-\>".
68	
69	When you define a transition between two states and the states are not already defined, the undefined states are defined
70	with the id from the transition. You can later add descriptions to states defined this way.
71	
72	```mermaid-example
73	stateDiagram-v2
74	    s1 --> s2
75	```
76	
77	It is possible to add text to a transition to describe what it represents:
78	
79	```mermaid-example
80	stateDiagram-v2
81	    s1 --> s2: A transition
82	```
83	
84	## Start and End
85	
86	There are two special states indicating the start and stop of the diagram. These are written with the [\*] syntax and
87	the direction of the transition to it defines it either as a start or a stop state.
88	
89	```mermaid-example
90	stateDiagram-v2
91	    [*] --> s1
92	    s1 --> [*]
93	```
94	
95	## Composite states
96	
97	In a real world use of state diagrams you often end up with diagrams that are multidimensional as one state can
98	have several internal states. These are called composite states in this terminology.
99	
100	In order to define a composite state you need to use the state keyword followed by an id and the body of the composite
101	state between \{\}. You can name a composite state on a separate line just like a simple state. See the example below:
102	
103	```mermaid-example
104	stateDiagram-v2
105	    [*] --> First
106	    state First {
107	        [*] --> second
108	        second --> [*]
109	    }
110	
111	    [*] --> NamedComposite
112	    NamedComposite: Another Composite
113	    state NamedComposite {
114	        [*] --> namedSimple
115	        namedSimple --> [*]
116	        namedSimple: Another simple
117	    }
118	```
119	
120	You can do this in several layers:
121	
122	```mermaid-example
123	stateDiagram-v2
124	    [*] --> First
125	
126	    state First {
127	        [*] --> Second
128	
129	        state Second {
130	            [*] --> second
131	            second --> Third
132	
133	            state Third {
134	                [*] --> third
135	                third --> [*]
136	            }
137	        }
138	    }
139	```
140	
141	You can also define transitions also between composite states:
142	
143	```mermaid-example
144	stateDiagram-v2
145	    [*] --> First
146	    First --> Second
147	    First --> Third
148	
149	    state First {
150	        [*] --> fir
151	        fir --> [*]
152	    }
153	    state Second {
154	        [*] --> sec
155	        sec --> [*]
156	    }
157	    state Third {
158	        [*] --> thi
159	        thi --> [*]
160	    }
161	```
162	
163	_You cannot define transitions between internal states belonging to different composite states_
164	
165	## Choice
166	
167	Sometimes you need to model a choice between two or more paths, you can do so using <<choice>>.
168	
169	```mermaid-example
170	stateDiagram-v2
171	    state if_state <<choice>>
172	    [*] --> IsPositive
173	    IsPositive --> if_state
174	    if_state --> False: if n < 0
175	    if_state --> True : if n >= 0
176	```
177	
178	## Forks
179	
180	It is possible to specify a fork in the diagram using <<fork>> <<join>>.
181	
182	```mermaid-example
183	   stateDiagram-v2
184	    state fork_state <<fork>>
185	      [*] --> fork_state
186	      fork_state --> State2
187	      fork_state --> State3
188	
189	      state join_state <<join>>
190	      State2 --> join_state
191	      State3 --> join_state
192	      join_state --> State4
193	      State4 --> [*]
194	```
195	
196	## Notes
197	
198	Sometimes nothing says it better than a Post-it note. That is also the case in state diagrams.
199	
200	Here you can choose to put the note to the _right of_ or to the _left of_ a node.
201	
202	```mermaid-example
203	    stateDiagram-v2
204	        State1: The state with a note
205	        note right of State1
206	            Important information! You can write
207	            notes.
208	        end note
209	        State1 --> State2
210	        note left of State2 : This is the note to the left.
211	```
212	
213	## Concurrency
214	
215	As in plantUml you can specify concurrency using the -- symbol.
216	
217	```mermaid-example
218	stateDiagram-v2
219	    [*] --> Active
220	
221	    state Active {
222	        [*] --> NumLockOff
223	        NumLockOff --> NumLockOn : EvNumLockPressed
224	        NumLockOn --> NumLockOff : EvNumLockPressed
225	        --
226	        [*] --> CapsLockOff
227	        CapsLockOff --> CapsLockOn : EvCapsLockPressed
228	        CapsLockOn --> CapsLockOff : EvCapsLockPressed
229	        --
230	        [*] --> ScrollLockOff
231	        ScrollLockOff --> ScrollLockOn : EvScrollLockPressed
232	        ScrollLockOn --> ScrollLockOff : EvScrollLockPressed
233	    }
234	```
235	
236	## Setting the direction of the diagram
237	
238	With state diagrams you can use the direction statement to set the direction which the diagram will render like in this
239	example.
240	
241	```mermaid-example
242	stateDiagram
243	    direction LR
244	    [*] --> A
245	    A --> B
246	    B --> C
247	    state B {
248	      direction LR
249	      a --> b
250	    }
251	    B --> D
252	```
253	
254	## Comments
255	
256	Comments can be entered within a state diagram chart, which will be ignored by the parser. Comments must be prefaced with `%%` (double percent signs) and any text after their start to the next newline will be treated as a comment, including any diagram syntax. They can be on their own line or at the end of a statement.
257	
258	```mermaid
259	stateDiagram-v2
260	    [*] --> Still
261	    Still --> [*]
262	%% this is a comment
263	    Still --> Moving
264	    Moving --> Still %% another comment
265	    Moving --> Crash
266	    Crash --> [*]
267	```
268	
269	## Styling with classDefs
270	
271	As with other diagrams (like flowcharts), you can define a style in the diagram itself and apply that named style to a
272	state or states in the diagram.
273	
274	**These are the current limitations with state diagram classDefs:**
275	
276	1. Cannot be applied to start or end states
277	2. Cannot be applied to or within composite states
278	
279	_These are in development and will be available in a future version._
280	
281	You define a style using the `classDef` keyword, which is short for "class definition" (where "class" means something
282	like a _CSS class_)
283	followed by _a name for the style,_
284	and then one or more _property-value pairs_. Each _property-value pair_ is
285	a _[valid CSS property name](https://www.w3.org/TR/CSS/#properties)_ followed by a colon (`:`) and then a _value._
286	
287	Here is an example of a classDef with just one property-value pair:
288	
289	```txt
290	classDef movement font-style:italic;
291	```
292	
293	where
294	
295	- the _name_ of the style is `movement`
296	- the only _property_ is `font-style` and its _value_ is `italic`
297	
298	If you want to have more than one _property-value pair_ then you put a comma (`,`) between each _property-value pair._
299	
300	Here is an example with three property-value pairs:
301	
302	```txt
303	classDef badBadEvent fill:#f00,color:white,font-weight:bold,stroke-width:2px,stroke:yellow
304	```
305	
306	where
307	
308	- the _name_ of the style is `badBadEvent`
309	- the first _property_ is `fill` and its _value_ is `#f00`
310	- the second _property_ is `color` and its _value_ is `white`
311	- the third _property_ is `font-weight` and its _value_ is `bold`
312	- the fourth _property_ is `stroke-width` and its _value_ is `2px`
313	- the fifth _property_ is `stroke` and its _value_ is `yellow`
314	
315	### Apply classDef styles to states
316	
317	There are two ways to apply a `classDef` style to a state:
318	
319	1. use the `class` keyword to apply a classDef style to one or more states in a single statement, or
320	2. use the `:::` operator to apply a classDef style to a state as it is being used in a transition statement (e.g. with an arrow
321	   to/from another state)
322	
323	#### 1. `class` statement
324	
325	A `class` statement tells Mermaid to apply the named classDef to one or more classes. The form is:
326	
327	```txt
328	class [one or more state names, separated by commas] [name of a style defined with classDef]
329	```
330	
331	Here is an example applying the `badBadEvent` style to a state named `Crash`:
332	
333	```txt
334	class Crash badBadEvent
335	```
336	
337	Here is an example applying the `movement` style to the two states `Moving` and `Crash`:
338	
339	```txt
340	class Moving, Crash movement
341	```
342	
343	Here is a diagram that shows the examples in use. Note that the `Crash` state has two classDef styles applied: `movement`
344	and `badBadEvent`
345	
346	```mermaid-example
347	   stateDiagram
348	   direction TB
349	
350	   accTitle: This is the accessible title
351	   accDescr: This is an accessible description
352	
353	   classDef notMoving fill:white
354	   classDef movement font-style:italic
355	   classDef badBadEvent fill:#f00,color:white,font-weight:bold,stroke-width:2px,stroke:yellow
356	
357	   [*]--> Still
358	   Still --> [*]
359	   Still --> Moving
360	   Moving --> Still
361	   Moving --> Crash
362	   Crash --> [*]
363	
364	   class Still notMoving
365	   class Moving, Crash movement
366	   class Crash badBadEvent
367	   class end badBadEvent
368	```
369	
370	#### 2. `:::` operator to apply a style to a state
371	
372	You can apply a classDef style to a state using the `:::` (three colons) operator. The syntax is
373	
374	```txt
375	[state]:::[style name]
376	```
377	
378	You can use this in a diagram within a statement using a class. This includes the start and end states. For example:
379	
380	```mermaid-example
381	stateDiagram
382	   direction TB
383	
384	   accTitle: This is the accessible title
385	   accDescr: This is an accessible description
386	
387	   classDef notMoving fill:white
388	   classDef movement font-style:italic;
389	   classDef badBadEvent fill:#f00,color:white,font-weight:bold,stroke-width:2px,stroke:yellow
390	
391	   [*] --> Still:::notMoving
392	   Still --> [*]
393	   Still --> Moving:::movement
394	   Moving --> Still
395	   Moving --> Crash:::movement
396	   Crash:::badBadEvent --> [*]
397	```
398	
399	## Spaces in state names
400	
401	Spaces can be added to a state by first defining the state with an id and then referencing the id later.
402	
403	In the following example there is a state with the id **yswsii** and description **Your state with spaces in it**.
404	After it has been defined, **yswsii** is used in the diagram in the first transition (`[*] --> yswsii`)
405	and also in the transition to **YetAnotherState** (`yswsii --> YetAnotherState`).
406	(**yswsii** has been styled so that it is different from the other states.)
407	
408	```mermaid-example
409	stateDiagram
410	    classDef yourState font-style:italic,font-weight:bold,fill:white
411	
412	    yswsii: Your state with spaces in it
413	    [*] --> yswsii:::yourState
414	    [*] --> SomeOtherState
415	    SomeOtherState --> YetAnotherState
416	    yswsii --> YetAnotherState
417	    YetAnotherState --> [*]
418	```
419	
420	<!--- cspell:ignore yswsii --->
421

# State Diagram

**Source**: `mermaid-upstream/packages/mermaid/src/docs/syntax/stateDiagram.md` (420 lines)
**Detector**: `src/diagrams/state/stateDetector-V2.ts` — `/^\s*stateDiagram-v2/`, `/^\s*stateDiagram/`
**Registry id**: `state`

Syntax deliberately tracks PlantUML so diagrams can be shared between the two (`:7-8`).

## Header

`stateDiagram-v2` (current renderer) or `stateDiagram` (older renderer). Both render the
same source; offer `-v2` as the canonical completion.

## States (`:42-63`)

Three equivalent declarations:

```
stateId
state "This is a state description" as s2
s2 : This is a state description
```

Special states: `[*]` is start or end depending on transition direction (`:84-93`).

**Spaces in a state name require the id-then-description form** (`:399-418`): declare
`yswsii: Your state with spaces in it`, then reference `yswsii`.

## Transitions (`:65-82`)

`s1 --> s2`, with optional label `s1 --> s2: A transition`. Undefined states are created
implicitly by the transition and can be described later.

## Composite States (`:95-163`)

```
state First {
    [*] --> second
    second --> [*]
}
```

Nestable to arbitrary depth. Transitions between composite states are allowed;
**transitions between internal states of different composite states are not** (`:163`).

## Special Nodes

- `state if_state <<choice>>` (`:165-176`)
- `state fork_state <<fork>>` / `state join_state <<join>>` (`:178-194`)

## Notes (`:196-211`)

Two forms, `right of` and `left of` only — no `over`:

```
note right of State1
    multi-line body
end note

note left of State2 : single line
```

## Concurrency (`:213-234`)

`--` on its own line inside a composite state separates concurrent regions. This is the
same token as part of an arrow, so tokenization must treat a bare `--` line as a region
separator, not a malformed transition.

## Direction (`:236-252`)

`direction LR` at diagram level and inside composite states.

## Comments (`:254-267`)

`%%`, on their own line **or at the end of a statement** — unlike flowchart and class,
where comments must occupy the whole line.

## Styling (`:269-397`)

`classDef name prop:value,prop:value`, applied either with `class` or `:::`.

- `class Crash badBadEvent`
- `class Moving, Crash movement` — comma-separated, spaces allowed after the comma
- `[*] --> Still:::notMoving` — `:::` works inline in a transition

**Documented limitations of `classDef`** (`:274-279`):

1. Cannot be applied to start or end states.
2. Cannot be applied to, or within, composite states.

Upstream calls these in development. Note the tension: `:::` is documented as working on
start and end states (`:378`), while limitation 1 says it does not. Verify empirically
before writing a diagnostic — do not encode either claim as fact yet.

## Accessibility

`accTitle:` and `accDescr:` appear in the examples (`:350-351`) and are the standard
mermaid accessibility directives, shared across diagram types.

## Editor Notes

- Fold `state X { … }` and `note … end note`.
- A Lezer grammar is justified: the visual editor needs the nesting tree.
- Completion after `state <id>` should offer `<<choice>>`, `<<fork>>`, `<<join>>`.
- Distinguish a bare `--` line (concurrency) from `-->` at tokenization time.
- Identifier completion should include implicitly created states, not just declared ones.

1	# Entity Relationship Diagrams
2	
3	> An entity–relationship model (or ER model) describes interrelated things of interest in a specific domain of knowledge. A basic ER model is composed of entity types (which classify the things of interest) and specifies relationships that can exist between entities (instances of those entity types) [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Entity%E2%80%93relationship_model).
4	
5	Note that practitioners of ER modelling almost always refer to _entity types_ simply as _entities_. For example the `CUSTOMER` entity _type_ would be referred to simply as the `CUSTOMER` entity. This is so common it would be inadvisable to do anything else, but technically an entity is an abstract _instance_ of an entity type, and this is what an ER diagram shows - abstract instances, and the relationships between them. This is why entities are always named using singular nouns.
6	
7	Mermaid can render ER diagrams
8	
9	```mermaid-example
10	---
11	title: Order example
12	---
13	erDiagram
14	    CUSTOMER ||--o{ ORDER : places
15	    ORDER ||--|{ LINE-ITEM : contains
16	    CUSTOMER }|..|{ DELIVERY-ADDRESS : uses
17	```
18	
19	Entity names are often capitalised, although there is no accepted standard on this, and it is not required in Mermaid.
20	
21	Relationships between entities are represented by lines with end markers representing cardinality. Mermaid uses the most popular crow's foot notation. The crow's foot intuitively conveys the possibility of many instances of the entity that it connects to.
22	
23	ER diagrams can be used for various purposes, ranging from abstract logical models devoid of any implementation details, through to physical models of relational database tables. It can be useful to include attribute definitions on ER diagrams to aid comprehension of the purpose and meaning of entities. These do not necessarily need to be exhaustive; often a small subset of attributes is enough. Mermaid allows them to be defined in terms of their _type_ and _name_.
24	
25	```mermaid-example
26	erDiagram
27	    CUSTOMER ||--o{ ORDER : places
28	    CUSTOMER {
29	        string name
30	        string custNumber
31	        string sector
32	    }
33	    ORDER ||--|{ LINE-ITEM : contains
34	    ORDER {
35	        int orderNumber
36	        string deliveryAddress
37	    }
38	    LINE-ITEM {
39	        string productCode
40	        int quantity
41	        float pricePerUnit
42	    }
43	```
44	
45	When including attributes on ER diagrams, you must decide whether to include foreign keys as attributes. This probably depends on how closely you are trying to represent relational table structures. If your diagram is a _logical_ model which is not meant to imply a relational implementation, then it is better to leave these out because the associative relationships already convey the way that entities are associated. For example, a JSON data structure can implement a one-to-many relationship without the need for foreign key properties, using arrays. Similarly an object-oriented programming language may use pointers or references to collections. Even for models that are intended for relational implementation, you might decide that inclusion of foreign key attributes duplicates information already portrayed by the relationships, and does not add meaning to entities. Ultimately, it's your choice.
46	
47	## Syntax
48	
49	### Entities and Relationships
50	
51	Mermaid syntax for ER diagrams is compatible with PlantUML, with an extension to label the relationship. Each statement consists of the following parts:
52	
53	```
54	    <first-entity> [<relationship> <second-entity> : <relationship-label>]
55	```
56	
57	Where:
58	
59	- `first-entity` is the name of an entity. Names support any unicode characters and can include spaces if surrounded by double quotes (e.g. "name with space").
60	- `relationship` describes the way that both entities inter-relate. See below.
61	- `second-entity` is the name of the other entity.
62	- `relationship-label` describes the relationship from the perspective of the first entity.
63	
64	For example:
65	
66	```
67	    PROPERTY ||--|{ ROOM : contains
68	```
69	
70	This statement can be read as _a property contains one or more rooms, and a room is part of one and only one property_. You can see that the label here is from the first entity's perspective: a property contains a room, but a room does not contain a property. When considered from the perspective of the second entity, the equivalent label is usually very easy to infer. (Some ER diagrams label relationships from both perspectives, but this is not supported here, and is usually superfluous).
71	
72	Only the `first-entity` part of a statement is mandatory. This makes it possible to show an entity with no relationships, which can be useful during iterative construction of diagrams. If any other parts of a statement are specified, then all parts are mandatory.
73	
74	#### Unicode text
75	
76	Entity names, relationships, and attributes all support unicode text.
77	
78	```mermaid-example
79	erDiagram
80	    "This ❤ Unicode"
81	```
82	
83	#### Markdown formatting
84	
85	Markdown formatting and text is also supported.
86	
87	```mermaid-example
88	erDiagram
89	    "This **is** _Markdown_"
90	```
91	
92	### Relationship Syntax
93	
94	The `relationship` part of each statement can be broken down into three sub-components:
95	
96	- the cardinality of the first entity with respect to the second
97	- whether the relationship confers identity on a 'child' entity
98	- the cardinality of the second entity with respect to the first
99	
100	Cardinality is a property that describes how many elements of another entity can be related to the entity in question. In the above example a `PROPERTY` can have one or more `ROOM` instances associated to it, whereas a `ROOM` can only be associated with one `PROPERTY`. In each cardinality marker there are two characters. The outermost character represents a maximum value, and the innermost character represents a minimum value. The table below summarises possible cardinalities.
101	
102	| Value (left) | Value (right) | Meaning                       |
103	| :----------: | :-----------: | ----------------------------- |
104	|    `\|o`     |     `o\|`     | Zero or one                   |
105	|    `\|\|`    |    `\|\|`     | Exactly one                   |
106	|     `}o`     |     `o{`      | Zero or more (no upper limit) |
107	|    `}\|`     |     `\|{`     | One or more (no upper limit)  |
108	
109	**Aliases**
110	
111	| Value (left) | Value (right) | Alias for    |
112	| :----------: | :-----------: | ------------ |
113	| one or zero  |  one or zero  | Zero or one  |
114	| zero or one  |  zero or one  | Zero or one  |
115	| one or more  |  one or more  | One or more  |
116	| one or many  |  one or many  | One or more  |
117	|   many(1)    |    many(1)    | One or more  |
118	|      1+      |      1+       | One or more  |
119	| zero or more | zero or more  | Zero or more |
120	| zero or many | zero or many  | Zero or more |
121	|   many(0)    |    many(0)    | Zero or more |
122	|      0+      |      0+       | Zero or more |
123	|   only one   |   only one    | Exactly one  |
124	|      1       |       1       | Exactly one  |
125	
126	### Identification
127	
128	Relationships may be classified as either _identifying_ or _non-identifying_ and these are rendered with either solid or dashed lines respectively. This is relevant when one of the entities in question cannot have independent existence without the other. For example a firm that insures people to drive cars might need to store data on `NAMED-DRIVER`s. In modelling this we might start out by observing that a `CAR` can be driven by many `PERSON` instances, and a `PERSON` can drive many `CAR`s - both entities can exist without the other, so this is a non-identifying relationship that we might specify in Mermaid as: `PERSON }|..|{ CAR : "driver"`. Note the two dots in the middle of the relationship that will result in a dashed line being drawn between the two entities. But when this many-to-many relationship is resolved into two one-to-many relationships, we observe that a `NAMED-DRIVER` cannot exist without both a `PERSON` and a `CAR` - the relationships become identifying and would be specified using hyphens, which translate to a solid line:
129	
130	| Value |     Alias for     |
131	| :---: | :---------------: |
132	|  --   |   _identifying_   |
133	|  ..   | _non-identifying_ |
134	
135	**Aliases**
136	
137	|     Value     |     Alias for     |
138	| :-----------: | :---------------: |
139	|      to       |   _identifying_   |
140	| optionally to | _non-identifying_ |
141	
142	```mermaid-example
143	erDiagram
144	    CAR ||--o{ NAMED-DRIVER : allows
145	    PERSON }o..o{ NAMED-DRIVER : is
146	```
147	
148	```mermaid-example
149	erDiagram
150	    CAR 1 to zero or more NAMED-DRIVER : allows
151	    PERSON many(0) optionally to 0+ NAMED-DRIVER : is
152	```
153	
154	### Attributes
155	
156	Attributes can be defined for entities by specifying the entity name followed by a block containing multiple `type name` pairs, where a block is delimited by an opening `{` and a closing `}`. The attributes are rendered inside the entity boxes. For example:
157	
158	```mermaid-example
159	erDiagram
160	    CAR ||--o{ NAMED-DRIVER : allows
161	    CAR {
162	        string registrationNumber
163	        string make
164	        string model
165	    }
166	    PERSON ||--o{ NAMED-DRIVER : is
167	    PERSON {
168	        string firstName
169	        string lastName
170	        int age
171	    }
172	```
173	
174	The `type` values must begin with an alphabetic character and may contain digits, hyphens, underscores, parentheses and square brackets. The `name` values follow a similar format to `type`, but may start with an asterisk as another option to indicate an attribute is a primary key. Other than that, there are no restrictions, and there is no implicit set of valid data types.
175	
176	#### Optional attribute types (v11.16.0+)
177	
178	Attribute `type` values may end with `?` to indicate an optional or nullable type.
179	
180	```mermaid-example
181	erDiagram
182	    PERSON {
183	        string firstName
184	        string? middleName
185	        string lastName
186	    }
187	```
188	
189	### Entity Name Aliases
190	
191	An alias can be added to an entity using square brackets. If provided, the alias will be showed in the diagram instead of the entity name. Alias names follow all of the same rules as entity names.
192	
193	```mermaid-example
194	erDiagram
195	    p[Person] {
196	        string firstName
197	        string lastName
198	    }
199	    a["Customer Account"] {
200	        string email
201	    }
202	    p ||--o| a : has
203	```
204	
205	#### Attribute Keys and Comments
206	
207	Attributes may also have a `key` or comment defined. Keys can be `PK`, `FK` or `UK`, for Primary Key, Foreign Key or Unique Key (markdown formatting and unicode is not supported for keys). To specify multiple key constraints on a single attribute, separate them with a comma (e.g., `PK, FK`). A `comment` is defined by double quotes at the end of an attribute. Comments themselves cannot have double-quote characters in them.
208	
209	```mermaid-example
210	erDiagram
211	    CAR ||--o{ NAMED-DRIVER : allows
212	    CAR {
213	        string registrationNumber PK
214	        string make
215	        string model
216	        string[] parts
217	    }
218	    PERSON ||--o{ NAMED-DRIVER : is
219	    PERSON {
220	        string driversLicense PK "The license #"
221	        string(99) firstName "Only 99 characters are allowed"
222	        string lastName
223	        string phone UK
224	        int age
225	    }
226	    NAMED-DRIVER {
227	        string carRegistrationNumber PK, FK
228	        string driverLicence PK, FK
229	    }
230	    MANUFACTURER only one to zero or more CAR : makes
231	```
232	
233	### Direction
234	
235	The direction statement declares the direction of the diagram.
236	
237	This declares that the diagram is oriented from top to bottom (`TB`). This can be reversed to be oriented from bottom to top (`BT`).
238	
239	```mermaid-example
240	erDiagram
241	    direction TB
242	    CUSTOMER ||--o{ ORDER : places
243	    CUSTOMER {
244	        string name
245	        string custNumber
246	        string sector
247	    }
248	    ORDER ||--|{ LINE-ITEM : contains
249	    ORDER {
250	        int orderNumber
251	        string deliveryAddress
252	    }
253	    LINE-ITEM {
254	        string productCode
255	        int quantity
256	        float pricePerUnit
257	    }
258	```
259	
260	This declares that the diagram is oriented from left to right (`LR`). This can be reversed to be oriented from right to left (`RL`).
261	
262	```mermaid-example
263	erDiagram
264	    direction LR
265	    CUSTOMER ||--o{ ORDER : places
266	    CUSTOMER {
267	        string name
268	        string custNumber
269	        string sector
270	    }
271	    ORDER ||--|{ LINE-ITEM : contains
272	    ORDER {
273	        int orderNumber
274	        string deliveryAddress
275	    }
276	    LINE-ITEM {
277	        string productCode
278	        int quantity
279	        float pricePerUnit
280	    }
281	```
282	
283	Possible diagram orientations are:
284	
285	- TB - Top to bottom
286	- BT - Bottom to top
287	- RL - Right to left
288	- LR - Left to right
289	
290	### Subgraphs (v<MERMAID_RELEASE_VERSION>+)
291	
292	Subgraphs allow grouping entities into logical sections within an ER diagram. They are useful for organizing
293	complex diagrams and improving readability.
294	
295	Subgraphs can contain entities, relationships, and even other subgraphs (nested subgraphs).
296	
297	```
298	subgraph title
299	    graph definition
300	end
301	```
302	
303	An example below:
304	
305	```mermaid-example
306	erDiagram
307	    subgraph title1
308	        CUSTOMER
309	        CUSTOMER {
310	            string name
311	            string custNumber
312	            string sector
313	        }
314	    end
315	    subgraph title2
316	        CAR ||--o{ NAMED-DRIVER : allows
317	        subgraph title3
318	            PERSON
319	            PERSON {
320	                string firstName
321	                string lastName
322	                int age
323	            }
324	        end
325	    end
326	```
327	
328	A subgraph always has an `id`, and optionally a `title`.
329	
330	If the subgraph name is a single word, it is used as both id and title:
331	
332	```mermaid-example
333	erDiagram
334	    subgraph title1
335	        CUSTOMER
336	    end
337	```
338	
339	If the subgraph identifier contains more than one word, it must be written in `quotes`. In this case, the quoted value is used both as the id and the title.
340	
341	```mermaid-example
342	erDiagram
343	    subgraph "Customer Domain"
344	        CUSTOMER
345	    end
346	```
347	
348	You can also set an explicit id for the subgraph.
349	
350	```mermaid-example
351	erDiagram
352	    subgraph id1 [title 1]
353	        CUSTOMER
354	    end
355	```
356	
357	````note
358	Subgraphs are always referenced by their id, never by their title.
359	
360	This is important when defining relationships involving subgraphs.
361	
362	**If a subgraph id contains spaces, it must be referenced using quotes:**
363	
364	```"Customer Domain" ||--o{ ORDER : contains```
365	````
366	
367	#### Relationships involving subgraphs
368	
369	It is also possible to define relationships to and from subgraphs.
370	
371	```mermaid-example
372	erDiagram
373	    subgraph title1
374	        A1 ||--|| A2 : links
375	    end
376	
377	    subgraph title2
378	        B1 ||--|| B2 : links
379	    end
380	
381	    subgraph title3
382	        C1 ||--|| C2 : links
383	    end
384	
385	    title1 ||--|| title2 : links
386	    title2 ||--|| title3 : links
387	    title2 ||--|| C2 : links
388	```
389	
390	#### Direction in subgraphs
391	
392	A subgraph can define its own layout direction.
393	
394	```mermaid-example
395	erDiagram
396	    direction LR
397	    subgraph TOP
398	        direction TB
399	        subgraph B1
400	            direction RL
401	            I1 ||--|| F1 : links
402	        end
403	        subgraph B2
404	            direction BT
405	            I2 ||--|| F2 : links
406	        end
407	    end
408	    A ||--|| TOP : links
409	    TOP ||--|| B : links
410	    B1 ||--|| B2 : links
411	```
412	
413	### Styling a node
414	
415	It is possible to apply specific styles such as a thicker border or a different background color to a node.
416	
417	```mermaid-example
418	erDiagram
419	    id1||--||id2 : label
420	    style id1 fill:#f9f,stroke:#333,stroke-width:4px
421	    style id2 fill:#bbf,stroke:#f66,stroke-width:2px,color:#fff,stroke-dasharray: 5 5
422	```
423	
424	It is also possible to attach styles to a list of nodes in one statement:
425	
426	```
427	    style nodeId1,nodeId2 styleList
428	```
429	
430	#### Classes
431	
432	More convenient than defining the style every time is to define a class of styles and attach this class to the nodes that
433	should have a different look.
434	
435	A class definition looks like the example below:
436	
437	```
438	    classDef className fill:#f9f,stroke:#333,stroke-width:4px
439	```
440	
441	It is also possible to define multiple classes in one statement:
442	
443	```
444	    classDef firstClassName,secondClassName font-size:12pt
445	```
446	
447	Attachment of a class to a node is done as per below:
448	
449	```
450	    class nodeId1 className
451	```
452	
453	It is also possible to attach a class to a list of nodes in one statement:
454	
455	```
456	    class nodeId1,nodeId2 className
457	```
458	
459	Multiple classes can be attached at the same time as well:
460	
461	```
462	    class nodeId1,nodeId2 className1,className2
463	```
464	
465	A shorter form of adding a class is to attach the classname to the node using the `:::`operator as per below:
466	
467	```mermaid-example
468	erDiagram
469	    direction TB
470	    CAR:::someclass {
471	        string registrationNumber
472	        string make
473	        string model
474	    }
475	    PERSON:::someclass {
476	        string firstName
477	        string lastName
478	        int age
479	    }
480	    HOUSE:::someclass
481	
482	    classDef someclass fill:#f96
483	```
484	
485	This form can be used when declaring relationships between entities:
486	
487	```mermaid-example
488	erDiagram
489	    CAR {
490	        string registrationNumber
491	        string make
492	        string model
493	    }
494	    PERSON {
495	        string firstName
496	        string lastName
497	        int age
498	    }
499	    PERSON:::foo ||--|| CAR : owns
500	    PERSON o{--|| HOUSE:::bar : has
501	
502	    classDef foo stroke:#f00
503	    classDef bar stroke:#0f0
504	    classDef foobar stroke:#00f
505	```
506	
507	Similar to the class statement, the shorthand syntax can also apply multiple classes at once:
508	
509	```
510	    nodeId:::className1,className2
511	```
512	
513	### Default class
514	
515	If a class is named default it will be assigned to all classes without specific class definitions.
516	
517	```
518	    classDef default fill:#f9f,stroke:#333,stroke-width:4px;
519	```
520	
521	> **Note:** Custom styles from style or other class statements take priority and will overwrite the default styles. (e.g. The `default` class gives nodes a background color of pink but the `blue` class will give that node a background color of blue if applied.)
522	
523	```mermaid-example
524	erDiagram
525	    CAR {
526	        string registrationNumber
527	        string make
528	        string model
529	    }
530	    PERSON {
531	        string firstName
532	        string lastName
533	        int age
534	    }
535	    PERSON:::foo ||--|| CAR : owns
536	    PERSON o{--|| HOUSE:::bar : has
537	
538	    classDef default fill:#f9f,stroke-width:4px
539	    classDef foo stroke:#f00
540	    classDef bar stroke:#0f0
541	    classDef foobar stroke:#00f
542	```
543	
544	## Configuration
545	
546	### Layout
547	
548	The layout of the diagram is handled by [`render()`](../config/setup/mermaid/interfaces/Mermaid.md#render). The default layout is dagre.
549	
550	For larger or more-complex diagrams, you can alternatively apply the ELK (Eclipse Layout Kernel) layout using your YAML frontmatter's `config`. For more information, see [Customizing ELK Layout](../intro/syntax-reference.md#customizing-elk-layout).
551	
552	```yaml
553	---
554	config:
555	  layout: elk
556	---
557	```
558	
559	Your Mermaid code should be similar to the following:
560	
561	```mermaid-example
562	---
563	title: Order example
564	config:
565	    layout: elk
566	---
567	erDiagram
568	    CUSTOMER ||--o{ ORDER : places
569	    ORDER ||--|{ LINE-ITEM : contains
570	    CUSTOMER }|..|{ DELIVERY-ADDRESS : uses
571	```
572	
573	```note
574	Note that the site needs to use mermaid version 9.4+ for this to work and have this featured enabled in the lazy-loading configuration.
575	```
576	
577	<!--- cspell:locale en,en-gb --->

1	# User Journey Diagram
2	
3	> User journeys describe at a high level of detail exactly what steps different users take to complete a specific task within a system, application or website. This technique shows the current (as-is) user workflow, and reveals areas of improvement for the to-be workflow. (Wikipedia)
4	
5	Mermaid can render user journey diagrams:
6	
7	```mermaid-example
8	journey
9	    title My working day
10	    section Go to work
11	      Make tea: 5: Me
12	      Go upstairs: 3: Me
13	      Do work: 1: Me, Cat
14	    section Go home
15	      Go downstairs: 5: Me
16	      Sit down: 5: Me
17	```
18	
19	Each user journey is split into sections, these describe the part of the task
20	the user is trying to complete.
21	
22	Tasks syntax is `Task name: <score>: <comma separated list of actors>`
23	
24	Score is a number between 1 and 5, inclusive.

1	# Pie chart diagrams
2	
3	> A pie chart (or a circle chart) is a circular statistical graphic, which is divided into slices to illustrate numerical proportion. In a pie chart, the arc length of each slice (and consequently its central angle and area), is proportional to the quantity it represents. While it is named for its resemblance to a pie which has been sliced, there are variations on the way it can be presented. The earliest known pie chart is generally credited to William Playfair's Statistical Breviary of 1801
4	> -Wikipedia
5	
6	Mermaid can render Pie Chart diagrams.
7	
8	```mermaid-example
9	pie title Pets adopted by volunteers
10	    "Dogs" : 386
11	    "Cats" : 85
12	    "Rats" : 15
13	```
14	
15	## Syntax
16	
17	Drawing a pie chart is really simple in mermaid.
18	
19	- Start with `pie` keyword to begin the diagram
20	  - `showData` to render the actual data values after the legend text. This is **_OPTIONAL_**
21	- Followed by `title` keyword and its value in string to give a title to the pie-chart. This is **_OPTIONAL_**
22	- Followed by dataSet. Pie slices will be ordered clockwise in the same order as the labels.
23	  - `label` for a section in the pie diagram within `" "` quotes.
24	  - Followed by `:` colon as separator
25	  - Followed by `positive numeric value` (supported up to two decimal places)
26	
27	**Note:**
28	
29	> Pie chart values must be **positive numbers greater than zero**.
30	> **Negative values are not allowed** and will result in an error.
31	
32	[pie] [showData] (OPTIONAL)
33	[title] [titlevalue] (OPTIONAL)
34	"[datakey1]" : [dataValue1]
35	"[datakey2]" : [dataValue2]
36	"[datakey3]" : [dataValue3]
37	.
38	.
39	
40	## Donut chart diagram (v11.16.0+)
41	
42	By setting `donutHole` parameter on config, Mermaid can render Donut Chart Diagram.
43	
44	## Legend Position (v11.16.0+)
45	
46	By setting `legendPosition` parameter on config, you can set where the legend is positioned.
47	
48	## Highlight Slice (v11.16.0+)
49	
50	By setting `highlightSlice` parameter on config, you can highlight specific slice. You can also highlight slice by hovering on it.
51	
52	## Example
53	
54	```mermaid-example
55	---
56	config:
57	  pie:
58	    textPosition: 0.5
59	    donutHole: 0.2
60	    highlightSlice: Potassium
61	  themeVariables:
62	    pieOuterStrokeWidth: "5px"
63	---
64	pie showData
65	    title Key elements in Product X
66	    "Calcium" : 42.96
67	    "Potassium" : 50.05
68	    "Magnesium" : 10.01
69	    "Iron" :  5
70	```
71	
72	## Configuration
73	
74	Possible pie diagram configuration parameters:
75	
76	| Parameter        | Description                                                                                                  | Default value |
77	| ---------------- | ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------ | ------------- |
78	| `textPosition`   | The axial position of the pie slice labels, from 0.0 at the center to 1.0 at the outside edge of the circle. | `0.75`        |
79	| `donutHole`      | Donut hole ratio. Valid values are from `0` to `0.9`.                                                        | `0`           |
80	| `legendPosition` | Legend's position relative to the chart. Valid values are `top`, `bottom`, `left`, `right`, and `center`.    | `right`       |
81	| `highlightSlice` | Highlight specific slice with matching label. Set to 'hover' to highlight hovered slice.                     |               |

# Entity Relationship Diagram

**Source**: `mermaid-upstream/packages/mermaid/src/docs/syntax/entityRelationshipDiagram.md` (577 lines)
**Detector**: `src/diagrams/er/erDetector.ts` — `/^\s*erDiagram/`
**Registry id**: `er`

PlantUML-compatible, with an extension for relationship labels (`:51`). Crow's foot notation.

## Statement Shape (`:53-72`)

```
<first-entity> [<relationship> <second-entity> : <relationship-label>]
```

Only `first-entity` is mandatory — a lone entity with no relationship is valid, which
makes iterative construction possible. **If any other part is present, all parts become
mandatory** (`:72`).

Entity names accept any unicode and may contain spaces when double-quoted. Markdown
formatting is supported in names (`:74-90`).

## Cardinality (`:100-124`)

| Left | Right | Meaning |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `\|o` | `o\|` | Zero or one |
| `\|\|` | `\|\|` | Exactly one |
| `}o` | `o{` | Zero or more |
| `}\|` | `\|{` | One or more |

Outermost character is the maximum, innermost the minimum.

**Word aliases** — a distinctive ER feature worth full completion support:

- Zero or one: `one or zero`, `zero or one`
- One or more: `one or more`, `one or many`, `many(1)`, `1+`
- Zero or more: `zero or more`, `zero or many`, `many(0)`, `0+`
- Exactly one: `only one`, `1`

So `CAR 1 to zero or more NAMED-DRIVER : allows` is valid (`:148-152`).

## Identification (`:126-140`)

| Value | Meaning |
| --- | --- |
| `--` | identifying (solid line) |
| `..` | non-identifying (dashed line) |
| `to` | alias for identifying |
| `optionally to` | alias for non-identifying |

## Attributes (`:154-231`)

Block of `type name` pairs inside `{ }`.

- `type` must begin with a letter; may contain digits, hyphens, underscores, parentheses
  and square brackets — so `string(99)` and `string[]` are valid.
- `name` follows the same rules and may additionally start with `*` to mark a primary key.
- There is **no implicit set of valid data types** (`:174`) — do not validate type names.
- **Optional types (v11.16.0+)**: a trailing `?`, e.g. `string? middleName`.
- Keys: `PK`, `FK`, `UK`, combinable with a comma — `PK, FK`. Keys do not support markdown
  or unicode.
- Comment: a double-quoted string at the end of the attribute. **Comments cannot contain
  double quotes** (`:207`).

## Entity Aliases (`:189-203`)

`p[Person] { … }` or `a["Customer Account"] { … }`. The alias displays instead of the
entity name and follows the same naming rules.

## Direction (`:233-288`)

`direction TB | BT | RL | LR`.

## Subgraphs

Version gate is the unresolved placeholder `v<MERMAID_RELEASE_VERSION>+` (`:290`).

```
subgraph title
    graph definition
end
```

- Nestable. May contain entities, relationships and other subgraphs.
- One-word name is used as both id and title.
- A multi-word identifier must be quoted; the quoted value becomes both id and title.
- Explicit id: `subgraph id1 [title 1]`.
- **Subgraphs are always referenced by id, never by title** (`:358`), and an id with
  spaces must be quoted in relationships: `"Customer Domain" ||--o{ ORDER : contains`.
- Subgraphs can take part in relationships and can set their own `direction`.

## Styling (`:413-542`)

- `style id1 fill:…`, and lists: `style nodeId1,nodeId2 styleList`
- `classDef className …`, multiple: `classDef firstName,secondName font-size:12pt`
- `class nodeId1 className`, lists, and **multiple classes at once**:
  `class nodeId1,nodeId2 className1,className2`
- `:::` shorthand, including multiple: `nodeId:::className1,className2`, usable on an
  entity with or without an attribute block, and inside a relationship statement.
- `classDef default` applies to unstyled nodes; explicit styles and classes override it.

Note the divergence: ER uses `class nodeId className` (unquoted, like flowchart), while
the class diagram uses `cssClass "nodeId" className`. Easy to get wrong across dialects.

## Configuration (`:544-575`)

`config.layout: elk` for larger diagrams; default is dagre. Requires v9.4+.

## Editor Notes

- Completion for cardinality should offer **both** the symbol forms and the word aliases,
  with the symbols first — they are what people actually type.
- Fold entity `{ … }` blocks and `subgraph` … `end`.
- Diagnostic: a partially-specified relationship (entity + arrow, no second entity or
  label) is an error, because partial statements are all-or-nothing.
- Diagnostic: a double quote inside an attribute comment.
- A Lezer grammar is justified — the visual editor needs entity and attribute structure.

```

| `legendPosition` | `top`, `bottom`, `left`, `right`, `center` | `right` |

`donutHole`, `legendPosition` and `highlightSlice` are all **v11.16.0+** (`:40-50`) — the
exact version this project pins, so they work but must be marked as very recent for users
on older runtimes.

Theme variable used in the example: `pieOuterStrokeWidth`.

- Simplest dialect in the product. A `StreamLanguage` with three tokens.
- Completion: `showData` only immediately after `pie`; `title` only on the second line.
