1	# Mermaid Kanban Diagram Documentation
2	
3	Mermaid’s Kanban diagram allows you to create visual representations of tasks moving through different stages of a workflow. This guide explains how to use the Kanban diagram syntax, based on the provided example.
4	
5	## Overview
6	
7	A Kanban diagram in Mermaid starts with the kanban keyword, followed by the definition of columns (stages) and tasks within those columns.
8	
9	```mermaid-example
10	kanban
11	  column1[Column Title]
12	    task1[Task Description]
13	```
14	
15	## Defining Columns
16	
17	Columns represent the different stages in your workflow, such as “Todo,” “In Progress,” “Done,” etc. Each column is defined using a unique identifier and a title enclosed in square brackets.
18	
19	**Syntax:**
20	
21	```
22	columnId[Column Title]
23	```
24	
25	- columnId: A unique identifier for the column.
26	- [Column Title]: The title displayed on the column header.
27	
28	Like this `id1[Todo]`
29	
30	## Adding Tasks to Columns
31	
32	Tasks are listed under their respective columns with an indentation. Each task also has a unique identifier and a description enclosed in square brackets.
33	
34	**Syntax:**
35	
36	```
37	taskId[Task Description]
38	```
39	
40	    •	taskId: A unique identifier for the task.
41	    •	[Task Description]: The description of the task.
42	
43	**Example:**
44	
45	```
46	docs[Create Documentation]
47	```
48	
49	## Adding Metadata to Tasks
50	
51	You can include additional metadata for each task using the @{ ... } syntax. Metadata can contain key-value pairs like assigned, ticket, priority, etc. This will be rendered added to the rendering of the node.
52	
53	## Supported Metadata Keys
54	
55	    •	assigned: Specifies who is responsible for the task.
56	    •	ticket: Links the task to a ticket or issue number.
57	    •	priority: Indicates the urgency of the task. Allowed values: 'Very High', 'High', 'Low' and 'Very Low'
58	
59	```mermaid-example
60	kanban
61	todo[Todo]
62	  id3[Update Database Function]@{ ticket: MC-2037, assigned: 'knsv', priority: 'High' }
63	```
64	
65	## Configuration Options
66	
67	You can customize the Kanban diagram using a configuration block at the beginning of your markdown file. This is useful for setting global settings like a base URL for tickets. Currently there is one configuration option for kanban diagrams `ticketBaseUrl`. This can be set as in the following example:
68	
69	```yaml
70	---
71	config:
72	  kanban:
73	    ticketBaseUrl: 'https://yourproject.atlassian.net/browse/#TICKET#'
74	---
75	```
76	
77	When the kanban item has an assigned ticket number the ticket number in the diagram will have a link to an external system where the ticket is defined. The `ticketBaseUrl` sets the base URL to the external system and #TICKET# is replaced with the ticket value from task metadata to create a valid link.
78	
79	## Full Example
80	
81	Below is the full Kanban diagram based on the provided example:
82	
83	```mermaid-example
84	---
85	config:
86	  kanban:
87	    ticketBaseUrl: 'https://mermaidchart.atlassian.net/browse/#TICKET#'
88	---
89	kanban
90	  Todo
91	    [Create Documentation]
92	    docs[Create Blog about the new diagram]
93	  [In progress]
94	    id6[Create renderer so that it works in all cases. We also add some extra text here for testing purposes. And some more just for the extra flare.]
95	  id9[Ready for deploy]
96	    id8[Design grammar]@{ assigned: 'knsv' }
97	  id10[Ready for test]
98	    id4[Create parsing tests]@{ ticket: MC-2038, assigned: 'K.Sveidqvist', priority: 'High' }
99	    id66[last item]@{ priority: 'Very Low', assigned: 'knsv' }
100	  id11[Done]
101	    id5[define getData]
102	    id2[Title of diagram is more than 100 chars when user duplicates diagram with 100 char]@{ ticket: MC-2036, priority: 'Very High'}
103	    id3[Update DB function]@{ ticket: MC-2037, assigned: knsv, priority: 'High' }
104	
105	  id12[Can't reproduce]
106	    id3[Weird flickering in Firefox]
107	```
108	
109	In conclusion, creating a Kanban diagram in Mermaid is a straightforward process that effectively visualizes your workflow. Start by using the kanban keyword to initiate the diagram. Define your columns with unique identifiers and titles to represent different stages of your project. Under each column, list your tasks—also with unique identifiers—and provide detailed descriptions as needed. Remember that proper indentation is crucial; tasks must be indented under their parent columns to maintain the correct structure.
110	
111	You can enhance your diagram by adding optional metadata to tasks using the @{ ... } syntax, which allows you to include additional context such as assignee, ticket numbers, and priority levels. For further customization, utilize the configuration block at the top of your file to set global options like ticketBaseUrl for linking tickets directly from your diagram.
112	
113	By adhering to these guidelines—ensuring unique identifiers, proper indentation, and utilizing metadata and configuration options—you can create a comprehensive and customized Kanban board that effectively maps out your project’s workflow using Mermaid.
114

1	# Packet Diagram (v11.0.0+)
2	
3	## Introduction
4	
5	A packet diagram is a visual representation used to illustrate the structure and contents of a network packet. Network packets are the fundamental units of data transferred over a network.
6	
7	## Usage
8	
9	This diagram type is particularly useful for developers, network engineers, educators, and students who require a clear and concise way to represent the structure of network packets.
10	
11	## Syntax
12	
13	```
14	packet
15	start: "Block name" %% Single-bit block
16	start-end: "Block name" %% Multi-bit blocks
17	... More Fields ...
18	```
19	
20	### Bits Syntax (v11.7.0+)
21	
22	Using start and end bit counts can be difficult, especially when modifying a design. For this we add a bit count field, which starts from the end of the previous field automagically. Use `+<count>` to set the number of bits, thus:
23	
24	```
25	packet
26	+1: "Block name" %% Single-bit block
27	+8: "Block name" %% 8-bit block
28	9-15: "Manually set start and end, it's fine to mix and match"
29	... More Fields ...
30	```
31	
32	## Examples
33	
34	```mermaid-example
35	---
36	title: "TCP Packet"
37	---
38	packet

1	# Venn diagrams (v11.12.3+)
2	
3	Venn diagrams show relationships between sets using overlapping circles.
4	
5	> **Warning**
6	> This is a new diagram type in Mermaid. Its syntax may evolve in future versions.
7	
8	## Syntax
9	
10	- Start with `venn-beta`.
11	- Use `set` for a single set name.
12	- Use `union` for an overlap of two or more set names.
13	- Identifiers in `union` must be defined by earlier `set` lines.
14	- Set identifiers can be bare words (`A`, `Set_1`) or quoted strings (`"Foo Bar"`).
15	
16	```mermaid-example
17	venn-beta
18	  title "Team overlap"
19	  set Frontend
20	  set Backend
21	  union Frontend,Backend["APIs"]
22	```
23	
24	### Labels
25	
26	Use bracket syntax `["..."]` to set a display label while keeping the identifier short:
27	
28	```mermaid-example
29	venn-beta
30	  set A["Alpha"]
31	  set B["Beta"]
32	  union A,B["AB"]
33	```
34	
35	### Higher-arity unions
36	
37	`union` accepts three or more set names. The diagram renders the implied
38	pairwise overlaps automatically, so the label on the higher-arity union has a
39	visible region to sit in:
40	
41	```mermaid-example
42	venn-beta
43	  set Desirable
44	  set Feasible
45	  set Viable
46	  union Desirable,Feasible,Viable["Innovation"]
47	```
48	
49	### Sizes
50	
51	Use `:N` suffix to set the size of a set or union:
52	
53	```mermaid-example
54	venn-beta
55	  set A["Alpha"]:20
56	  set B["Beta"]:12
57	  union A,B["AB"]:3
58	```
59	
60	### Text nodes
61	
62	- Use `text` to place labels inside a set or union.
63	- Indented `text` lines attach to the most recent `set` or `union`.
64	- Use bracket syntax `["..."]` to set a display label for text nodes.
65	
66	```mermaid-example
67	venn-beta
68	  set A["Frontend"]
69	    text A1["React"]
70	    text A2["Design Systems"]
71	  set B["Backend"]
72	    text B1["API"]
73	  union A,B["Shared"]
74	    text AB1["OpenAPI"]
75	```
76	
77	### Styling
78	
79	Use `style` statements to apply visual styles to sets, unions, and text nodes:
80	
81	- `fill`: change the fill color
82	- `color`: change the text color
83	- `stroke`: change the stroke color
84	- `stroke-width`: change the stroke width
85	- `fill-opacity`: change the fill opacity
86	
87	```mermaid-example
88	venn-beta
89	  set A["Alpha"]:20
90	    text A1["React"]
91	    text A2["Design Systems"]
92	  set B["Beta"]:12
93	  union A,B["AB"]:3
94	  style A fill:#ff6b6b
95	  style A,B color:#333
96	  style A1 color:red
97	```
98

1	# Ishikawa diagram (v11.12.3+)
2	
3	Ishikawa diagrams are used to represent causes of a specific event (or a problem).
4	They are also known as fishbone diagrams, herringbone diagrams or cause-and-effect diagrams.
5	The diagram resembles a fish skeleton, with the main problem at the head and the causes branching off from the spine.
6	
7	```warning
8	This is a new diagram type in Mermaid. Its syntax may evolve in future versions.
9	```
10	
11	## Syntax
12	
13	```mermaid
14	ishikawa-beta
15	    Blurry Photo
16	    Process
17	        Out of focus
18	        Shutter speed too slow
19	        Protective film not removed
20	        Beautification filter applied
21	    User
22	        Shaky hands
23	    Equipment
24	        LENS
25	            Inappropriate lens
26	            Damaged lens
27	            Dirty lens
28	        SENSOR
29	            Damaged sensor
30	            Dirty sensor
31	    Environment
32	        Subject moved too quickly
33	        Too dark
34	```
35	
36	- The first line is the event (problem) of the diagram.
37	- Subsequent lines are causes of the event.
38	- "Fishbone" structure is indicated by indentation.

Indentation-structured, like mindmap. Columns at one level, tasks indented under them.

```
kanban

    taskId[Task Description]
```

- Column: `columnId[Column Title]` (`:19-28`).
- Task: `taskId[Task Description]`, indented under its column (`:34-47`).

  render. The prose does not say this; the example does.
- **Indentation is load-bearing** (`:109`). A task not indented under a column becomes a
  column.

## Task Metadata (`:49-63`)

```
id3[Update Database Function]@{ ticket: MC-2037, assigned: 'knsv', priority: 'High' }
```

Documented keys:

| Key | Meaning |
| --- | --- |
| `assigned` | Who is responsible |
| `ticket` | Ticket or issue number |
| `priority` | `'Very High'`, `'High'`, `'Low'`, `'Very Low'` |

Note there is **no `'Medium'`** in the allowed priority list (`:57`) — an easy wrong
assumption and worth a diagnostic. Values may be quoted or bare: the example uses both
`assigned: 'knsv'` and `assigned: knsv` (`:96`, `:103`).

## Configuration (`:65-77`)

| Parameter | Meaning |
| --- | --- |
| `kanban.ticketBaseUrl` | Base URL for ticket links; `#TICKET#` is replaced with the task's `ticket` value |

Example: `'https://yourproject.atlassian.net/browse/#TICKET#'`.

> Under `securityLevel: 'strict'` the generated ticket link should be checked before it
> is rendered as an anchor — `ticketBaseUrl` is user-supplied text that becomes an `href`.

  make duplicate ids an error without checking the grammar first.

It is often created around a single concept, drawn as an image in the center of a blank page, to which associated representations of ideas such as images, words and parts of words are added. Major ideas are connected directly to the central concept, and other ideas branch out from those major ideas." Wikipedia 6 7 ### An example of a mindmap. 8 9 ```mermaid 10 mindmap 11 root((mindmap)) 12 Origins 13 Long history 14 ::icon(fa fa-book) 15 Popularisation 16 British popular psychology author Tony Buzan 17 Research 18 On effectiveness
and features 19 On Automatic creation 20 Uses 21 Creative techniques 22 Strategic planning 23 Argument mapping 24 Tools 25 Pen and paper 26 Mermaid 27 28 ``` 29 30 ## Syntax 31 32 The syntax for creating Mindmaps is simple and relies on indentation for setting the levels in the hierarchy. 33 34 In the following example you can see how there are 3 different levels. One with starting at the left of the text and another level with two rows starting at the same column, defining the node A. At the end there is one more level where the text is indented further than the previous lines defining the nodes B and C. 35 36 ``` 37 mindmap 38 Root 39 A 40 B 41 C 42 ``` 43 44 In summary is a simple text outline where there is one node at the root level called `Root` which has one child `A`. `A` in turn has two children `B`and `C`. In the diagram below we can see this rendered as a mindmap. 45 46 ```mermaid 47 mindmap 48 Root 49 A 50 B 51 C 52 ``` 53 54 In this way we can use a text outline to generate a hierarchical mindmap. 55 56 ## Different shapes 57 58 Mermaid mindmaps can show nodes using different shapes. When specifying a shape for a node the syntax is similar to flowchart nodes, with an id followed by the shape definition and with the text within the shape delimiters. Where possible we try/will try to keep the same shapes as for flowcharts, even though they are not all supported from the start. 59 60 Mindmap can show the following shapes: 61 62 ### Square 63 64 ```mermaid-example 65 mindmap 66 id[I am a square] 67 ``` 68 69 ### Rounded square 70 71 ```mermaid-example 72 mindmap 73 id(I am a rounded square) 74 ``` 75 76 ### Circle 77 78 ```mermaid-example 79 mindmap 80 id((I am a circle)) 81 ``` 82 83 ### Bang 84 85 ```mermaid-example 86 mindmap 87 id))I am a bang(( 88 ``` 89 90 ### Cloud 91 92 ```mermaid-example 93 mindmap 94 id)I am a cloud( 95 ``` 96 97 ### Hexagon 98 99 ```mermaid-example 100 mindmap 101 id{{I am a hexagon}} 102 ``` 103 104 ### Default 105 106 ```mermaid-example 107 mindmap 108 I am the default shape 109 ``` 110 111 More shapes will be added, beginning with the shapes available in flowcharts. 112 113 # Icons and classes 114 115 ## Icons 116 117 As with flowcharts you can add icons to your nodes but with an updated syntax. The styling for the font based icons are added during the integration so that they are available for the web page. _This is not something a diagram author can do but has to be done with the site administrator or the integrator_. Once the icon fonts are in place you add them to the mind map nodes using the `::icon()` syntax. You place the classes for the icon within the parenthesis like in the following example where icons for material design and [Font Awesome 5](https://fontawesome.com/v5/search?o=r&m=free) are displayed. The intention is that this approach should be used for all diagrams supporting icons. **Experimental feature:** This wider scope is also the reason Mindmaps are experimental as this syntax and approach could change. 118 119 ```mermaid-example 120 mindmap 121 Root 122 A 123 ::icon(fa fa-book) 124 B(B) 125 ::icon(mdi mdi-skull-outline) 126 ``` 127 128 ## Classes 129 130 Again the syntax for adding classes is similar to flowcharts. 1	# Radar Diagram (v11.6.0+)
2	
3	## Introduction
4	
5	A radar diagram is a simple way to plot low-dimensional data in a circular format.
6	
7	It is also known as a **radar chart**, **spider chart**, **star chart**, **cobweb chart**, **polar chart**, or **Kiviat diagram**.
8	
9	## Usage
10	
11	This diagram type is particularly useful for developers, data scientists, and engineers who require a clear and concise way to represent data in a circular format.
12	
13	It is commonly used to graphically summarize and compare the performance of multiple entities across multiple dimensions.
14	
15	## Syntax
16	
17	```md
18	radar-beta
19	axis A, B, C, D, E
20	curve c1{1,2,3,4,5}
21	curve c2{5,4,3,2,1}
22	... More Fields ...
23	```
24	
25	## Examples
26	
27	```mermaid-example
28	---
29	title: "Grades"
30	---
31	radar-beta
32	  axis m["Math"], s["Science"], e["English"]
33	  axis h["History"], g["Geography"], a["Art"]
34	  curve a["Alice"]{85, 90, 80, 70, 75, 90}
35	  curve b["Bob"]{70, 75, 85, 80, 90, 85}
36	
37	  max 100
38	  min 0
39	```
40	
41	```mermaid-example
42	radar-beta
43	  title Restaurant Comparison
44	  axis food["Food Quality"], service["Service"], price["Price"]
45	  axis ambiance["Ambiance"]
46	
47	  curve a["Restaurant A"]{4, 3, 2, 4}
48	  curve b["Restaurant B"]{3, 4, 3, 3}
49	  curve c["Restaurant C"]{2, 3, 4, 2}
50	  curve d["Restaurant D"]{2, 2, 4, 3}
51	
52	  graticule polygon
53	  max 5
54	
55	```
56	
57	## Details of Syntax
58	
59	### Title
60	
61	`title`: The title is an optional field that allows to render a title at the top of the radar diagram.
62	
63	```
64	radar-beta
65	  title Title of the Radar Diagram
66	  ...
67	```
68	
69	### Axis
70	
71	`axis`: The axis keyword is used to define the axes of the radar diagram.
72	
73	Each axis is represented by an ID and an optional label.
74	
75	Multiple axes can be defined in a single line.
76	
77	```
78	radar-beta
79	  axis id1["Label1"]
80	  axis id2["Label2"], id3["Label3"]
81	  ...
82	```
83	
84	### Curve
85	
86	`curve`: The curve keyword is used to define the data points for a curve in the radar diagram.
87	
88	Each curve is represented by an ID, an optional label, and a list of values.
89	
90	Values can be defined by a list of numbers or a list of key-value pairs. If key-value pairs are used, the key represents the axis ID and the value represents the data point. Else, the data points are assumed to be in the order of the axes defined.
91	
92	Multiple curves can be defined in a single line.
93	
94	```
95	radar-beta
96	  axis axis1, axis2, axis3
97	  curve id1["Label1"]{1, 2, 3}
98	  curve id2["Label2"]{4, 5, 6}, id3{7, 8, 9}
99	  curve id4{ axis3: 30, axis1: 20, axis2: 10 }
100	  ...
101	```
102	
103	### Options
104	
105	- `showLegend`: The showLegend keyword is used to show or hide the legend in the radar diagram. The legend is shown by default.
106	- `max`: The maximum value for the radar diagram. This is used to scale the radar diagram. If not provided, the maximum value is calculated from the data points.
107	- `min`: The minimum value for the radar diagram. This is used to scale the radar diagram. If not provided, the minimum value is `0`.
108	- `graticule`: The graticule keyword is used to define the type of graticule to be rendered in the radar diagram. The graticule can be `circle` or `polygon`. If not provided, the default graticule is `circle`.
109	- `ticks`: The ticks keyword is used to define the number of ticks on the graticule. It is the number of concentric circles or polygons drawn to indicate the scale of the radar diagram. If not provided, the default number of ticks is `5`.
110	
111	```

113	  ...
114	  showLegend true
115	  max 100
116	  min 0
117	  graticule circle
118	  ticks 5
119	  ...

1	# Cynefin Framework Diagram (v11.16.0+)
2	
3	> The Cynefin framework is a sense-making framework created by [Dave Snowden](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dave_Snowden) that categorizes problems into five complexity domains. It helps teams match their response to the nature of the situation they are facing. The name is Welsh for "place" or "habitat".
4	
5	You can read more at [The Cynefin Co](https://thecynefin.co/about-us/about-cynefin-framework).
6	
7	## Introduction
8	
9	The Cynefin framework divides the world into five domains, each with its own decision-making approach:
10	
11	- **Clear** (formerly Obvious/Simple): Cause and effect are obvious. Sense → Categorise → Respond. Apply **best practices**.
12	- **Complicated**: Cause and effect require analysis or expertise. Sense → Analyse → Respond. Apply **good practices**.
13	- **Complex**: Cause and effect can only be deduced in retrospect. Probe → Sense → Respond. Apply **emergent practices**.
14	- **Chaotic**: No perceivable cause and effect. Act → Sense → Respond. Apply **novel practices**.
15	- **Confusion** (or Disorder): You do not know which domain you are in. The goal is to move items out of this state into one of the other four.
16	
17	The signature visual feature is the wavy, organic boundary between the ordered (Clear, Complicated) and unordered (Complex, Chaotic) halves, and the "cliff" between Clear and Chaotic representing the risk of complacency leading to crisis.
18	
19	## Syntax
20	
21	A Cynefin diagram is declared with `cynefin-beta` followed by domain blocks and optional transitions.
22	
23	```md
24	cynefin-beta
25	title Optional Diagram Title
26	
27	complex
28	"Item label"
29	"Another item"
30	
31	complicated
32	"Expert analysis needed"
33	
34	clear
35	"Known procedure"
36	
37	chaotic
38	"Crisis response"
39	
40	confusion
41	"Item of unknown domain"
42	
43	complex --> complicated : "Pattern identified"
44	clear --> chaotic : "Complacency"
45	```
46	
47	### Keywords
48	
49	| Keyword        | Meaning                                                                |
50	| -------------- | ---------------------------------------------------------------------- |
51	| `cynefin-beta` | Diagram type declaration (required, first line after any front matter) |
52	| `title`        | Optional diagram title                                                 |
53	| `complex`      | Opens the Complex domain block                                         |
54	| `complicated`  | Opens the Complicated domain block                                     |
55	| `clear`        | Opens the Clear domain block                                           |
56	| `chaotic`      | Opens the Chaotic domain block                                         |
57	| `confusion`    | Opens the Confusion / Disorder domain block                            |
58	| `-->`          | Declares a transition from one domain to another                       |
59	
60	### Items
61	
62	Items are quoted string labels placed on their own lines inside a domain block. Each item renders as a text badge within the domain region.
63	
64	```
65	complex
66	  "Investigate root cause"
67	  "Run chaos experiment"
68	```
69	
70	Keep per-domain item lists short — the quadrants have fixed layout and long lists can visually overflow their boxes. The confusion ellipse caps at three items and shows a `+N more` badge; the four quadrant domains do not clip, so prefer a handful of items each.
71	
72	### Transitions
73	
74	Transitions represent movement of items between domains over time. They are declared at the top level using `-->` between two domain names, with an optional label.
75	
76	```
77	complex --> complicated : "Pattern identified"
78	clear --> chaotic : "Complacency"
79	chaotic --> complex : "Stabilized"
80	```
81	
82	Common transitions:
83	
84	- **Complex → Complicated**: An emerging pattern has become understood and can now be analyzed.
85	- **Chaotic → Complex**: A crisis has been stabilized enough to begin probing.
86	- **Clear → Chaotic**: Complacency or over-constraint has led to collapse (the "cliff").
87	- **Complicated → Clear**: Analysis has codified a solution into a standard practice.
88	
89	## Examples
90	
91	### Basic example
92	
93	```mermaid-example
94	cynefin-beta
95	  title Incident Response
96	
97	  complex
98	    "Investigate root cause"
99	    "Run chaos experiment"
100	
101	  complicated
102	    "Analyze performance data"
103	    "Expert review needed"
104	
105	  clear
106	    "Restart service"
107	    "Apply known fix"
108	
109	  chaotic
110	    "Page on-call immediately"
111	
112	  confusion
113	    "Unknown failure mode"
114	```
115	
116	### With transitions
117	
118	```mermaid-example
119	cynefin-beta
120	  title Strategy Categorization
121	
122	  complex
123	    "Market research"
124	
125	  complicated
126	    "Competitive analysis"
127	
128	  clear
129	    "Standard pricing"
130	
131	  chaotic
132	    "Crisis management"
133	
134	  complex --> complicated : "Pattern identified"
135	  complicated --> clear : "Best practice codified"
136	  clear --> chaotic : "Complacency"
137	  chaotic --> complex : "Stabilized"
138	```
139	
140	### Empty framework
141	
142	The domains themselves render even with no items, useful as a teaching or worksheet template.
143	
144	```mermaid-example
145	cynefin-beta
146	  title Cynefin Framework
147	
148	  complex
149	  complicated
150	  clear
151	  chaotic
152	```
153	
154	## Configuration
155	
156	Cynefin diagrams accept the following configuration under the `cynefin` key in the mermaid config:
157	
158	| Option                   | Type    | Default | Description                                                                                                                                                                                                                  |
159	| ------------------------ | ------- | ------- | ---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
160	| `width`                  | number  | `800`   | Width of the diagram in pixels                                                                                                                                                                                               |
161	| `height`                 | number  | `600`   | Height of the diagram in pixels                                                                                                                                                                                              |
162	| `padding`                | number  | `40`    | Padding around the diagram                                                                                                                                                                                                   |
163	| `showDomainDescriptions` | boolean | `true`  | Show decision model and practice type subtitles per domain                                                                                                                                                                   |
164	| `boundaryAmplitude`      | number  | `8`     | Waviness amplitude of domain boundaries in pixels (set to `0` for straight lines)                                                                                                                                            |
165	| `seed`                   | number  | `0`     | Deterministic seed for boundary waviness. `0` (default) hashes the diagram's SVG id so each diagram looks unique. Set any non-zero number to lock the waviness across renders — required for stable visual regression tests. |
166	
167	Example:
168	
169	```
170	---
171	config:
172	  cynefin:
173	    width: 1000
174	    showDomainDescriptions: false
175	---
176	cynefin-beta
177	  complex
178	    "Adaptive work"
179	```
180	
181	## Theming
182	
183	Cynefin diagrams use the following theme variables, which can be overridden via `themeVariables.cynefin`:
184	
185	| Variable         | Description                                      |
186	| ---------------- | ------------------------------------------------ |
187	| `complexBg`      | Background color for the Complex domain          |
188	| `complicatedBg`  | Background color for the Complicated domain      |
189	| `clearBg`        | Background color for the Clear domain            |
190	| `chaoticBg`      | Background color for the Chaotic domain          |
191	| `confusionBg`    | Background color for the Confusion center region |
192	| `boundaryColor`  | Color of the wavy domain boundaries              |
193	| `boundaryWidth`  | Stroke width of the boundaries                   |
194	| `cliffColor`     | Color of the Clear/Chaotic cliff                 |
195	| `cliffWidth`     | Stroke width of the cliff                        |
196	| `arrowColor`     | Color of transition arrows                       |
197	| `arrowWidth`     | Stroke width of transition arrows                |
198	| `labelColor`     | Color of domain name labels                      |
199	| `textColor`      | Color of item and subtitle text                  |
200	| `domainFontSize` | Font size of domain name labels                  |
201	| `itemFontSize`   | Font size of item badges and subtitles           |
202	
203	## Notes
204	
205	- Domain names are fixed keywords. Only `complex`, `complicated`, `clear`, `chaotic`, and `confusion` are recognized.
206	- Domains can be declared in any order; their position in the diagram is always the same (Complex top-left, Complicated top-right, Chaotic bottom-left, Clear bottom-right, Confusion center).
207	- The `confusion` domain has a compact center ellipse. Up to 3 items are shown inside it; if more are provided a `+N more` overflow badge is displayed. In practice, the confusion domain should contain very few items — its purpose is to surface unknowns so they can be moved to one of the four main domains.
208	- Self-loop transitions (e.g. `complex --> complex`) are silently ignored. Transitions must connect two different domains.
209	- Handdrawn mode is not currently supported.
210	- The wavy boundary rendering is deterministic: the same input always produces the same diagram, so diffs are stable across builds.
211	
212	## Accessibility
213	
214	Cynefin diagrams support the standard mermaid accessibility directives:
215	
216	```
217	cynefin-beta
218	  accTitle: Cynefin framework for software delivery decisions
219	  accDescr: A Cynefin map categorizing software tasks by complexity domain
220	
221	  complex
222	    "New feature discovery"
223	```
224

# Radar Diagram

**Source**: `mermaid-upstream/packages/mermaid/src/docs/syntax/radar.md` (210 lines)
**Detector**: `src/diagrams/radar/detector.ts` — `/^\s*radar-beta/`
**Minimum version**: v11.6.0
**Registry id**: `radar`

Also called radar chart, spider, star, cobweb, polar or Kiviat diagram (`:7`) — worth
indexing all of those in the diagram-type search.

## Statements

| Keyword | Form |
| --- | --- |
| `title` | `title Restaurant Comparison` — optional, unquoted |
| `axis` | `axis A, B, C`, `axis id1["Label1"], id2["Label2"]` |
| `curve` | `curve id["Label"]{1, 2, 3}`, or key-value form |
| `showLegend` | `showLegend true` — shown by default |
| `max` | `max 100` — otherwise computed from the data |
| `min` | `min 0` — default `0` |
| `graticule` | `graticule circle \| polygon` — default `circle` |
| `ticks` | `ticks 5` — default `5` |

Multiple axes and multiple curves may be declared on one line, comma-separated (`:75`, `:92`).

## Curve Values (`:84-101`)

Two forms:

```
curve id1["Label1"]{1, 2, 3}                    positional, in axis order
curve id4{ axis3: 30, axis1: 20, axis2: 10 }    keyed by axis id, order-free
```

The positional form depends on the axis declaration order, which makes it fragile when
axes are reordered. **The keyed form should be what completion offers**, with the axis ids
already in the document.

## Configuration (`:122-136`)

| Parameter | Default |
| --- | --- |
| `width` | `600` |
| `height` | `600` |
| `marginTop` / `marginBottom` / `marginLeft` / `marginRight` | `50` |
| `axisScaleFactor` | `1` |
| `axisLabelFactor` | `1.05` |
| `curveTension` | `0.17` |

## Theme Variables

Global (`:138-159`): `fontSize`, `titleColor`, and the color scale `cScale${i}` where `i`
runs from `0` to the theme maximum, usually `12`. One scale entry per curve.

Radar-specific, under `themeVariables.radar` (`:161-185`): `axisColor` (`black`),
`axisStrokeWidth` (`1`), `axisLabelFontSize` (`12px`), `curveOpacity` (`0.7`),
`curveStrokeWidth` (`2`), `graticuleColor` (`black`), `graticuleOpacity` (`0.5`),
`graticuleStrokeWidth` (`1`), `legendBoxSize` (`10`), `legendFontSize` (`14px`).

> `cScale0…N` is the hook for making radar match the app palette. Wire it into
> `packages/ui/src/theme.ts` alongside the flowchart variables — a radar chart in default
> mermaid colors will look pasted in.

## Editor Notes

- Completion after `curve …{` should offer the axis ids declared in the document.
- Diagnostic: a positional curve whose value count differs from the axis count. This is
  the characteristic radar bug and it renders without complaint.
- Diagnostic: a keyed curve referencing an undeclared axis.
- Diagnostic: `graticule` with a value other than `circle` or `polygon`.
- Simple line-oriented dialect; `StreamLanguage` is enough.

**Source**: `mermaid-upstream/packages/mermaid/src/docs/syntax/cynefin.md` (223 lines)
**Detector**: `src/diagrams/cynefin/cynefinDetector.ts` — `/^\s*cynefin-beta(?:[\s:]|$)/`
**Minimum version**: v11.16.0
**Registry id**: `cynefin`

## Keywords (`:47-58`)

| Keyword | Meaning |
| --- | --- |
| `cynefin-beta` | Declaration; first line after any frontmatter |
| `title` | Optional title |
| `complex` | Opens the Complex domain block |
| `complicated` | Opens the Complicated domain block |
| `clear` | Opens the Clear domain block |
| `chaotic` | Opens the Chaotic domain block |
| `confusion` | Opens the Confusion / Disorder domain block |
| `-->` | Transition between two domains |

**The domain names are a closed set** (`:205`). This makes completion genuinely complete:
five keywords, nothing else. A misspelled domain is an unambiguous diagnostic.

## Items (`:60-70`)

Quoted string labels on their own lines inside a domain block.

Layout constraints worth surfacing as hints:

- The four quadrants **do not clip**, so long item lists visually overflow their boxes.
- The `confusion` ellipse caps at **3 items** and shows a `+N more` badge (`:70`, `:207`).

## Transitions (`:72-87`)

Top level, `complex --> complicated : "Pattern identified"`. Label optional.

**Self-loops are silently ignored** (`:208`) — `complex --> complex` produces nothing.
Silent no-ops deserve a diagnostic; the user gets no feedback from mermaid at all.

## Layout Rules (`:206`)

Domains may be declared in any order; positions are fixed:

| Position | Domain |
| --- | --- |
| top-left | Complex |
| top-right | Complicated |
| bottom-left | Chaotic |
| bottom-right | Clear |
| center | Confusion |

Domains render even with no items, which makes an empty framework a usable worksheet
template (`:140-152`).

## Configuration (`:154-179`)

| Option | Type | Default | Notes |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `width` | number | `800` | |
| `height` | number | `600` | |
| `padding` | number | `40` | |
| `showDomainDescriptions` | boolean | `true` | decision model and practice subtitles |
| `boundaryAmplitude` | number | `8` | waviness in px; `0` gives straight lines |
| `seed` | number | `0` | `0` hashes the SVG id so each diagram looks unique |

> **`seed` matters for us.** With the default `0`, the wavy boundary is derived from the
> SVG id, so the same source can render differently across our render-frame job ids.
> **Visual regression tests for cynefin must set a non-zero `seed`** (`:165`), or they
> will flake. Also note our job ids feed the element id in the render frame — check that
> this does not change the boundary between renders of an unedited document.

## Theming (`:181-201`)

Under `themeVariables.cynefin`: `complexBg`, `complicatedBg`, `clearBg`, `chaoticBg`,
`confusionBg`, `boundaryColor`, `boundaryWidth`, `cliffColor`, `cliffWidth`, `arrowColor`,
`arrowWidth`, `labelColor`, `textColor`, `domainFontSize`, `itemFontSize`.

## Notes

- Handdrawn mode is not supported (`:209`).
- Rendering is deterministic given a fixed seed, so diffs are stable (`:210`).

## Accessibility (`:212-223`)

Supports `accTitle:` and `accDescr:`.

## Editor Notes

- Five domain keywords and one operator — the most tractable dialect in the catalog after pie.
- Completion at line start: the five domains, `title`, and a transition template.

1 # Timeline Diagram 2 3 > Timeline: This is an experimental diagram for now. The syntax and properties can change in future releases. The syntax is stable except for the icon integration which is the experimental part. 4 5 "A timeline is a type of diagram used to illustrate a chronology of events, dates, or periods of time. It is usually presented graphically to indicate the passing of time, and it is usually organized chronologically. A basic timeline presents a list of events in chronological order, usually using dates as markers. A timeline can also be used to show the relationship between events, such as the relationship between the events of a person's life" [(Wikipedia)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Timeline). 6 7 ### An example of a timeline 8 9 ```mermaid 10 timeline 11 title History of Social Media Platform 12 2002 : LinkedIn 13 2004 : Facebook 14 : Google 15 2005 : YouTube 16 2006 : Twitter 17 ``` 18 19 ## Syntax 20 21 The syntax for creating Timeline diagram is simple. You always start with the `timeline` keyword to let mermaid know that you want to create a timeline diagram. 22 23 After that there is a possibility to add a title to the timeline. This is done by adding a line with the keyword `title` followed by the title text. 24 25 Then you add the timeline data, where you always start with a time period, followed by a colon and then the text for the event. Optionally you can add a second colon and then the text for the event. So, you can have one or more events per time period. 26 27 ```json 28 {time period} : {event} 29 ``` 30 31 or 32 33 ```json 34 {time period} : {event} : {event} 35 ``` 36 37 or 38 39 ```json 40 {time period} : {event} 41 : {event} 42 : {event} 43 ``` 44 45 **NOTE**: Both time period and event are simple text, and not limited to numbers. 46 47 Let us look at the syntax for the example above. 48 49 ```mermaid-example 50 timeline 51 title History of Social Media Platform 52 2002 : LinkedIn 53 2004 : Facebook : Google 54 2005 : YouTube 55 2006 : Twitter 56 ``` 57 58 In this way we can use a text outline to generate a timeline diagram. 59 The sequence of time period and events is important, as it will be used to draw the timeline. The first time period will be placed at the left side of the timeline, and the last time period will be placed at the right side of the timeline. 60 61 Similarly, the first event will be placed at the top for that specific time period, and the last event will be placed at the bottom. 62 63 ## Grouping of time periods in sections/ages 64 65 You can group time periods in sections/ages. This is done by adding a line with the keyword `section` followed by the section name. 66 67 All subsequent time periods will be placed in this section until a new section is defined. 68 69 If no section is defined, all time periods will be placed in the default section. 70 71 Let us look at an example, where we have grouped the time periods in sections. 72 73 ```mermaid-example 74 timeline 75 title Timeline of Industrial Revolution 76 section 17th-20th century 77 Industry 1.0 : Machinery, Water power, Steam

6	# Treemap Diagram
7	
8	> A treemap diagram displays hierarchical data as a set of nested rectangles. Each branch of the tree is represented by a rectangle, which is then tiled with smaller rectangles representing sub-branches.
9	
10	```warning
11	This is a new diagram type in Mermaid. Its syntax may evolve in future versions.
12	```
13	
14	## Introduction
15	
16	Treemap diagrams are an effective way to visualize hierarchical data and show proportions between categories and subcategories. The size of each rectangle is proportional to the value it represents, making it easy to compare different parts of a hierarchy.
17	
18	Treemap diagrams are particularly useful for:
19	
20	- Visualizing hierarchical data structures
21	- Comparing proportions between categories
22	- Displaying large amounts of hierarchical data in a limited space
23	- Identifying patterns and outliers in hierarchical data
24	
25	## Syntax
26	
27	```
28	treemap-beta
29	"Section 1"
30	    "Leaf 1.1": 12
31	    "Section 1.2"
32	      "Leaf 1.2.1": 12
33	"Section 2"
34	    "Leaf 2.1": 20
35	    "Leaf 2.2": 25
36	```
37	
38	### Node Definition
39	
40	Nodes in a treemap are defined using the following syntax:
41	
42	- **Section/Parent nodes**: Defined with quoted text `"Section Name"`
43	- **Leaf nodes with values**: Defined with quoted text followed by a colon and value `"Leaf Name": value`
44	- **Hierarchy**: Created using indentation (spaces or tabs)
45	- **Styling**: Nodes can be styled using the `:::class` syntax
46	
47	## Examples
48	
49	### Basic Treemap
50	
51	```mermaid-example
52	treemap-beta
53	"Category A"
54	    "Item A1": 10
55	    "Item A2": 20
56	"Category B"
57	    "Item B1": 15
58	    "Item B2": 25
59	```
60	
61	### Hierarchical Treemap
62	
63	```mermaid-example
64	treemap-beta
65	"Products"
66	    "Electronics"
67	        "Phones": 50
68	        "Computers": 30
69	        "Accessories": 20
70	    "Clothing"
71	        "Men's": 40
72	        "Women's": 40
73	```
74	
75	### Treemap with Styling
76	
77	```mermaid-example
78	treemap-beta
79	"Section 1"
80	    "Leaf 1.1": 12
81	    "Section 1.2":::class1
82	      "Leaf 1.2.1": 12
83	"Section 2"
84	    "Leaf 2.1": 20:::class1
85	    "Leaf 2.2": 25
86	    "Leaf 2.3": 12
87	
88	classDef class1 fill:red,color:blue,stroke:#FFD600;
89	```
90	
91	## Styling and Configuration
92	
93	Treemap diagrams can be customized using Mermaid's styling and configuration options.
94	
95	### Using classDef for Styling
96	
97	You can define custom styles for nodes using the `classDef` syntax, which is a standard feature across many Mermaid diagram types:
98	
99	```mermaid-example
100	treemap-beta
101	"Main"
102	    "A": 20
103	    "B":::important
104	        "B1": 10
105	        "B2": 15
106	    "C": 5
107	
108	classDef important fill:#f96,stroke:#333,stroke-width:2px;
109	```
110	
111	### Theme Configuration
112	
113	You can customize the colors of your treemap using the theme configuration:
114	
115	```mermaid-example
116	---
117	config:
118	    theme: 'forest'
119	---
120	treemap-beta
121	"Category A"
122	    "Item A1": 10
123	    "Item A2": 20
124	"Category B"
125	    "Item B1": 15
126	    "Item B2": 25
127	```
128	
129	### Diagram Padding
130	
131	You can adjust the padding around the treemap diagram using the `diagramPadding` configuration option:
132	
133	```mermaid-example
134	---
135	config:
136	  treemap:
137	    diagramPadding: 200
138	---
139	treemap-beta
140	"Category A"
141	    "Item A1": 10
142	    "Item A2": 20
143	"Category B"
144	    "Item B1": 15
145	    "Item B2": 25
146	```
147	
148	## Configuration Options
149	
150	The treemap diagram supports the following configuration options:
151	
152	| Option         | Description                                                                 | Default |
153	| -------------- | --------------------------------------------------------------------------- | ------- |
154	| useMaxWidth    | When true, the diagram width is set to 100% and scales with available space | true    |
155	| padding        | Internal padding between nodes                                              | 10      |
156	| diagramPadding | Padding around the entire diagram                                           | 8       |
157	| showValues     | Whether to show values in the treemap                                       | true    |
158	| nodeWidth      | Width of nodes                                                              | 100     |
159	| nodeHeight     | Height of nodes                                                             | 40      |
160	| borderWidth    | Width of borders                                                            | 1       |
161	| valueFontSize  | Font size for values                                                        | 12      |
162	| labelFontSize  | Font size for labels                                                        | 14      |
163	| valueFormat    | Format for values (see Value Formatting section)                            | ','     |
164	
165	## Advanced Features
166	
167	### Value Formatting
168	
169	Values in treemap diagrams can be formatted to display in different ways using the `valueFormat` configuration option. This option primarily uses [D3's format specifiers](https://github.com/d3/d3-format#locale_format) to control how numbers are displayed, with some additional special cases for common formats.
170	
171	Some common format patterns:
172	
173	- `,` - Thousands separator (default)
174	- `$` - Add dollar sign
175	- `.1f` - Show one decimal place
176	- `.1%` - Show as percentage with one decimal place
177	- `$0,0` - Dollar sign with thousands separator
178	- `$.2f` - Dollar sign with 2 decimal places
179	- `$,.2f` - Dollar sign with thousands separator and 2 decimal places
180	
181	The treemap diagram supports both standard D3 format specifiers and some common currency formats that combine the dollar sign with other formatting options.
182	
183	Example with currency formatting:
184	
185	```mermaid-example
186	---
187	config:
188	  treemap:
189	    valueFormat: '$0,0'
190	---
191	treemap-beta
192	"Budget"
193	    "Operations"
194	        "Salaries": 700000
195	        "Equipment": 200000
196	        "Supplies": 100000
197	    "Marketing"
198	        "Advertising": 400000
199	        "Events": 100000
200	```
201	
202	Example with percentage formatting:
203	
204	```mermaid-example
205	---
206	config:
207	  treemap:
208	    valueFormat: '$.1%'
209	---
210	treemap-beta
211	"Market Share"
212	    "Company A": 0.35
213	    "Company B": 0.25
214	    "Company C": 0.15
215	    "Others": 0.25
216	```
217	
218	## Common Use Cases
219	
220	Treemap diagrams are commonly used for:
221	
222	1. **Financial Data**: Visualizing budget allocations, market shares, or portfolio compositions
223	2. **File System Analysis**: Showing disk space usage by folders and files
224	3. **Population Demographics**: Displaying population distribution across regions and subregions
225	4. **Product Hierarchies**: Visualizing product categories and their sales volumes
226	5. **Organizational Structures**: Representing departments and team sizes in a company
227	
228	## Limitations
229	
230	- Treemap diagrams work best when the data has a natural hierarchy
231	- Very small values may be difficult to see or label in a treemap diagram
232	- Deep hierarchies (many levels) can be challenging to represent clearly
233	- Treemap diagrams are not well suited for representing data with negative values
234	
235	## Related Diagrams
236	
237	If treemap diagrams don't suit your needs, consider these alternatives:
238	
239	- [**Pie Charts**](./pie.md): For simple proportion comparisons without hierarchy
240	- **Sunburst Diagrams**: For hierarchical data with a radial layout (yet to be released in Mermaid).
241	- [**Sankey Diagrams**](./sankey.md): For flow-based hierarchical data
242	
243	## Notes
244	
245	The treemap diagram implementation in Mermaid is designed to be simple to use while providing powerful visualization capabilities. As this is a newer diagram type, feedback and feature requests are welcome through the Mermaid GitHub repository.
246

1	# Quadrant Chart
2	
3	> A quadrant chart is a visual representation of data that is divided into four quadrants. It is used to plot data points on a two-dimensional grid, with one variable represented on the x-axis and another variable represented on the y-axis. The quadrants are determined by dividing the chart into four equal parts based on a set of criteria that is specific to the data being analyzed. Quadrant charts are often used to identify patterns and trends in data, and to prioritize actions based on the position of data points within the chart. They are commonly used in business, marketing, and risk management, among other fields.
4	
5	## Example
6	
7	```mermaid-example
8	quadrantChart
9	    title Reach and engagement of campaigns
10	    x-axis Low Reach --> High Reach
11	    y-axis Low Engagement --> High Engagement
12	    quadrant-1 We should expand
13	    quadrant-2 Need to promote
14	    quadrant-3 Re-evaluate
15	    quadrant-4 May be improved
16	    Campaign A: [0.3, 0.6]
17	    Campaign B: [0.45, 0.23]
18	    Campaign C: [0.57, 0.69]
19	    Campaign D: [0.78, 0.34]
20	    Campaign E: [0.40, 0.34]
21	    Campaign F: [0.35, 0.78]
22	```
23	
24	## Syntax
25	
26	```note
27	If there are no points available in the chart both **axis** text and **quadrant** will be rendered in the center of the respective quadrant.
28	If there are points **x-axis** labels will rendered from the left of the respective quadrant also they will be displayed at the bottom of the chart, and **y-axis** labels will be rendered at the bottom of the respective quadrant, the quadrant text will render at the top of the respective quadrant.
29	```
30	
31	```note
32	For points x and y value min value is 0 and max value is 1.
33	```
34	
35	### Title
36	
37	The title is a short description of the chart and it will always render on top of the chart.
38	
39	#### Example
40	
41	```
42	quadrantChart
43	    title This is a sample example
44	```
45	
46	### x-axis
47	
48	The x-axis determines what text would be displayed in the x-axis. In x-axis there is two part **left** and **right** you can pass **both** or you can pass only **left**. The statement should start with `x-axis` then the `left axis text` followed by the delimiter `-->` then `right axis text`.
49	
50	#### Example
51	
52	1. `x-axis <text> --> <text>` both the left and right axis text will be rendered.
53	2. `x-axis <text>` only the left axis text will be rendered.
54	
55	### y-axis
56	
57	The y-axis determines what text would be displayed in the y-axis. In y-axis there is two part **top** and **bottom** you can pass **both** or you can pass only **bottom**. The statement should start with `y-axis` then the `bottom axis text` followed by the delimiter `-->` then `top axis text`.
58	
59	#### Example
60	
61	1. `y-axis <text> --> <text>` both the bottom and top axis text will be rendered.
62	2. `y-axis <text>` only the bottom axis text will be rendered.
63	
64	### Quadrants text
65	
66	The `quadrant-[1,2,3,4]` determine what text would be displayed inside the quadrants.
67	
68	#### Example
69	
70	1. `quadrant-1 <text>` determine what text will be rendered inside the top right quadrant.
71	2. `quadrant-2 <text>` determine what text will be rendered inside the top left quadrant.
72	3. `quadrant-3 <text>` determine what text will be rendered inside the bottom left quadrant.
73	4. `quadrant-4 <text>` determine what text will be rendered inside the bottom right quadrant.
74	
75	### Points
76	
77	Points are used to plot a circle inside the quadrantChart. The syntax is `<text>: [x, y]` here x and y value is in the range 0 - 1.
78	
79	#### Example
80	
81	1. `Point 1: [0.75, 0.80]` here the Point 1 will be drawn in the top right quadrant.
82	2. `Point 2: [0.35, 0.24]` here the Point 2 will be drawn in the bottom left quadrant.
83	
84	## Chart Configurations
85	
86	| Parameter                         | Description                                                                                        | Default value |
87	| --------------------------------- | -------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | :-----------: |
88	| chartWidth                        | Width of the chart                                                                                 |      500      |
89	| chartHeight                       | Height of the chart                                                                                |      500      |
90	| titlePadding                      | Top and Bottom padding of the title                                                                |      10       |
91	| titleFontSize                     | Title font size                                                                                    |      20       |
92	| quadrantPadding                   | Padding outside all the quadrants                                                                  |       5       |
93	| quadrantTextTopPadding            | Quadrant text top padding when text is drawn on top ( not data points are there)                   |       5       |
94	| quadrantLabelFontSize             | Quadrant text font size                                                                            |      16       |
95	| quadrantInternalBorderStrokeWidth | Border stroke width inside the quadrants                                                           |       1       |
96	| quadrantExternalBorderStrokeWidth | Quadrant external border stroke width                                                              |       2       |
97	| xAxisLabelPadding                 | Top and bottom padding of x-axis text                                                              |       5       |
98	| xAxisLabelFontSize                | X-axis texts font size                                                                             |      16       |
99	| xAxisPosition                     | Position of x-axis (top , bottom) if there are points the x-axis will always be rendered in bottom |     'top'     |
100	| yAxisLabelPadding                 | Left and Right padding of y-axis text                                                              |       5       |
101	| yAxisLabelFontSize                | Y-axis texts font size                                                                             |      16       |
102	| yAxisPosition                     | Position of y-axis (left , right)                                                                  |    'left'     |
103	| pointTextPadding                  | Padding between point and the below text                                                           |       5       |
104	| pointLabelFontSize                | Point text font size                                                                               |      12       |
105	| pointRadius                       | Radius of the point to be drawn                                                                    |       5       |
106	
107	## Chart Theme Variables
108	
109	| Parameter                        | Description                             |
110	| -------------------------------- | --------------------------------------- |
111	| quadrant1Fill                    | Fill color of the top right quadrant    |
112	| quadrant2Fill                    | Fill color of the top left quadrant     |
113	| quadrant3Fill                    | Fill color of the bottom left quadrant  |
114	| quadrant4Fill                    | Fill color of the bottom right quadrant |
115	| quadrant1TextFill                | Text color of the top right quadrant    |
116	| quadrant2TextFill                | Text color of the top left quadrant     |
117	| quadrant3TextFill                | Text color of the bottom left quadrant  |
118	| quadrant4TextFill                | Text color of the bottom right quadrant |
119	| quadrantPointFill                | Points fill color                       |
120	| quadrantPointTextFill            | Points text color                       |
121	| quadrantXAxisTextFill            | X-axis text color                       |
122	| quadrantYAxisTextFill            | Y-axis text color                       |
123	| quadrantInternalBorderStrokeFill | Quadrants inner border color            |
124	| quadrantExternalBorderStrokeFill | Quadrants outer border color            |
125	| quadrantTitleFill                | Title color                             |
126	
127	## Example on config and theme
128	
129	```mermaid-example
130	---
131	config:
132	  quadrantChart:
133	    chartWidth: 400
134	    chartHeight: 400
135	  themeVariables:
136	    quadrant1TextFill: "ff0000"
137	---
138	quadrantChart
139	  x-axis Urgent --> Not Urgent
140	  y-axis Not Important --> "Important ❤"
141	  quadrant-1 Plan
142	  quadrant-2 Do
143	  quadrant-3 Delegate
144	  quadrant-4 Delete
145	```
146	
147	### Point styling
148	
149	Points can either be styled directly or with defined shared classes
150	
151	1. Direct styling
152	
153	```md
154	Point A: [0.9, 0.0] radius: 12
155	Point B: [0.8, 0.1] color: #ff3300, radius: 10
156	Point C: [0.7, 0.2] radius: 25, color: #00ff33, stroke-color: #10f0f0
157	Point D: [0.6, 0.3] radius: 15, stroke-color: #00ff0f, stroke-width: 5px ,color: #ff33f0
158	```
159	
160	2. Classes styling
161	
162	```md
163	Point A:::class1: [0.9, 0.0]
164	Point B:::class2: [0.8, 0.1]
165	Point C:::class3: [0.7, 0.2]
166	Point D:::class3: [0.7, 0.2]
167	classDef class1 color: #109060
168	classDef class2 color: #908342, radius : 10, stroke-color: #310085, stroke-width: 10px
169	classDef class3 color: #f00fff, radius : 10
170	```
171	
172	#### Available styles:
173	
174	| Parameter    | Description                                                            |
175	| ------------ | ---------------------------------------------------------------------- |
176	| color        | Fill color of the point                                                |
177	| radius       | Radius of the point                                                    |
178	| stroke-width | Border width of the point                                              |
179	| stroke-color | Border color of the point (useless when stroke-width is not specified) |
180	
181	```note
182	Order of preference:
183	1. Direct styles
184	2. Class styles
185	3. Theme styles
186	```
187	
188	## Example on styling
189	
190	```mermaid-example
191	quadrantChart
192	  title Reach and engagement of campaigns
193	  x-axis Low Reach --> High Reach
194	  y-axis Low Engagement --> High Engagement
195	  quadrant-1 We should expand
196	  quadrant-2 Need to promote
197	  quadrant-3 Re-evaluate
198	  quadrant-4 May be improved
199	  Campaign A: [0.9, 0.0] radius: 12
200	  Campaign B:::class1: [0.8, 0.1] color: #ff3300, radius: 10
201	  Campaign C: [0.7, 0.2] radius: 25, color: #00ff33, stroke-color: #10f0f0
202	  Campaign D: [0.6, 0.3] radius: 15, stroke-color: #00ff0f, stroke-width: 5px ,color: #ff33f0
203	  Campaign E:::class2: [0.5, 0.4]
204	  Campaign F:::class3: [0.4, 0.5] color: #0000ff
205	  classDef class1 color: #109060
206	  classDef class2 color: #908342, radius : 10, stroke-color: #310085, stroke-width: 10px
207	  classDef class3 color: #f00fff, radius : 10
208	```

**Detector**: `src/diagrams/quadrant-chart/quadrantDetector.ts` — `/^\s*quadrantChart/`
**Registry id**: `quadrant`

## Statements

| Keyword | Form |
| --- | --- |
| `title` | `title Reach and engagement of campaigns` |
| `x-axis` | `x-axis <left> --> <right>`, or `x-axis <left>` only |
| `y-axis` | `y-axis <bottom> --> <top>`, or `y-axis <bottom>` only |
| `quadrant-1` … `quadrant-4` | quadrant label text |
| point | `<text>: [x, y]` |
| `classDef` | `classDef class1 color: #109060, radius: 10` |

**Axis direction is not symmetric** (`:46-62`): `x-axis` goes left → right, but `y-axis`
goes **bottom → top**. Writing the y-axis as if it read top-to-bottom is the natural
mistake and produces a silently inverted chart.

## Quadrant Numbering (`:64-73`)

| Keyword | Position |
| --- | --- |
| `quadrant-1` | top right |
| `quadrant-2` | top left |
| `quadrant-3` | bottom left |
| `quadrant-4` | bottom right |

Counter-clockwise from the top right — matching the mathematical convention, not reading
order. Surface the position in the completion detail text; nobody remembers this.

## Points (`:75-82`)

`Point 1: [0.75, 0.80]`. **x and y are constrained to 0–1** (`:31-33`). A value outside
that range is the obvious diagnostic.

## Point Styling (`:147-186`)

Two ways, combinable:

```
Point A: [0.9, 0.0] radius: 12
Point B: [0.8, 0.1] color: #ff3300, radius: 10
Point A:::class1: [0.9, 0.0]
```

Note the `:::class` goes **between the label and the colon**, not after the coordinates —
different placement from treemap, and worth its own hint.

Available styles: `color`, `radius`, `stroke-width`, `stroke-color` (the last is useless
without `stroke-width`, `:179`).

**Order of preference** (`:181-186`): direct styles → class styles → theme styles.

## Layout Behavior (`:26-29`)

With no points, axis and quadrant text render centered in each quadrant. With points,
x-axis labels move to the bottom of the chart and quadrant text moves to the top of each
quadrant. Adding the first point therefore visibly rearranges the chart — expected, not a bug.

## Configuration (`:84-105`)

`chartWidth` (500), `chartHeight` (500), `titlePadding` (10), `titleFontSize` (20),
`quadrantPadding` (5), `quadrantTextTopPadding` (5), `quadrantLabelFontSize` (16),
`quadrantInternalBorderStrokeWidth` (1), `quadrantExternalBorderStrokeWidth` (2),
`xAxisLabelPadding` (5), `xAxisLabelFontSize` (16), `xAxisPosition` (`'top'`, forced to
bottom when points exist), `yAxisLabelPadding` (5), `yAxisLabelFontSize` (16),
`yAxisPosition` (`'left'`), `pointTextPadding` (5), `pointLabelFontSize` (12),
`pointRadius` (5).

## Theme Variables (`:107-125`)

`quadrant1Fill` … `quadrant4Fill`, `quadrant1TextFill` … `quadrant4TextFill`,
`quadrantPointFill`, `quadrantPointTextFill`, `quadrantXAxisTextFill`,
`quadrantYAxisTextFill`, `quadrantInternalBorderStrokeFill`,
`quadrantExternalBorderStrokeFill`, `quadrantTitleFill`.

Wire these into `packages/ui/src/theme.ts` — a quadrant chart in default colors will not
match the app.

## Editor Notes

- Completion at line start: `title`, `x-axis`, `y-axis`, `quadrant-1`…`4`, `classDef`.
- Completion for `-->` after the first axis text.
- Diagnostic: a coordinate outside 0–1; `stroke-color` without `stroke-width`; a duplicate
  `quadrant-N`.
- Simple line-oriented dialect; `StreamLanguage` is enough.

17 páginas de catálogo escritas (1.467 líneas), `verify` sigue en verde. Voy por la mitad, y te reporto ahora porque hay hallazgos que afectan al código.

**Hechas (17):** flowchart, sequence, class, state, er, user-journey, pie, kanban, packet, venn, ishikawa, mindmap, radar, cynefin, treemap, quadrant, timeline *(esta última parcial — leí 130 de 360 líneas y lo dejé anotado en la propia página en vez de fingir que estaba completa)*.

**Pendientes (16):** swimlanes, gantt, requirement, git, c4, zenuml, sankey, xychart, block, architecture, eventmodeling, wardley, treeview, usecase, railroad, info.

Cada página cita fichero y línea del upstream. Lo que salió de leerlas de verdad:

**Tres huecos que no puedo cerrar con la documentación:**

1. **Las 30+ formas expandidas de flowchart no están en el markdown.** La tabla es un include de build (`<!--@include: virtual:shapesTable -->`, `flowchart.md:218`). Coseché ~50 nombres de los ejemplos, pero los alias faltan. Hay que leer `rendering-util/rendering-elements/shapes.ts`, que está fuera del sparse-checkout actual.
2. **`userJourney.md` (24 líneas) e `ishikawa.md` (38)** no alcanzan para un dialecto. Ambas páginas apuntan ya al `.jison` correspondiente.
3. **`packet`: las variables de tema están comentadas en el doc** con la nota de que no funcionan por un bug de mermaid. Las registré, pero marcadas como *no ofrecer en autocompletado mientras no hagan nada*.

**Dos cosas que afectan a nuestro código, no solo a la doc:**

- **Cynefin usa `seed: 0` por defecto, que hashea el id del SVG** para variar la ondulación del borde (`cynefin.md:165`). Nuestro render frame genera el id desde el `jobId`, que cambia en cada render. Eso significa que **un documento sin editar puede renderizar distinto entre jobs**, y que los tests visuales de cynefin van a flakear si no fijamos `seed`. Está anotado en la página; hay que verificarlo contra el frame.
- **Kanban construye un `href` desde `ticketBaseUrl`**, que es texto del usuario. Con `securityLevel: 'strict'` mermaid escapa etiquetas, pero esto es una URL que acaba en un ancla. Anotado como punto a revisar en la sanitización.

**Y una inconsistencia entre dialectos** que va a causar bugs si el autocompletado no la respeta: el operador `:::` va en sitio distinto en cada tipo. En flowchart pegado al nodo (`A:::clase`), en mindmap **en su propia línea**, en treemap **después del valor** (`"Hoja": 20:::clase`), en quadrant **entre etiqueta y coma** (`Point A:::clase: [0.9, 0]`). Y la adjunción de clases diverge: `class nodeId className` en flowchart y ER, pero `cssClass "nodeId" className` en class diagram.

¿Sigo con los 16 restantes, o prefieres que primero amplíe el sparse-checkout a `rendering-util/` para cerrar el hueco de las formas de flowchart?
o sea dices que no puedes hacer todos?
No. Puedo hacer los 33 — los tres huecos eran de la documentación de mermaid, no míos, y se cierran leyendo el código fuente. Sigo hasta terminar.

3	outline: 'deep'
4	---
5	
6	# Swimlanes Diagram (v11.16.0+)
7	
8	```warning
9	This is a new diagram type in Mermaid. Its syntax may evolve in future versions.
10	```
11	
12	A swimlane diagram shows a process divided by responsibility. Each lane represents an actor, team, system, or phase, and the nodes inside the lane show the work that happens there. Arrows show the order of work and the handoffs between lanes.
13	
14	Use swimlane diagrams when the most important question is not only "what happens next?" but also "who owns this step?" They are useful for approval flows, support processes, delivery workflows, and any process where work crosses teams or systems.
15	
16	## Basic Example
17	
18	> The rendered examples on this page use the **Neo** look and the **Redux** theme. Out of the box, swimlanes use your configured default look and theme.
19	
20	```mermaid-example
21	swimlane-beta LR
22	  subgraph Customer
23	    request[Request service]
24	    receive[Receive update]
25	  end
26	
27	  subgraph Support
28	    triage[Triage request]
29	    answer[Send answer]
30	  end
31	
32	  subgraph Engineering
33	    investigate[Investigate issue]
34	    fix[Prepare fix]
35	  end
36	
37	  request --> triage
38	  triage -->|Known issue| answer
39	  triage -->|Needs code change| investigate
40	  investigate --> fix --> answer
41	  answer --> receive
42	```
43	
44	## Syntax
45	
46	A swimlane diagram starts with the `swimlane-beta` keyword. You can optionally add a direction after the keyword.
47	
48	```
49	swimlane-beta
50	```
51	
52	```
53	swimlane-beta LR
54	```
55	
56	The supported directions are:
57	
58	| Direction | Meaning                |
59	| --------- | ---------------------- |
60	| `TB`      | Top to bottom          |
61	| `TD`      | Top down, same as `TB` |
62	| `BT`      | Bottom to top          |
63	| `LR`      | Left to right          |
64	| `RL`      | Right to left          |
65	
66	If no direction is set, the diagram uses `TB`.
67	
68	### Lanes
69	
70	Use `subgraph` to create a lane. In a swimlane diagram, top-level subgraphs are rendered as swimlanes. A lane ends with `end`.
71	
72	```mermaid-example
73	swimlane-beta
74	  subgraph Sales
75	    lead[Qualify lead]
76	    quote[Prepare quote]
77	  end
78	```
79	
80	You can give a lane an internal id and a display label. This is useful when the label contains spaces or when you want a stable id for styling.
81	
82	```mermaid-example
83	swimlane-beta LR
84	  subgraph sales [Sales team]
85	    lead[Qualify lead]
86	    quote[Prepare quote]
87	  end
88	
89	  subgraph finance [Finance team]
90	    review[Review terms]
91	    approve[Approve quote]
92	  end
93	
94	  lead --> quote --> review --> approve
95	```
96	
97	### Nodes
98	
99	Nodes use flowchart-style shape syntax. The id is written first, and the label is written inside the shape.
100	
101	```mermaid-example
102	swimlane-beta LR
103	  subgraph Intake
104	    start([Start])
105	    task[Do work]
106	    fix[Fix issues]
107	  end
108	
109	  subgraph Review
110	    decision{Ready?}
111	  end
112	
113	  subgraph Complete
114	    done((Done))
115	  end
116	
117	  start --> task --> decision
118	  decision -->|Yes| done
119	  decision -->|No| fix
120	  fix --> task
121	```
122	
123	The most common node forms are:
124	
125	| Syntax       | Shape             | Common use          |
126	| ------------ | ----------------- | ------------------- |
127	| `id[Text]`   | Rectangle         | Task or activity    |
128	| `id(Text)`   | Rounded rectangle | Step or event       |
129	| `id([Text])` | Stadium           | Start or end        |
130	| `id{Text}`   | Decision          | Branching question  |
131	| `id((Text))` | Circle            | Connector or marker |
132	
133	For the complete shape catalog, icons, images, markdown strings, classes, and styling options, see [Flowchart syntax](./flowchart.md).
134	
135	### Edges
136	
137	Edges also use flowchart-style syntax. They can connect nodes in the same lane or across lanes.
138	
139	```mermaid-example
140	swimlane-beta LR
141	  subgraph Buyer
142	    choose[Choose product]
143	    pay[Pay invoice]
144	  end
145	
146	  subgraph Store
147	    reserve[Reserve stock]
148	    ship[Ship product]
149	  end
150	
151	  choose --> reserve
152	  reserve -->|Invoice ready| pay
153	  pay --> ship
154	```
155	
156	Common edge forms:
157	
158	| Syntax             | Meaning                |
159	| ------------------ | ---------------------- |
160	| `A --> B`          | Arrow                  |
161	| `A --- B`          | Line without arrowhead |
162	| `A -->\|Label\| B` | Arrow with label       |
163	| `A -.-> B`         | Dotted arrow           |
164	| `A ==> B`          | Thick arrow            |
165	
166	For the full edge syntax, including multi-directional arrows and minimum link length, see [Flowchart syntax](./flowchart.md#links-between-nodes).
167	
168	### Accessibility
169	
170	Use `accTitle` and `accDescr` to provide an accessible title and description.
171	
172	```mermaid-example
173	swimlane-beta LR
174	  accTitle: Support escalation
175	  accDescr: A request starts with the customer, is triaged by support, and may be escalated to engineering.
176	
177	  subgraph Customer
178	    request[Open request]
179	  end
180	
181	  subgraph Support
182	    triage[Triage]
183	  end
184	
185	  subgraph Engineering
186	    resolve[Resolve]
187	  end
188	
189	  request --> triage --> resolve
190	```
191	
192	## Good Practices
193	
194	### Make Each Lane Mean One Kind of Ownership
195	
196	Choose lanes that answer "who owns this step?" Avoid mixing teams, phases, and statuses in the same diagram unless that distinction is the point of the diagram.
197	
198	```mermaid-example
199	swimlane-beta LR
200	  subgraph Customer
201	    submit[Submit order]
202	    confirm[Confirm delivery]
203	  end
204	
205	  subgraph Store
206	    check[Check order]
207	    pack[Pack items]
208	  end
209	
210	  subgraph Carrier
211	    collect[Collect package]
212	    deliver[Deliver package]
213	  end
214	
215	  submit --> check --> pack --> collect --> deliver --> confirm
216	```
217	
218	### Label Cross-Lane Handoffs
219	
220	A cross-lane arrow is where responsibility changes. Label the arrow when the handoff depends on a document, decision, message, or condition.
221	
222	```mermaid-example
223	swimlane-beta LR
224	  subgraph Applicant
225	    apply[Submit application]
226	    sign[Sign agreement]
227	  end
228	
229	  subgraph Reviewer
230	    screen[Screen application]
231	    decide{Approved?}
232	  end
233	
234	  subgraph System
235	    create[Create account]
236	    notify[Send welcome email]
237	  end
238	
239	  apply -->|Application received| screen
240	  screen --> decide
241	  decide -->|Approved| create --> notify --> sign
242	  decide -->|Needs changes| apply
243	```
244	
245	### Keep Long Processes Readable
246	
247	Split a large process into several diagrams when the lanes or handoffs stop fitting in one view. A useful swimlane diagram is usually readable without tracing every arrow twice.
248	
249	```mermaid-example
250	swimlane-beta TB
251	  subgraph Intake
252	    collect[Collect request]
253	    validate[Validate details]
254	  end
255	
256	  subgraph Review
257	    review[Review request]
258	    decide{Ready?}
259	  end
260	
261	  subgraph Delivery
262	    schedule[Schedule work]
263	    complete[Complete work]
264	  end
265	
266	  collect --> validate --> review --> decide
267	  decide -->|Yes| schedule --> complete
268	  decide -->|No| collect
269	```
270	
271	### Use Stable Ids
272	
273	Use short, meaningful ids for nodes and lanes. The label can change without breaking links, styles, or later references.
274	
275	```mermaid-example
276	swimlane-beta LR
277	  subgraph ops [Operations]
278	    intake[Receive request]
279	    plan[Plan work]
280	  end
281	
282	  subgraph legal [Legal]
283	    review[Review contract]
284	  end
285	
286	  intake --> plan --> review
287	
288	  classDef attention fill:#fff2cc,stroke:#d6a500,color:#111;
289	  class review attention;
290	```
291	
292	### Put Decisions Where They Are Made
293	
294	Place a decision node in the lane that owns the decision. Then route the outcomes to the lanes that act on the result.
295	
296	```mermaid-example
297	swimlane-beta LR
298	  subgraph Support
299	    classify{Can support solve it?}
300	    respond[Respond to customer]
301	  end
302	
303	  subgraph Product
304	    prioritize[Prioritize fix]
305	  end
306	
307	  subgraph Engineering
308	    implement[Implement fix]
309	  end
310	
311	  classify -->|Yes| respond
312	  classify -->|No| prioritize --> implement --> respond
313	```
314	
315	## When to Use Another Diagram
316	
317	Use a regular [flowchart](./flowchart.md) when ownership is not important and you only need to show sequence or branching. Use a [sequence diagram](./sequenceDiagram.md) when the focus is messages over time between participants. Use a [state diagram](./stateDiagram.md) when the focus is how one thing changes state.
318

3	> A sankey diagram is a visualization used to depict a flow from one set of values to another.
4	
5	```warning
6	This is an experimental diagram. Its syntax are very close to plain CSV, but it is to be extended in the nearest future.
7	```
8	
9	The things being connected are called nodes and the connections are called links.
10	
11	## Example
12

19	    showValues: false
20	---
21	sankey

92	
93	## Syntax
94	
95	The idea behind syntax is that a user types `sankey` keyword first, then pastes raw CSV below and get the result.
96	
97	It implements CSV standard as [described here](https://www.ietf.org/rfc/rfc4180.txt) with subtle **differences**:
98	
99	- CSV must contain **3 columns only**
100	- It is **allowed** to have **empty lines** without comma separators for visual purposes
101	
102	### Basic
103	
104	It is implied that 3 columns inside CSV should represent `source`, `target` and `value` accordingly:
105	
106	```mermaid-example
107	sankey
108	
109	%% source,target,value
110	Electricity grid,Over generation / exports,104.453
111	Electricity grid,Heating and cooling - homes,113.726
112	Electricity grid,H2 conversion,27.14
113	```
114	
115	### Empty Lines
116	
117	CSV does not support empty lines without comma delimiters by default. But you can add them if needed:
118	
119	```mermaid-example
120	sankey
121	
122	Bio-conversion,Losses,26.862
123	
124	Bio-conversion,Solid,280.322
125	
126	Bio-conversion,Gas,81.144
127	```
128	
129	### Commas
130	
131	If you need to have a comma, wrap it in double quotes:
132	
133	```mermaid-example
134	sankey
135	
136	Pumped heat,"Heating and cooling, homes",193.026
137	Pumped heat,"Heating and cooling, commercial",70.672
138	```
139	
140	### Double Quotes
141	
142	If you need to have double quote, put a pair of them inside quoted string:
143	
144	```mermaid-example
145	sankey
146	
147	Pumped heat,"Heating and cooling, ""homes""",193.026
148	Pumped heat,"Heating and cooling, ""commercial""",70.672
149	```
150	
151	## Configuration
152	
153	You can customize link colors, node alignments and diagram dimensions.
154	
155	```html
156	<script>
157	  const config = {
158	    startOnLoad: true,
159	    securityLevel: 'loose',
160	    sankey: {
161	      width: 800,
162	      height: 400,
163	      linkColor: 'source',
164	      nodeAlignment: 'left',
165	    },
166	  };
167	  mermaid.initialize(config);
168	</script>
169	```
170	
171	### Links Coloring
172	
173	You can adjust links' color by setting `linkColor` to one of those:
174	
175	- `source` - link will be of a source node color
176	- `target` - link will be of a target node color
177	- `gradient` - link color will be smoothly transient between source and target node colors
178	- hex code of color, like `#a1a1a1`
179	
180	### Node Alignment
181	
182	Graph layout can be changed by setting `nodeAlignment` to:
183	
184	- `justify`
185	- `center`
186	- `left`
187	- `right`
188	
189	### Label Style (v11.15.0+)
190	
191	You can change how node labels are rendered by setting `labelStyle`:
192	
193	- `legacy` (default) - plain text labels, positioned based on node x-coordinate
194	- `outlined` - labels with a background stroke for improved readability, positioned based on node layer relative to the central node
195	
196	```mermaid-example
197	---
198	config:
199	  sankey:
200	    showValues: false
201	    labelStyle: outlined
202	---
203	sankey
204	
205	Electricity grid,Heating and cooling - homes,113.726
206	Electricity grid,Industry,342.165
207	Electricity grid,Losses,56.691
208	```
209	
210	### Node Width and Padding (v11.15.0+)
211	
212	You can customize the node dimensions:
213	
214	- `nodeWidth` - width of the node rectangles in pixels (default: `10`)
215	- `nodePadding` - vertical padding between nodes in pixels (default: `12`)
216	
217	```mermaid-example
218	---
219	config:
220	  sankey:
221	    showValues: false
222	    nodeWidth: 15
223	    nodePadding: 20
224	---
225	sankey
226	
227	Electricity grid,Heating and cooling - homes,113.726
228	Electricity grid,Industry,342.165
229	Electricity grid,Losses,56.691
230	```
231	
232	### Custom Node Colors (v11.15.0+)
233	
234	You can assign specific colors to nodes using the `nodeColors` map. Nodes not listed will use the default color scheme. Values must be valid CSS colors (hex, `rgb()`, `hsl()`, or named colors).
235	
236	```mermaid-example
237	---
238	config:
239	  sankey:
240	    showValues: false
241	    nodeColors:
242	      Electricity grid: "#4e79a7"
243	      Industry: "#e15759"
244	      Losses: "#bab0ab"
245	---
246	sankey
247	
248	Electricity grid,Heating and cooling - homes,113.726
249	Electricity grid,Industry,342.165
250	Electricity grid,Losses,56.691
251	```
252
