# Use Case Diagram

**Source**: `mermaid-upstream/packages/mermaid/src/docs/syntax/usecase.md` (438 lines)
**Detector**: `src/diagrams/usecase/usecaseDetector.ts` — `/^\s*usecase-beta(?:\s|$)/`
**Minimum version**: **unknown** — the page still carries the literal placeholder
`<MERMAID_RELEASE_VERSION>+` (`:1`), so upstream has not cut the release.
**Registry id**: `usecase`
**Not published on the mermaid.ai documentation site.** Merged 2026-08-14.

> **Partial extraction.** Lines 1–230 captured. Lines 230–438 — remaining edge features,
> JSON nodes, notes, styling and configuration — are **not yet extracted**.

The best-specified page in the whole catalog: it states tokenization rules explicitly,
which most pages do not.

## Identifiers (`:21`)

Match `[A-Za-z0-9_]+`, **so they may start with a digit** — `1`, `1mg`, `3rd` are valid.
Identifiers are **diagram-wide**, shared by actors, use cases, boundaries, JSON nodes and
explicit edges.

A quoted declaration such as `"Reset password"` gets a deterministic identifier by
**replacing each non-word character with `_`** → `Reset_password` (`:36`, `:148`).

## Declarations (`:19-38`)

```
actor Customer
actor Admin("Main administrator")
Login("Sign in")      ellipse use case
Report[Generate report]   rectangle use case
"Reset password"          quoted, id derived
```

Resolution rules (`:38`):

- An endpoint may appear **before** its declaration; final order does not affect kind,
  shape or label.
- An undeclared endpoint becomes an **ellipse use case**.
- **Actors are never inferred** — they always require an `actor` declaration.

## Actor Variants (`:40-60`)

`@{ type: hollow }`, `@{ type: awesome }`, `@{ icon: "fa:user" }`. Default is the normal
stick actor.

Metadata accepts **only** `type`, `icon`, `business`. An icon **cannot** combine with a
non-normal `type` or with `business: true`. A missing icon renders the unknown-icon
fallback rather than failing the diagram (`:58`).

## Business Elements And Stereotypes (`:62-79`)

`business: true` adds the business slash — valid on normal/hollow actors and ellipse use
cases only. **Not** on rectangular use cases, awesome actors, or icon actors.

Stereotype: `<<Employee>>`, placed **after metadata and before a `:::` class suffix**.
Case is preserved; renders above the main label. Stereotypes create no CSS classes.

Suffix order, used consistently by actors, use cases and boundaries (`:132`):

```
<id><label>@{ … }<<stereotype>>:::<classes>
```

## Labels (`:81-110`)

Unquoted labels are taken **literally** from the source: digits, markdown markers,
punctuation, non-ASCII all pass through. One physical line; leading/trailing spaces dropped.

**Reserved inside an unquoted label** — the only things excluded (`:85`):
delimiters `(` `)` `[` `]` `{` `}`, quotes `"` `'`, and the sequences
`--`, `-->`, `<--`, `--o`, `--x`, `--|>`, `..>`, `:::`, `@{`, `<<`.
A lone `-`, `.`, `:`, `@`, `<`, `>` is ordinary text.

Plain strings stay plain — markdown markers display literally. Mermaid Markdown strings
use `"` outside and backticks inside, and may contain **physical newlines**.

**No backslash escapes**: `"First\nSecond"` shows a literal backslash-n (`:110`). Use
entity codes — `#quot;`, `#39;`, `#40;`, `#41;`, `#91;`, `#93;`, `#96;` — or a physical
newline inside a markdown string.

## Lines And Comments (`:112-128`)

- One statement per physical line, except markdown strings, multiline metadata, JSON
  objects, accessibility blocks and boundary blocks.
- `%%` starts a whole-line comment, after optional indentation.
- **`//` and `#` are not comments. A semicolon is not a separator.**
- **Any token after a complete statement on the same line is an error** — unusually strict,
  and a precise diagnostic.
- Blank lines and comments retain source order in the public AST.

## System Boundaries (`:130-162`)

```
systemBoundary sb1["Payment service"]@{ type: package }:::system
  actor Clerk("Payment clerk")
  Authorize("Authorize payment")
end
```

- Bracket form does **not** select a shape here; geometry comes from `type` only.
- `type` defaults to `rect`; `package` renders a title tab. A later metadata statement
  overrides inline metadata for the same key.
- **Boundaries are one level deep.** Contents may contain only actor and use case
  declarations, blank lines and comments. Relationships, notes, JSON nodes, `direction`,
  class/style statements, boundary metadata and nested boundaries stay at top level.
- An element belongs to **at most one** boundary.

## Relationships (`:164-213`)

Seven solid associations: `-->`, `<--`, `--`, `--o`, `o--`, `--x`, `x--`. Marker direction
and type are preserved. Labels allowed; **a label containing `include` or `extend` is
still an ordinary association** (`:185`).

Explicit UML operators:

| Operator | Meaning | Constraint |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `..> : include X` | source includes target | both must be use cases |
| `..> : extend X` | source extends target | both must be use cases |
| `--\|>` | generalization | two actors **or** two use cases |

JSON nodes accept only point, reversed-point and markerless solid associations — not
circle, cross, include, extend or generalization (`:194`).

## Edge IDs (`:215-230`)

`Customer opens@-- "starts checkout" ---> Checkout`. The id goes immediately before the
operator, shares the diagram-wide namespace, and can be targeted by `class`, `style` and
metadata — including `opens@{ animation: fast }` and `payment@{ animate: false }`.

## Editor Notes

- The reserved-sequence list at `:85` is a tokenizer specification — implement it exactly.
- Diagnostics with real value, all explicitly specified upstream:
  - a token after a complete statement on the same line;
  - `//` or `#` used as a comment;
  - `icon` combined with a non-normal `type` or `business: true`;
  - `business: true` on a rectangular use case, awesome actor or icon actor;
  - `include`/`extend` with a non-use-case endpoint;
  - generalization mixing an actor and a use case;
  - a relationship endpoint used as an actor without an `actor` declaration;
  - a nested `systemBoundary`, or a non-declaration statement inside one.
- Completion: identifiers already in the document; the three metadata keys; `hollow` /
  `awesome` after `type`.
- Fold `systemBoundary … end`.

## The Thing That Matters Most

ZenUML is **not part of the `mermaid` package**. There is no detector under
`src/diagrams/`; the renderer ships as `@mermaid-js/mermaid-zenuml` and must be registered
with `registerExternalDiagrams` before a `zenuml` document will render at all.

This is why the registry marks it `external: true`. Two consequences for us:

1. **It will not render in our render frame until we add and register that package.**
   Without it, a valid `zenuml` document produces an "unknown diagram type" error, which
   our normalizer must map to the `external-diagram-not-registered` error kind rather than
   a generic parse failure.
2. It is a **third-party sequence-diagram engine with its own syntax** (`:5-6`), unrelated
   to mermaid's own `sequenceDiagram`. Nothing from the sequence dialect carries over.

## Participants (`:18-61`)

- Implicit by first appearance, or declared explicitly on their own line to control order.
- **Annotators**: `@Actor Alice`, `@Database Bob`. The full list of annotators is only in
  an image (`img/zenuml-participant-annotators.png`, `:48`) — **not extractable from
  text**. Get it from the `@mermaid-js/mermaid-zenuml` source when we add the dependency.
- Aliases: `A as Alice`.

## Messages (`:63-144`)

Four kinds:

| Kind | Syntax |
| --- | --- |
| Sync | `A.SyncMessage`, `A.SyncMessage(with, parameters) { … }` |
| Async | `Alice->Bob: How are you?` |
| Creation | `new A1`, `new A2(with, parameters)` |
| Reply | three forms, below |

Reply messages (`:106-128`):

```
a = A.SyncMessage()              assign a variable
SomeType a = A.SyncMessage()     optionally typed
A.SyncMessage() { return result }
@return
A->B: result                     annotator form, returns one level up
```

## Nesting (`:146-156`)

Sync and creation messages nest naturally with `{ }` — this is a **block-structured,
code-like syntax**, closer to a programming language than to any other mermaid dialect.

## Comments (`:158-173`)

**`//`, not `%%`** — the only mermaid diagram type where this is true. Markdown is
supported inside comments. Comments render **above** messages and fragments; comments
elsewhere (for example on a participant) are ignored.

## Editor Notes

- The dialect is closer to a C-like language than to mermaid: braces, dot-calls,
  assignments, `new`, `return`, `if`. Indentation-aware bracket matching and auto-closing
  pay off more here than anywhere else.
- **Comment token differs**: `//`. The shared preamble layer in `packages/editor/core`
  assumes `%%` — this dialect must override it. Getting that wrong makes every comment
  highlight incorrectly.
- Before building the dialect, decide whether to take on the `@mermaid-js/mermaid-zenuml`
  dependency. It is the only diagram type that costs an extra package, and it duplicates
  a capability we already have in `sequenceDiagram`.
- If we do **not** ship it, the catalog status must say so plainly and the editor should
  tell the user why their `zenuml` document does not render — not fail with a confusing
  parse error.

# Block Diagram

**Source**: `mermaid-upstream/packages/mermaid/src/docs/syntax/block.md` (520 lines)
**Detector**: `src/diagrams/block/blockDetector.ts` — `/^\s*block(-beta)?/`
**Registry id**: `block`

> **Partial extraction.** Lines 1–280 captured. Lines 280–520 — remaining block arrows,
> space blocks, edges, styling and configuration — are **not yet extracted**.

## Why It Exists (`:33`)

The point of this type, in upstream's own words: people use flowcharts for architecture
sketches, and *"the automatic layout sometimes move shapes to positions that the diagram
maker does not want. Block diagrams use a different approach… we give the author full
control over where the shapes are positioned."*

**Layout is manual.** That reframes what the editor should help with: not connectivity,
but grid position.

## Layout

```
block
  a b c              blocks on one line, laid out horizontally
```

- `columns <n>` sets the column count; blocks wrap to the next row (`:71-86`).
- `columns auto` is the default inside a nested block (`:149`).
- **Width span**: `b:2` makes a block span 2 columns (`:103-109`).
- **Nested / composite blocks**: `block … end`, and with an id and span:
  `block:group1:2 … end` (`:111-152`).
- Column widths adjust dynamically to the widest block in the column (`:130-154`).
- Vertical stacking is achieved by nesting a block with `columns 1` (`:156-167`).

So the grammar for a block reference is `id[:span]` and for a nested block
`block[:id[:span]]`.

## Shapes (`:171-268`)

Same delimiters as flowchart, but **labels are quoted in every example**:

| Syntax | Shape |
| --- | --- |
| `id1("text")` | round edges |
| `id1(["text"])` | stadium |
| `id1[["text"]]` | subroutine |
| `id1[("text")]` | cylinder |
| `id1(("text"))` | circle |
| `id1>"text"]` | asymmetric |
| `id1{"text"}` | rhombus |
| `id1{{"text"}}` | hexagon |
| `id1[/"text"/]`, `id1[\"text"\]` | parallelogram |
| `A[/"Christmas"\]`, `B[\"Go shopping"/]` | trapezoid |
| `id1((("text")))` | double circle |

## Block Arrows And Space (`:270-280+`)

- **Block arrow**: `blockArrowId<["Label"]>(right)` — the direction is a separate
  parenthesized argument. The intro example uses `(down)` (`:14`).
- **`space`** is a keyword producing an empty grid cell (`:20`), used to control layout.
  There is a `space:N` form to skip several cells — details past the extraction boundary.

## Edges And Styling

Flowchart-style edges (`ID --> D`, `:22`) and `style` statements (`:24`) work. A nested
block's id can be an edge endpoint — `ID --> D` where `ID` is the composite block.

Details past line 280.

## Editor Notes

- **The highest-value editor feature here is a grid preview**, not completion: show the
  current column count and which cell the cursor's block will land in. Manual layout is
  the whole point of the type, and no editor helps with it today.
- Completion: `columns`, `space`, `block`, `end`, and the direction words inside
  `blockArrow…(…)`.
- Diagnostics: a `:span` larger than the current `columns`; an edge referencing an
  undefined id; a nested `block` without `end`.
- Fold `block … end`.
- Shares the flowchart shape tokenizer, so build it on the same core — but note labels are
  conventionally quoted here, and `space` is a reserved word that is not an id.

# C4 Diagram

**Source**: `mermaid-upstream/packages/mermaid/src/docs/syntax/c4.md` (378 lines)
**Detector**: `src/diagrams/c4/c4Detector.ts`
**Registry id**: `c4`

> **Experimental, and upstream says so bluntly** (`:3`): *"The syntax and properties can
> change in future releases. Proper documentation will be provided when the syntax is
> stable."* The mermaid.ai navigation marks this type with warning icons.
>
> **Partial extraction.** Lines 1–130 captured. Lines 130–378 — remaining relationship
> types, styling helpers and layout config — are **not yet extracted**.

Syntax is compatible with PlantUML's C4-PlantUML (`:5`), and upstream defers to
[that README](https://github.com/plantuml-stdlib/C4-PlantUML/blob/master/README.md) rather
than documenting the language itself (`:64`). That is the real reference for this type.

## Detector Quirk

The upstream regex is:

```
/^\s*C4Context|C4Container|C4Component|C4Dynamic|C4Deployment/
```

Because `|` has lower precedence than the anchor, **only the first alternative is
anchored**. The other four match anywhere in the text. This is an upstream defect; our
registry transcribes it faithfully so detection behaves identically, but it means a
document mentioning `C4Container` in a comment can be detected as C4. Worth a note in the
detection tests.

## Five Diagram Kinds (`:56-62`)

`C4Context`, `C4Container`, `C4Component`, `C4Dynamic`, `C4Deployment`.

## Elements (`:85-122`)

All use a call-like form: `Name(alias, label, ?descr, ?sprite, ?tags, $link)`.

**System Context**: `Person`, `Person_Ext`, `System`, `SystemDb`, `SystemQueue`,
`System_Ext`, `SystemDb_Ext`, `SystemQueue_Ext`, `Boundary(alias, label, ?type, ?tags, $link)`,
`Enterprise_Boundary`, `System_Boundary`.

**Container**: `Container(alias, label, ?techn, ?descr, ?sprite, ?tags, $link)`,
`ContainerDb`, `ContainerQueue`, `Container_Ext`, `ContainerDb_Ext`, `ContainerQueue_Ext`,
`Container_Boundary`.

**Component**: `Component(alias, label, ?techn, ?descr, …)`, `ComponentDb`,
`ComponentQueue`, `Component_Ext`, `ComponentDb_Ext`, `ComponentQueue_Ext`.

**Dynamic**: `RelIndex(index, from, to, label, ?tags, $link)`.

**Deployment**: `Deployment_Node(alias, label, ?type, ?descr, …)`, `Node` (short form),
`Node_L` (left aligned), `Node_R` (right aligned).

Boundaries take a `{ … }` block containing nested elements.

## Relationships (`:124-130`)

`Rel(from, to, label, ?techn, ?descr, ?sprite, ?tags, $link)`, `BiRel`, and the directional
variants `Rel_U`/`Rel_Up`, `Rel_D`/`Rel_Down`, `Rel_L`/`Rel_Left`, `Rel_R`/`Rel_Right`.

## Styling And Layout (`:43-76`)

- `UpdateElementStyle(alias, $fontColor=…, $bgColor=…, $borderColor=…)`
- `UpdateRelStyle(from, to, $textColor=…, $lineColor=…, $offsetX=…, $offsetY=…)`
- `UpdateLayoutConfig($c4ShapeInRow="3", $c4BoundaryInRow="1")`

Style statements go **last in the diagram** (`:67`).

> **C4 is fixed-style**: *"such as css color, so different css is not provided under
> different skins"* (`:66`). It will **not follow our theme tokens**, unlike every other
> type. Either accept that C4 looks different from the rest of the app, or generate
> `UpdateElementStyle` calls from the token set. Worth a product decision, and worth
> saying plainly in the UI rather than letting it look like a bug.

**Layout is manual**: shape position is controlled by statement order, and upstream has
*"no plan to support"* the `Lay_U`/`Lay_D`/`Lay_L`/`Lay_R` statements (`:69-76`).

## Not Supported (`:78-83`)

`sprite`, `tags`, `link`, `Legend` — all listed as unfinished. Note the element signatures
still *accept* `?sprite`, `?tags` and `$link` positionally, so a user can pass them and
have them silently ignored. Diagnostic candidate.

## Editor Notes

- The dialect is a call-syntax language: identifier, parentheses, comma-separated
  arguments, optional `$key="value"` pairs. Closer to railroad's IR form than to flowchart.
- Completion is genuinely valuable: ~30 element constructors with distinct argument lists.
  Show the signature as detail text.
- Completion for `from`/`to` in `Rel(…)`: aliases already defined.
- Diagnostics: unknown constructor; wrong argument count; `sprite`/`tags`/`link` passed
  but unsupported; a `Rel` referencing an undefined alias; a style statement not at the end.
- Fold boundary `{ … }` blocks.
- Because upstream defers to C4-PlantUML for the real language, that README must be read
  before this dialect is considered complete — and cited here.

1	# GitGraph Diagrams
2	
3	> A Git Graph is a pictorial representation of git commits and git actions(commands) on various branches.
4	
5	These kind of diagram are particularly helpful to developers and devops teams to share their Git branching strategies. For example, it makes it easier to visualize how git flow works.
6	
7	Mermaid can render Git diagrams
8	
9	```mermaid-example
10	---
11	title: Example Git diagram
12	---
13	gitGraph
14	   commit
15	   commit
16	   branch develop
17	   checkout develop
18	   commit
19	   commit
20	   checkout main
21	   merge develop
22	   commit
23	   commit
24	```
25	
26	In Mermaid, we support the basic git operations like:
27	
28	- _commit_ : Representing a new commit on the current branch.
29	- _branch_ : To create & switch to a new branch, setting it as the current branch.
30	- _checkout_ : To checking out an existing branch and setting it as the current branch.
31	- _merge_ : To merge an existing branch onto the current branch.
32	
33	With the help of these key git commands, you will be able to draw a gitgraph in Mermaid very easily and quickly.
34	Entity names are often capitalized, although there is no accepted standard on this, and it is not required in Mermaid.
35	
36	**NOTE**: `checkout` and `switch` can be used interchangeably.
37	
38	## Syntax
39	
40	Mermaid syntax for a gitgraph is very straight-forward and simple. It follows a declarative-approach, where each commit is drawn on the timeline in the diagram, in order of its occurrences/presence in code. Basically, it follows the insertion order for each command.
41	
42	First thing you do is to declare your diagram type using the **gitgraph** keyword. This `gitgraph` keyword, tells Mermaid that you wish to draw a gitgraph, and parse the diagram code accordingly.
43	
44	Each gitgraph, is initialized with **_main_** branch. So unless you create a different branch, by-default the commits will go to the main branch. This is driven with how git works, where in the beginning you always start with the main branch (formerly called as **_master_** branch). And by-default, `main` branch is set as your **_current branch_**.
45	
46	You make use of **_commit_** keyword to register a commit on the current branch. Let see how this works:
47	
48	A simple gitgraph showing three commits on the default (**_main_**) branch:
49	
50	```mermaid-example
51	    gitGraph
52	       commit
53	       commit
54	       commit
55	```
56	
57	If you look closely at the previous example, you can see the default branch `main` along with three commits. Also, notice that by default each commit has been given a unique & random ID. What if you wanted to give your own custom ID to a commit? Yes, it is possible to do that with Mermaid.
58	
59	### Adding custom commit id
60	
61	For a given commit you may specify a custom ID at the time of declaring it using the `id` attribute, followed by `:` and your custom value within a `""` quote. For example: `commit id: "your_custom_id"`
62	
63	Let us see how this works with the help of the following diagram:
64	
65	```mermaid-example
66	    gitGraph
67	       commit id: "Alpha"
68	       commit id: "Beta"
69	       commit id: "Gamma"
70	```
71	
72	In this example, we have given our custom IDs to the commits.
73	
74	### Modifying commit type
75	
76	In Mermaid, a commit can be of three type, which render a bit different in the diagram. These types are:
77	
78	- `NORMAL` : Default commit type. Represented by a solid circle in the diagram
79	- `REVERSE` : To emphasize a commit as a reverse commit. Represented by a crossed solid circle in the diagram.
80	- `HIGHLIGHT` : To highlight a particular commit in the diagram. Represented by a filled rectangle in the diagram.
81	
82	For a given commit you may specify its type at the time of declaring it using the `type` attribute, followed by `:` and the required type option discussed above. For example: `commit type: HIGHLIGHT`
83	
84	NOTE: If no commit type is specified, `NORMAL` is picked as default.
85	
86	Let us see how these different commit type look with the help of the following diagram:
87	
88	```mermaid-example
89	    gitGraph
90	       commit id: "Normal"
91	       commit
92	       commit id: "Reverse" type: REVERSE
93	       commit
94	       commit id: "Highlight" type: HIGHLIGHT
95	       commit
96	```
97	
98	In this example, we have specified different types to each commit. Also, see how we have included both `id` and `type` together at the time of declaring our commits.
99	
100	### Adding Tags
101	
102	For a given commit you may decorate it as a **tag**, similar to the concept of tags or release version in git world.
103	You can attach a custom tag at the time of declaring a commit using the `tag` attribute, followed by `:` and your custom value within `""` quote. For example: `commit tag: "your_custom_tag"`
104	
105	Let us see how this works with the help of the following diagram:
106	
107	```mermaid-example
108	    gitGraph
109	       commit
110	       commit id: "Normal" tag: "v1.0.0"
111	       commit
112	       commit id: "Reverse" type: REVERSE tag: "RC_1"
113	       commit
114	       commit id: "Highlight" type: HIGHLIGHT tag: "8.8.4"
115	       commit
116	```
117	
118	In this example, we have given custom tags to the commits. Also, see how we have combined all these attributes in a single commit declaration. You can mix-match these attributes as you like.
119	
120	### Create a new branch
121	
122	In Mermaid, in-order to create a new branch, you make use of the `branch` keyword. You also need to provide a name of the new branch. The name has to be unique and cannot be that of an existing branch. A branch name that could be confused for a keyword must be quoted within `""`. Usage examples: `branch develop`, `branch "cherry-pick"`
123	
124	When Mermaid, reads the `branch` keyword, it creates a new branch and sets it as the current branch. Equivalent to you creating a new branch and checking it out in Git world.
125	
126	Let see this in an example:
127	
128	```mermaid-example
129	    gitGraph
130	       commit
131	       commit
132	       branch develop
133	       commit
134	       commit
135	       commit
136	```
137	
138	In this example, see how we started with default `main` branch, and pushed two commits on that.
139	Then we created the `develop` branch, and all commits afterwards are put on the `develop` branch as it became the current branch.
140	
141	### Checking out an existing branch
142	
143	In Mermaid, in order to switch to an existing branch, you make use of the `checkout` keyword. You also need to provide a name of an existing branch. If no branch is found with the given name, it will result in console error. Usage example: `checkout develop`
144	
145	When Mermaid, reads the `checkout` keyword, it finds the given branch and sets it as the current branch. Equivalent to checking out a branch in the Git world.
146	
147	Let see modify our previous example:
148	
149	```mermaid-example
150	    gitGraph
151	       commit
152	       commit
153	       branch develop
154	       commit
155	       commit
156	       commit
157	       checkout main
158	       commit
159	       commit
160	```
161	
162	In this example, see how we started with default `main` branch, and pushed two commits on that.
163	Then we created the `develop` branch, and all three commits afterwards are put on the `develop` branch as it became the current branch.
164	After this we made use of the `checkout` keyword to set the current branch as `main`, and all commit that follow are registered against the current branch, i.e. `main`.
165	
166	### Merging two branches
167	
168	In Mermaid, in order to merge or join to an existing branch, you make use of the `merge` keyword. You also need to provide the name of an existing branch to merge from. If no branch is found with the given name, it will result in console error. Also, you can only merge two separate branches, and cannot merge a branch with itself. In such case an error is throw.
169	
170	Usage example: `merge develop`
171	
172	When Mermaid, reads the `merge` keyword, it finds the given branch and its head commit (the last commit on that branch), and joins it with the head commit on the **current branch**. Each merge results in a **_merge commit_**, represented in the diagram with **filled double circle**.
173	
174	Let us modify our previous example to merge our two branches:
175	
176	```mermaid-example
177	    gitGraph
178	       commit
179	       commit
180	       branch develop
181	       commit
182	       commit
183	       commit
184	       checkout main
185	       commit
186	       commit
187	       merge develop
188	       commit
189	       commit
190	```
191	
192	In this example, see how we started with default `main` branch, and pushed two commits on that.
193	Then we created the `develop` branch, and all three commits afterwards are put on the `develop` branch as it became the current branch.
194	After this we made use of the `checkout` keyword to set the current branch as `main`, and all commits that follow are registered against the current branch, i.e. `main`.
195	After this we merge the `develop` branch onto the current branch `main`, resulting in a merge commit.
196	Since the current branch at this point is still `main`, the last two commits are registered against that.
197	
198	You can also decorate your merge with similar attributes as you did for the commit using:
199	
200	- `id`--> To override the default ID with custom ID
201	- `tag`--> To add a custom tag to your merge commit
202	- `type`--> To override the default shape of merge commit. Here you can use other commit type mentioned earlier.
203	
204	And you can choose to use none, some or all of these attributes together.
205	For example: `merge develop id: "my_custom_id" tag: "my_custom_tag" type: REVERSE`
206	
207	Let us see how this works with the help of the following diagram:
208	
209	```mermaid-example
210	    gitGraph
211	       commit id: "1"
212	       commit id: "2"
213	       branch nice_feature
214	       checkout nice_feature
215	       commit id: "3"
216	       checkout main
217	       commit id: "4"
218	       checkout nice_feature
219	       branch very_nice_feature
220	       checkout very_nice_feature

# GitGraph Diagram

**Source**: `mermaid-upstream/packages/mermaid/src/docs/syntax/gitgraph.md` (1242 lines)
**Detector**: `src/diagrams/git/gitGraphDetector.ts` — `/^\s*gitGraph/`

> **Partial extraction.** Lines 1–220 captured. Lines 220–1242 — `cherry-pick`, orientation,
> `parallelCommits`, themes, the large configuration surface and `gitGraph:` alternate
> header forms — are **not yet extracted**. This is the second-largest page in the catalog.

Note the **camelCase keyword** `gitGraph`, while the file and the type are called
"gitgraph". The detector is case-sensitive.

## Model (`:38-44`)

Declarative and **insertion-ordered**: each command is drawn in source order. Every graph
starts on a `main` branch, which is the current branch until changed.

## Commands (`:26-36`)

| Keyword | Meaning |
| --- | --- |
| `commit` | new commit on the current branch |
| `branch <name>` | create **and switch to** a new branch |
| `checkout <name>` / `switch <name>` | switch to an existing branch |
| `merge <name>` | merge a branch into the current one |
| `cherry-pick` | past the extraction boundary |

**`checkout` and `switch` are interchangeable** (`:36`).

## Commit Attributes (`:59-118`)

```
commit id: "Alpha"
commit type: HIGHLIGHT
commit tag: "v1.0.0"
commit id: "Reverse" type: REVERSE tag: "RC_1"
```

- `id: "…"` — custom id, quoted. Otherwise a unique random id is generated.
- `type:` — `NORMAL` (default, solid circle), `REVERSE` (crossed solid circle),
  `HIGHLIGHT` (filled rectangle). **Unquoted, uppercase.**
- `tag: "…"` — quoted.
- Attributes are freely mix-and-matchable.

Note the asymmetry: `id` and `tag` take **quoted** values, `type` takes a **bare
uppercase keyword**. That is exactly the kind of thing completion should get right.

## Branch Rules (`:120-139`)

- The name must be **unique** and cannot collide with an existing branch.
- **A branch name that could be confused with a keyword must be quoted**:
  `branch "cherry-pick"` (`:122`).
- `branch` both creates and checks out.

## Merge (`:166-205`)

- Both branches must exist, or it is a console error.
- **A branch cannot be merged with itself** — that throws.
- Produces a merge commit, drawn as a filled double circle.
- Accepts the same `id`, `tag` and `type` attributes as `commit`:
  `merge develop id: "my_custom_id" tag: "my_custom_tag" type: REVERSE`.

## Editor Notes

- **This is the type where a document-aware editor wins biggest.** Every command references
  branch state that the editor can track exactly:
  - completion after `checkout`, `switch` and `merge` → branches that exist **at that point
    in the document**, not just anywhere in it;
  - completion after `branch` → nothing, but a diagnostic if the name already exists;
  - a status hint showing the current branch at the cursor, which the source does not make
    visible and which is the main thing people lose track of.
- Diagnostics, all documented as hard errors upstream:
  - `checkout`/`merge` of a branch that does not exist yet;
  - `branch` with a duplicate name;
  - `merge` of the current branch with itself;
  - an unquoted branch name that collides with a keyword;
  - a duplicate `commit id`.
- Completion for `type:` → the three uppercase constants, unquoted.
- No block structure, so folding has little to offer; effort belongs in the branch-state
  tracking above.

**Source**: **none** — there is no page under `docs/syntax/`.
**Detector**: `mermaid-upstream/packages/mermaid/src/diagrams/info/infoDetector.ts` —

From `infoDb.ts`:

```ts
export const DEFAULT_INFO_DB: InfoFields = {
  version: injected.version + (injected.includeLargeFeatures ? '' : '-tiny'),
}
```

It renders the **installed mermaid version**. That is the whole diagram. The `-tiny`
suffix appears when the build excludes large features.

## Syntax

`info` on the first line. Nothing else is documented, and the DB exposes only `getVersion`.

Historically this type also accepted a `showInfo` token; that is **not** verifiable from
the files in the current sparse checkout. Read `infoParser.ts`, `info.spec.ts` and the
Langium grammar under `packages/parser/src/language/` before claiming anything more.

## Editor Notes

- No dialect is needed beyond recognizing the single keyword.
- **Do not offer it in the diagram-type picker.** It is a diagnostic tool for checking
  which mermaid version is running, not a diagram anyone authors deliberately.
- It is genuinely useful to us in exactly one place: a developer panel that renders `info`
  to confirm the render frame is running the version we pinned. That is a better check
  than trusting the hardcoded string currently returned in the frame's `ready` message.
- Because the detector is the bare `/^\s*info/`, any document starting with the word
  "info" is detected as this type. A user writing prose that begins with "info" gets a
  version badge. Worth a hint rather than silent surprise.

Los 33, hechos. `verify` en verde, y comprobado que **cada id del registro tiene su página** — 33 archivos, 3.247 líneas, todas con cita a fichero y línea del upstream.

Para ser exacto sobre qué significa "hechos": **25 páginas cubren su documento completo**. Las otras **8 son parciales** (git, gantt, block, wardley, usecase, c4, timeline, zenuml) — son los documentos largos, y cada página dice en su cabecera qué líneas leí y qué falta. No las marqué como completas porque no lo están; el catálogo tiene la tabla con los rangos exactos.

Cerré además el hueco que había señalado: **las 53 formas de flowchart** están en `docs/knowledge/flowchart-shapes.md`, extraídas de `shapes.ts`. Y confirmó lo que sospechaba — los ejemplos de la documentación usan **alias, no nombres canónicos** (`subproc`→`fr-rect`, `diamond`→`diam`, `das`→`h-cyl`, `processes`→`st-rect`…), y hay **siete formas que no aparecen en ninguna documentación**: `folder`, `bucket`, `console`, `browser`, `person`, `bang`, `cloud`.

**Lo que salió de leerlas todas, que cambia decisiones:**

- **ZenUML no se puede renderizar** sin añadir `@mermaid-js/mermaid-zenuml` y registrarlo. Hoy un documento `zenuml` válido da "tipo desconocido". Hay que decidir si vale la pena: es un motor de terceros que duplica algo que ya tenemos en `sequenceDiagram`, y es el único tipo que cuesta una dependencia extra. Su comentario además es `//`, no `%%` — el único del catálogo.
- **Dos tipos más necesitan `seed` fijo para tests visuales**: cynefin y architecture. Architecture lo dice explícitamente — *"`randomize: false` no basta, fcose sigue llamando a `Math.random()`"*.
- **C4 es de estilo fijo** y no seguirá nuestros tokens de tema. O generamos `UpdateElementStyle` desde el token set, o C4 se verá distinto al resto de la app. Es una decisión de producto, no un bug.
- **El detector de C4 tiene un fallo de upstream**: `/^\s*C4Context|C4Container|.../` — solo la primera alternativa está anclada. Lo transcribí tal cual para que la detección se comporte igual, pero está anotado.
- **TreeView y Architecture necesitan iconify**, que choca con la promesa de cero peticiones de red en fase 1. Ambas páginas apuntan a la misma decisión: empaquetar un subconjunto dentro del render frame.

Y la incoherencia de `:::` que ya te mencioné se confirmó peor de lo que pensaba: son **cuatro posiciones distintas** según el tipo (flowchart pegado al nodo, mindmap en línea propia, treemap tras el valor, quadrant entre etiqueta y coma), más `cssClass "id"` con comillas solo en class diagram.

Siguiente: la tarea 4, los dialectos de CodeMirror. Empezaría por `pie` como implementación de referencia del contrato (es el más simple), y luego `flowchart`, que arrastra a `swimlanes` y `block` porque comparten tokenizador.

import type { DiagramTypeId } from '@mr/core'

/**
 * Per-dialect syntax data, derived from `docs/knowledge/diagrams/<id>.md`.
 *
 * This table is the single place keywords live. The tokenizer, the completion sources and
 * the starter snippets all read from here, so a keyword can never be right in one and
 * wrong in another. If this table and the catalog disagree, the catalog is fixed first —
 * see the `add-diagram-type` skill.
 */

export interface DialectData {
  /** Statements valid at the start of a line. */
  readonly statements: readonly string[]
  /** Bare constants and enum values, highlighted as such. */
  readonly constants: readonly string[]
  /** Multi-character operators, longest first. Order matters for tokenizing. */
  readonly operators: readonly string[]
  /** Keywords that open a foldable block. */
  readonly blockOpen: readonly string[]
  /** Keyword that closes a foldable block, when the dialect has one. */
  readonly blockClose: string | null
  /** Line-comment prefix. `%%` everywhere except zenuml. */
  readonly lineComment: string
  /** A starter that renders and is genuinely useful, not a two-node stub. */
  readonly starter: string

Acabado. **162 archivos, 12.104 líneas, commit `c23f624`.** `bun run verify` en verde: format, lint, typecheck, **152 tests**, build. Servidor en http://localhost:5273 (app 200, frame 200).

**Los 33 tipos, en código y no solo en documentación:**

- `packages/core` — registro con las regex de detección transcritas de los detectores de upstream.
- `packages/editor` — **33 dialectos de CodeMirror** generados desde una tabla única (`data.ts`), derivada del catálogo. Un test verifica que **el starter de cada tipo se detecta como su propio tipo** — los 33 pasan, así que ninguno tiene la keyword mal.
- `packages/export` — SVG standalone (resolviendo las CSS variables, o el archivo sale negro sobre negro fuera de la app), PNG/WEBP con clamp al área máxima de canvas, y PDF vectorial con carga diferida.
- `packages/storage` — puertos + adaptador IndexedDB con migraciones numeradas y UUID v7.
- `apps/web` — dialecto y autocompletado en compartments (cambiar de flowchart a sequence no pierde el undo), errores en el gutter, selector de tipos, diálogo de export, autoguardado.

**Una corrección de fondo, la segunda del proyecto.** Documenté que el rasterizado iría en un Web Worker con `OffscreenCanvas`. Al implementarlo comprobé que tampoco es posible: rasterizar SVG necesita el decodificador de imágenes del navegador vía `HTMLImageElement`, y `createImageBitmap` no acepta blobs SVG en Firefox. Va en el hilo principal. Actualicé `stack.md`, `rendering.md`, `AGENTS.md` y el ADR 0003 para que el código y la documentación digan lo mismo.

**Lo que dejo sin terminar, explícitamente:**

- **8 páginas de catálogo siguen parciales** — git, gantt, block, wardley, usecase, c4, timeline, zenuml. Cada una dice qué líneas leí y qué falta, y la tabla está en `diagram-catalog.md`. Son los documentos largos.
- **Ningún tipo está marcado `supported`**, y es correcto: el criterio son cinco cosas (renderiza, resalta, autocompleta, diagnostica, exporta) y los diagnósticos específicos por dialecto no existen todavía. Hoy hay resaltado y autocompletado genéricos, no las comprobaciones concretas que documenté (el `end` en minúscula de flowchart, `m` vs `M` en gantt, coordenadas transpuestas en wardley).
- **Sin tests visuales.** Playwright está en el plan, no instalado. Y como te dije antes: `verify` en verde no prueba que se vea bien. **Ábrelo.**
- ZenUML sigue sin renderizar hasta que se decida si añadir su paquete.
Puedo probarlo en local o aún no está?
Sí, está corriendo ahora mismo. Lo dejé levantado.

**http://localhost:5273** — ábrelo.

Si lo cierras y quieres volver a levantarlo:

```bash
cd ~/Documentos/mermaid-render
bun run dev
```

**Qué probar, en orden de lo que más probable es que falle:**

1. **Carga inicial.** Debería aparecer el flowchart de ejemplo ya renderizado, con la barra de arriba diciendo `Flowchart` y `mermaid 11.16.1`.
2. **Rompe la sintaxis a propósito.** Borra un `-->` a medias. El diagrama **no debe desaparecer** — se atenúa y sale el error abajo en rojo, con un subrayado en la línea. Esto es lo que hace mal el playground oficial y es la razón principal del proyecto.
3. **"New diagram"** → busca cualquiera de los 32 tipos. Elige algo raro: `wardley-beta`, `cynefin-beta`, `treeView-beta`, `radar-beta`. Cada uno trae un starter que debería renderizar solo.
4. **Autocompletado** — `Ctrl+Espacio` a principio de línea. Ofrece los statements del dialecto actual; en medio de una línea ofrece identificadores del documento.
5. **Export** → SVG, PNG a 4×, PDF. El PDF tarda un poco la primera vez porque carga jspdf bajo demanda.
6. **Recarga la página.** Lo que escribiste debe seguir ahí (IndexedDB, autoguardado a los 700 ms).
7. **Pan y zoom** en el canvas: rueda para zoom, arrastrar para mover, botón "Fit".

git add -A && git commit -q -m "fix: make the diagram actually render, and install shadcn/ui

Three defects kept the preview blank, each found by opening a real browser
rather than by reading the code:

- The render frame never booted. sandbox=\"allow-scripts\" without
  allow-same-origin gives the frame an opaque origin, so loading its own
  module became a cross-origin request needing CORS. That combination is
  therefore not a usable security boundary; the boundary has to be a
  separate origin, and in phase 1 the defence that holds is strict mode
  plus DOMPurify.
- mermaid threw 'Unsupported color format: oklch(...)'. Neither
  getComputedStyle nor canvas.fillStyle converts it — both preserve the
  colour space under CSS Color 4 — so tokens are now resolved by painting
  a pixel and reading it back. mermaid.initialize also moved inside the
  try block: a job that threw before it never answered, so the host waited
  for its 20s timeout instead of reporting the error.

**Tres bugs, y ninguno se veía leyendo el código.** Los encontré abriendo Chromium:

Mi ADR decía que ese sandbox era la frontera de seguridad; era un bloqueo total. Corregido en el código y en el ADR: la frontera real es servir el frame desde otro origen, y en fase 1 lo que protege es `strict` + DOMPurify.
2. **`Unsupported color format: "oklch(...)"`.** Mis tokens están en oklch y mermaid no los parsea. Probé `getComputedStyle` y `canvas.fillStyle`: **ninguno convierte**, porque CSS Color 4 preserva el espacio de color en ambos. La única vía fiable es pintar un píxel y leerlo. Además `mermaid.initialize` estaba fuera del `try`, así que el error no se reportaba y el host esperaba 20 s en silencio.

# /loop — schedule a recurring or self-paced prompt

Parse the input below into `[interval] <prompt…>` and schedule it.

## Parsing (in priority order)

1. **Leading token**: if the first whitespace-delimited token matches `^\d+[smhd]$` (e.g. `5m`, `2h`), that's the interval; the rest is the prompt.
2. **Trailing "every" clause**: otherwise, if the input ends with `every <N><unit>` or `every <N> <unit-word>` (e.g. `every 20m`, `every 5 minutes`, `every 2 hours`), extract that as the interval and strip it from the prompt. Only match when what follows "every" is a time expression — `check every PR` has no interval.
3. **No interval**: otherwise, the entire input is the prompt and you'll self-pace dynamically (see "Dynamic mode" below).

If the resulting prompt is empty, show usage `/loop [interval] <prompt>` and stop.

Examples:
- `5m /babysit-prs` → interval `5m`, prompt `/babysit-prs` (rule 1)
- `check the deploy every 20m` → interval `20m`, prompt `check the deploy` (rule 2)
- `run tests every 5 minutes` → interval `5m`, prompt `run tests` (rule 2)
- `check the deploy` → no interval → dynamic mode, prompt `check the deploy` (rule 3)
- `check every PR` → no interval → dynamic mode, prompt `check every PR` (rule 3 — "every" not followed by time)
- `5m` → empty prompt → show usage

## Offer cloud first

Before any scheduling step, check whether EITHER is true:
- the parsed interval (rule 1 or 2) is **≥60 minutes**, or
- regardless of which rule matched, the original input uses daily phrasing ("every morning", "daily", "every day", "each night", "every weekday")

If either is true, call AskUserQuestion first:
- `question`: "This loop stops when you close this session. Set it up as a cloud schedule instead so it keeps running?"
- `header`: "Schedule"
- `options`: `[{label: "Cloud schedule (recommended)", description: "Runs in Anthropic's cloud even after you close this session"}, {label: "This session only", description: "Runs in this terminal until you exit"}]`

If they pick **Cloud schedule**: do NOT call CronCreate. Invoke the `schedule` skill directly via the Skill tool with `args` set to their original input verbatim (e.g. `Skill({skill: "schedule", args: "every morning tell me a joke"})`), then follow that skill's instructions to completion. Do NOT tell the user to run /schedule themselves. **Then stop — do not continue to any section below** (no CronCreate, no ScheduleWakeup, no "execute the prompt now").
If they pick **This session only**:
- If the trigger was a parsed ≥60-minute interval (rule 1 or 2): continue below with that interval.
- If the trigger was daily phrasing only (rule 3, no parsed interval): do NOT call CronCreate. Explain that a daily-cadence loop won't fire before this session closes, so there's nothing useful to schedule locally — suggest they either pick Cloud schedule, or re-run `/loop` with an explicit shorter interval (e.g. `/loop 1h <prompt>`) if they want a session loop. Then stop.
If neither trigger condition was met: continue below.

## Fixed-interval mode (rules 1 and 2)

Convert the interval to a cron expression:

| Interval pattern      | Cron expression     | Notes                                    |
|-----------------------|---------------------|------------------------------------------|
| `Nm` where N ≤ 59   | `*/N * * * *`     | every N minutes                          |
| `Nm` where N ≥ 60   | `0 */H * * *`     | round to hours (H = N/60, must divide 24)|
| `Nh` where N ≤ 23   | `0 */N * * *`     | every N hours                            |
| `Nd`                | `0 0 */N * *`     | every N days at midnight local           |
| `Ns`                | treat as `ceil(N/60)m` | cron minimum granularity is 1 minute  |

**If the interval doesn't cleanly divide its unit** (e.g. `7m` → `*/7 * * * *` gives uneven gaps at :56→:00; `90m` → 1.5h which cron can't express), pick the nearest clean interval and tell the user what you rounded to before scheduling.

Then:
1. Call CronCreate with: `cron` (the expression above), `prompt` (the parsed prompt verbatim), `recurring: true`.
2. Briefly confirm: what's scheduled, the cron expression, the human-readable cadence, that recurring tasks auto-expire after 7 days, and that the user can cancel sooner with CronDelete (include the job ID). Only if you did NOT show the cloud-offer AskUserQuestion above (i.e., neither trigger condition applied), end the confirmation with this exact line on its own, italicized: `_Runs until you close this session · For durable cloud-based loops, use /schedule_`. If the user already answered that question, omit this line.
3. **Then immediately execute the parsed prompt now** — don't wait for the first cron fire. If it's a slash command, invoke it via the Skill tool; otherwise act on it directly.

## Dynamic mode (rule 3 — no interval)

The user wants you to self-pace. Decide what makes the next iteration worth running — a passage of time, or an observable event.

1. **Run the parsed prompt now.** If it's a slash command, invoke it via the Skill tool; otherwise act on it directly.
2. **If the next run is gated on an event** (CI finishing, a log line matching, a file changing, a PR comment) and no Monitor is already running for it: arm one now with `persistent: true`. Its events arrive as `<task-notification>` messages and wake this loop immediately — you do not wait for the ScheduleWakeup deadline. Arm once; on later iterations call TaskList first and skip this step if a monitor is already running.
3. **Briefly confirm**: that you're self-pacing, whether a Monitor is the primary wake signal, that you ran the task now, and what fallback delay you're about to pick. Write this as text *before* calling ScheduleWakeup — the turn ends as soon as that tool returns.
4. **Then, as the last action of this turn, decide whether the loop continues.** If the task needs another iteration, call ScheduleWakeup with:
   - `delaySeconds`: with a Monitor armed this is the **fallback heartbeat** — how long to wait if no event fires (lean 1200–1800s; idle ticks more frequent than the task needs are pure overhead). Without a Monitor this is the cadence — pick based on what you observed. Read the tool's own description for cache-aware delay guidance.
   - `reason`: one short sentence on why you picked that delay.
   - `prompt`: the full original /loop input verbatim, prefixed with `/loop ` so the next firing re-enters this skill and continues the loop. For example, if the user typed `/loop check the deploy`, pass `/loop check the deploy` as the prompt.
   If it doesn't need another iteration, stop instead (step 6) — re-arming is a per-turn choice, not a default.
5. **If you were woken by a `<task-notification>`** rather than this prompt: handle the event in the context of the loop task, then make the same decision. If the loop should continue, call ScheduleWakeup again with the same `prompt` and the same 1200–1800s `delaySeconds` from step 4 (the Monitor remains the wake signal; the new wakeup is only the fallback heartbeat). If the event means the work is finished, stop (step 6).
6. **To stop the loop** — the task is complete, further iterations can't make progress, or the user asked you to stop — call ScheduleWakeup with `stop: true` (no other fields) and TaskStop any Monitor you armed (use TaskList to find the task ID if it is no longer in context). Stopping is the loop's normal ending — the user can restart it anytime with /loop.

input.content:
# Phase 1 remainder and phase 2 entry points

Phase 1 is complete and verified: `bun run verify` runs 220 unit tests and 37 end-to-end
tests in Chromium, including one per diagram type asserting its starter renders.

What follows is everything deliberately left open, with enough context to pick up cold.

## 1. Two product decisions, blocking their features

Neither can be resolved from the code; both change what the product promises.

### ZenUML

`zenuml` does not render. It ships as `@mermaid-js/mermaid-zenuml` and needs
`registerExternalDiagrams` — there is no detector for it inside the `mermaid` package.

- **Adopt it**: one extra dependency, and the only diagram type that costs one. Its
  syntax is a third-party sequence-diagram language unrelated to mermaid's own, and its
  comment token is `//`, not `%%`, so the shared preamble layer needs an override. Its
  annotator list exists only as an image in the docs and must come from that package's
  source.
- **Drop it**: the catalog stays honest at 32 renderable types, and the editor must say
  plainly why a `zenuml` document does not render — the `external-diagram-not-registered`
  error kind already exists for exactly this.

Recommendation: drop it for now. It duplicates `sequenceDiagram`, which is already
`supported`. Revisit if users ask.

### Icon packs

`architecture` ships five icons (`cloud`, `database`, `disk`, `internet`, `server`) and
`treeView` ships none. Everything else needs a registered iconify pack — which conflicts
with the phase-1 promise of **zero outbound requests**, asserted by an end-to-end test.

- **Bundle a curated subset** (`logos:` for architecture, `material-icon-theme:` for
  treeView) inside the render frame. Keeps the promise, costs bundle size.
- **Fetch on demand**, and drop the zero-network claim from the README and the test.

Recommendation: bundle a subset. The claim is worth more than the icons.

## 2. Eight catalog pages are partially extracted

Each page states its own boundary in its header. Finish before promoting those types
past `partial`.

| Type | Read | Total | Missing |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `git` | 1–220 | 1242 | cherry-pick, orientation, parallelCommits, themes, config |
| `gantt` | 1–300 | 559 | remaining config, styling, today marker |
| `block` | 1–280 | 520 | block arrows, space blocks, edges, styling, config |
| `wardley` | 1–240 | 461 | pipelines, annotations, markets, submaps, styling |
| `usecase` | 1–230 | 438 | JSON nodes, notes, styling, config |
| `c4` | 1–130 | 378 | relationship types, styling helpers, layout config |
| `timeline` | 1–130 | 360 | direction options, styling, config |
| `zenuml` | 1–180 | 314 | loops, opt, par, try/catch/finally, config |

Three types cannot be completed from documentation at all — `user-journey` (24-line page)
and `ishikawa` (38-line page) need their `.jison` grammars; `c4` defers to the
C4-PlantUML README. Each page names the file to read.

## 3. Fifteen types are `partial` for one reason: no diagnostics

`class`, `state`, `er`, `user-journey`, `requirement`, `git`, `c4`, `mindmap`, `timeline`,
`packet`, `architecture`, `eventmodeling`, `treeview`, `usecase`, `ishikawa`.

Each per-type catalog page already lists its candidate rules under "Editor Notes". The
highest-value ones, because they catch silent failures:

- **packet**: overlapping or gapped bit ranges — the entire point of the diagram type,
  and nothing else catches it.
- **architecture**: an `align` order that contradicts an edge direction makes the layout
  engine **fail to render**, and it is statically detectable.
- **class**: a method return type written without the required space before it.
- **er**: a partially specified relationship, which is all-or-nothing.
- **git**: `checkout`/`merge` of a branch that does not exist *at that point* in the
  document — this dialect is where document-aware analysis wins biggest.

Add them the same way as the existing sixteen: a rule in `packages/editor/src/diagnostics.ts`
citing its upstream line, plus a case in the suite. The starters must stay silent — that
test is the guard against false positives.

## 4. Known limitations worth fixing before phase 2

- **Coarse mode is documented but not implemented.** `rendering.md` describes downgrading
  the preview above a node threshold; `coarseThreshold` is passed to the frame and the
  result carries a `coarse` flag, but nothing consumes it. Large-diagram performance
  currently rests on cancellation alone.
- **The render frame's sandbox is not a boundary.** It needs `allow-same-origin` to load
  its own module, which negates the sandbox. The real boundary is a separate origin — a
  deployment task, recorded in `adr/0003-render-frame-not-worker.md`.
- **`parse` before `render` is specified but unused.** The frame implements a `parse`
  message; the host never sends one. Sending it first would make a half-typed document
  much cheaper.
- **No visual regression tests.** Playwright asserts that a diagram renders, not that it
  looks right. `cynefin` and `architecture` both need a pinned `seed` before snapshots
  can be stable.
- **No document rename in the UI.** `workspace.rename` exists and nothing calls it.

## 5. Phase 2 entry points

Designed, not built. See `docs/architecture/backend.md`, `authentication.md`,
`deployment.md`. The storage ports in `packages/storage/src/ports.ts` are the seam: the
server implements the same contract, and nothing above them changes.

content.text:
Aquí está el problema de cada uno, concreto.

## ZenUML

**No forma parte de mermaid.** Es un motor de terceros que se distribuye aparte (`@mermaid-js/mermaid-zenuml`, v0.2.3) y hay que registrarlo con `registerExternalDiagrams`. Por eso hoy, si escribes `zenuml`, no sale nada.

Añadirlo es fácil — una dependencia y unas 10 líneas. **El problema no es el coste, es si tiene sentido tenerlo:**

- Es **otro lenguaje distinto**, no una variante de mermaid. Sintaxis de llamadas con llaves, `A.metodo() { ... }`, `new`, `return`, `if`.
- Sus comentarios son **`//`**, no `%%`. Es el único tipo del catálogo así, y obliga a que el dialecto rompa la capa común del editor.
- **La lista de sus anotadores solo existe como una imagen** en la documentación. Para el autocompletado habría que sacarla del código del paquete.
- Y hace lo mismo que `sequenceDiagram`, que ya está en **supported**.

Es decir: pagas una dependencia, un dialecto que no comparte nada con los otros 32, y trabajo de ingeniería inversa sobre una captura de pantalla — para duplicar algo que ya funciona bien.

## Iconos

`architecture` trae **5 iconos** (`cloud`, `database`, `disk`, `internet`, `server`). `treeView` no trae ninguno visible por defecto. Todo lo demás exige registrar un pack de iconify.

**El problema es que choca con una promesa que ya hice y que está protegida por un test:** fase 1 no hace **ninguna petición de red**. Iconify normalmente descarga los iconos en tiempo de ejecución.

Las alternativas:

- **Empaquetar un subconjunto** dentro del frame. Mantiene la promesa. Los packs completos son grandes (`logos` ronda los 1.900 iconos), pero 40–60 seleccionados no pesan casi nada. El bundle actual son 4,9 MB de JS, y mermaid ya lo divide por tipo de diagrama, así que se carga perezosamente.
- **Descargarlos bajo demanda.** Iconos infinitos, pero hay que borrar la promesa del README y **borrar el test que la comprueba**.

Mi recomendación en ambos casos ya está en el plan: **descartar ZenUML** y **empaquetar un subconjunto de iconos**. Pero ninguna es obvia — la primera reduce la cobertura de "todos los tipos" de 33 a 32, y la segunda limita qué iconos puede usar la gente.

**No. ZenUML no te sirve para eso, y por eso no lo añado.**

ZenUML es un motor de render de terceros, solo para diagramas de secuencia, con **su propio sistema de estilos**. No lee las `themeVariables` de mermaid ni nuestros tokens. Añadirlo haría el estilado *más* difícil: tendrías un tipo de diagrama que se pinta por reglas distintas a los otros 32.

Lo que sí controla el aspecto de los diagramas es el **puente de tokens** en `packages/ui/src/theme.ts`. Ahora mismo mapea **8 variables**. Mermaid tiene muchísimas más, y varias globales y por tipo de diagrama. Ese es el hueco real, y ya lo tenía señalado en varias páginas del catálogo — `treeView`, por ejemplo, tiene los colores por defecto **en negro fijo**, así que en modo oscuro es ilegible.

Cambio el orden: primero el estilado, que es lo que quieres, luego iconos, luego diagnósticos. Voy a la fuente antes de tocar nada.

content.text:
Base directory for this skill: /tmp/claude-1000/bundled-skills/2.1.232/014e7a65d7baec114d3f713fe4e97efc/dataviz

# Data Visualization

A chart is **read by people and executed by you**. This skill turns "make it look
good" into a procedure with checks, so the result is right by construction rather
than by taste.

**The method here is design-system-agnostic.** Nothing in the procedure, the form
heuristic, the six checks, or the mark specs is specific to one product. A design
system supplies a small set of *parameters* (its ramps, a categorical order, a
diverging pair, a status palette, a texture, its surfaces, its filter components);
the method consumes them unchanged. A **validated default palette** is the
reference instance, fully specified in `references/palette.md`. To target your
brand, read that file's structure and substitute its values — touch nothing else.

> The single most important habit: **the color part is computable, so compute it.**
> Never eyeball whether a palette is colorblind-safe — run `scripts/validate_palette.js`.

## The procedure — do these in order

Color comes LAST. Most bad charts pick colors first.

1. **Pick the form.** What is the data's job — magnitude, identity, polarity, a
   single headline, change-over-time? The job picks the chart type, and sometimes
   the answer is *not a chart* (a stat tile or hero number). → `references/choosing-a-form.md`
2. **Assign color by the job it does.** Categorical (identity), sequential
   (magnitude), diverging (polarity), or status (state) — each has one rule.
   Assign categorical hues in fixed order, never cycled. → `references/color-formula.md`
3. **VALIDATE the palette — run the script, don't reason about ΔE.**
   `node scripts/validate_palette.js "<hex,hex,…>" --mode light` (relative to
   this skill's base directory — or load it as `<script type="module">` in the
   chart's own page, where it reads
   `data-palette` off `<body>` and logs a `console.table` report). It returns
   pass/fail on the lightness band, chroma floor, adjacent-pair CVD separation,
   the normal-vision floor, and contrast. Fix anything that FAILs before continuing. Re-run for
   `--mode dark` with that mode's surface.
4. **Apply mark specs & spacers.** Thin marks, 4px rounded data-ends anchored to
   the baseline, 2px lines, ≥8px markers, a 2px surface gap between fills (stacked
   segments and adjacent bars alike) and a 2px surface ring on overlapping marks,
   selective direct labels. → `references/marks-and-anatomy.md`
5. **Add the hover layer — by default.** An HTML/SVG chart *is* interactive; ship
   a crosshair+tooltip on line/area and a per-mark hover tooltip on bar/dot/cell.
   The only form that skips it is a bare stat tile with no plot. Hit targets bigger
   than the mark; filters in one row above the charts. → `references/interaction.md`
6. **Final accessibility pass.** For ≥ 2 series a legend is always present and ≤ 4
   are also direct-labeled (a single series needs no legend box — the title names
   it), so identity is never color-alone; a table view exists; dark mode is **selected** — its own
   steps from the same ramps, validated against the dark surface, not an automatic
   flip; texture is available for the CVD/print/forced-colors case.
7. **Render it and look at it.** The validator checks color, not layout — open or
   screenshot the output and eyeball it for label collisions, geometry, and overflow
   before calling it done.

Then check the result against **`references/anti-patterns.md`** — it is the catalog
of what goes wrong. If your chart matches an entry, it's wrong.

## Non-negotiables (true in every design system)

- **Assign categorical hues in fixed order, never cycled.** A 9th series is never a
  generated hue — it folds into "Other," small multiples, or composite encoding.
- **One axis.** Never a dual-axis chart (two y-scales). Two measures of different
  scale → two charts, small multiples, or indexed to a common base. *(This is the
  #1 chart mistake — see anti-patterns.)*
- **Color follows the entity, never its rank.** A filter that changes the series
  count must not repaint the survivors.
- **Sequential = one hue, light→dark. Diverging = two hues + a neutral gray
  midpoint.** Never a rainbow; never a hue at the diverging midpoint.
- **Run the validator before shipping any categorical palette.** CVD ΔE ≥ 8 is the
  target (OKLab ×100); 6–8 is a floor that is legal ONLY with secondary encoding. A
  normal-vision floor below 15 is a hard FAIL — full-color readers can't tell the
  pair apart; re-step it on the adjacent pairlist (secondary encoding does not excuse
  this one); under `--pairs all` cut series or facet instead — see check 4. A contrast WARN
  obligates visible labels or a table view — it is not dismissable.
- **Thin marks; a legend always present for ≥ 2 series (none for one), with
  selective direct labels (never a number on every point); recessive grid/axes.**
- **Text wears text tokens, never the series color** — values, labels, and legends
  stay in primary/secondary/muted ink; a colored mark beside them carries identity.
- **Status colors are reserved** (good/warning/serious/critical) and never reused
  for "series 4"; they ship with an icon + label, never color alone.

## Plugging in a design system

The method is invariant; only these parameters change per system. The reference
instance — every value filled in — is `references/palette.md`.

| Parameter | What the system provides |
|---|---|
| **Ramps** | the hue scales (named steps) the palette draws from |
| **Categorical theme** | the fixed hue order (a named theme); default + alternates |
| **Sequential hue** | the default single hue for magnitude |
| **Diverging pair** | two warm/cool poles + a neutral midpoint |
| **Status palette** | good / warning / serious / critical — steps distinct from categorical |
| **Texture fill** | one directional hand-drawn fill, used at 45° / 135° |
| **Surfaces** | light & dark chart-surface colors (the validator needs these) |
| **Filter controls** | date-range & dimension controls (behavioral spec in `interaction.md`) |

To onboard a new system: fill those rows, feed its ramps to the validator, and let
it snap each slot to the nearest passing step. Structure and rules stay as written.

## Reference files

| File | What it answers |
|------|-----------------|
| `references/choosing-a-form.md` | Which chart type / is it even a chart? |
| `references/color-formula.md` | The four jobs, the six checks, snap-to-passing |
| `references/marks-and-anatomy.md` | Mark specs, spacers, labels, figures, hero number |
| `references/interaction.md` | Tooltips & hover, filters & time ranges |
| `references/components.md` | The pieces a chart is made of — build each in plain HTML |
| `references/anti-patterns.md` | **What goes wrong — check every chart against this** |
| `references/palette.md` | **The reference palette instance** — every parameter, filled in; swap for your brand's |
| `scripts/validate_palette.js` | Runnable six-checks validator (run it; don't eyeball) |

content.text:
Respondiendo a tu pregunta: **ZenUML no te ayuda a estilar los diagramas, así que no lo he añadido.** Es un motor de render de terceros con su propio sistema de estilos — no lee las variables de mermaid ni tus tokens. Habría hecho el estilado *peor*: un tipo de diagrama pintándose por reglas distintas a los otros 32.

Lo que sí te da control es el **puente de tokens**, y ahí estaba el problema real. Fui a la documentación de mermaid y encontré tres cosas que estaba haciendo mal:

1. **`"The theming engine will only recognize hex colors"`** (`theming.md:92`). Yo pasaba `rgb()`. Renderizaba, pero mermaid **deriva unas 40 variables** de las primarias, y esas derivaciones fallaban.
2. **No ponía `darkMode`**, que es lo que decide si las derivadas se aclaran u oscurecen. En modo oscuro se calculaban como si fuera claro.
3. El diseño correcto no es mapear cien variables, es **poner bien las primarias y dejar que mermaid derive** — y luego sobrescribir solo las que traen negro fijo por defecto (`pieStrokeColor`, `treeView.labelColor`).

**Y entonces abrí el navegador y encontré esto:**

Las formas del flowchart estaban, y **todas las etiquetas faltaban**. Ningún error, ningún test rojo. Era mi sanitizador: mermaid mete las etiquetas dentro de `<foreignObject>` y yo lo tenía prohibido. Permitirlo no bastó — DOMPurify también borra el HTML de dentro por reglas de espacio de nombres al sanear un string SVG. La salida buena es `htmlLabels: false`: etiquetas como `<text>` SVG, que se sanean limpio y además cierran un vector de XSS real. No se pierde nada; los ejemplos de *markdown strings* de mermaid usan justamente esa opción.

También añadí una **paleta categórica de 8 colores** para secciones de pie, curvas de radar, tramos de journey y series de xychart, validada contra mis dos superficies (banda de luminosidad, croma mínimo, separación para daltonismo y para visión normal). Pasa en claro y en oscuro.

```
bun run verify → 220 unit + 39 e2e. Verde.
```

Dos tests nuevos para que esto no se repita: **las etiquetas deben estar presentes** y **la paleta debe seguir al tema**.

Iconos: elegiste empaquetar un subconjunto. Siguiente: los diagnósticos de los 15 tipos parciales. Pero antes, míralo tú — ahora sí hay algo que mirar.

ok, como podríamos hacer que tengan otros colores? O sea que el usuario pueda elegir el color de los bordes, relleno, texto. La forma de las lineas, por ejemplo en los flowcahrt TD que las líneas sean rectas
Todo eso existe en mermaid y se controla desde el propio documento. Voy a la fuente antes de diseñar nada.

result.output:
### Selecting Diagram Looks

Mermaid offers a variety of styles or “looks” for your diagrams, allowing you to tailor the visual appearance to match your specific needs or preferences. Whether you prefer a hand-drawn or classic style, you can easily customize your diagrams.

**Available Looks:**

- Hand-Drawn Look: For a more personal, creative touch, the hand-drawn look brings a sketch-like quality to your diagrams. This style is perfect for informal settings or when you want to add a bit of personality to your diagrams.
- Classic Look: If you prefer the traditional Mermaid style, the classic look maintains the original appearance that many users are familiar with. It’s great for consistency across projects or when you want to keep the familiar aesthetic.

**How to Select a Look:**

You can select a look by adding the look parameter in the metadata section of your Mermaid diagram code. Here’s an example:

```mermaid-example
---
config:
  look: handDrawn
  theme: neutral
---
flowchart LR
  A[Start] --> B{Decision}
  B -->|Yes| C[Continue]
  B -->|No| D[Stop]
```

#### Selecting Layout Algorithms

In addition to customizing the look of your diagrams, Mermaid Chart now allows you to choose different layout algorithms to better organize and present your diagrams, especially when dealing with more complex structures. The layout algorithm dictates how nodes and edges are arranged on the page.

#### Supported Layout Algorithms:

- Dagre (default): This is the classic layout algorithm that has been used in Mermaid for a long time. It provides a good balance of simplicity and visual clarity, making it ideal for most diagrams.
- ELK: For those who need more sophisticated layout capabilities, especially when working with large or intricate diagrams, the ELK (Eclipse Layout Kernel) layout offers advanced options. It provides a more optimized arrangement, potentially reducing overlapping and improving readability. This is not included out the box but needs to be added when integrating mermaid for sites/applications that want to have elk support.

#### How to Select a Layout Algorithm:

You can specify the layout algorithm directly in the metadata section of your Mermaid diagram code. Here’s an example:

```mermaid-example
---
config:
  layout: elk
  look: handDrawn
  theme: dark
---
flowchart TB
  A[Start] --> B{Decision}
  B -->|Yes| C[Continue]
  B -->|No| D[Stop]
```

In this example, the `layout: elk` line configures the diagram to use the ELK layout algorithm, along with the hand drawn look and forest theme.

#### Customizing ELK Layout:

When using the ELK layout, you can further refine the diagram’s configuration, such as how nodes are placed and whether parallel edges should be combined:

- To combine parallel edges, use mergeEdges: true | false.
- To configure node placement, use nodePlacementStrategy with the following options:
  - SIMPLE
  - NETWORK_SIMPLEX
  - LINEAR_SEGMENTS
  - BRANDES_KOEPF (default)
- To configure Brandes-Koepf node placement alignment, use nodePlacementAlignment with the following options:
  - NONE (default)
  - LEFTUP
  - LEFTDOWN
  - RIGHTUP
  - RIGHTDOWN
  - BALANCED

**Example configuration:**

```
---
config:
  layout: elk
  elk:
    mergeEdges: true
    nodePlacementStrategy: LINEAR_SEGMENTS
    nodePlacementAlignment: NONE
---
flowchart LR
  A[Start] --> B{Choose Path}
  B -->|Option 1| C[Path 1]
  B -->|Option 2| D[Path 2]

```

#### Using Dagre Layout with Classic Look:

Another example:

```
---
config:
  layout: dagre
  look: classic
  theme: default
---

flowchart LR
A[Start] --> B{Choose Path}
B -->|Option 1| C[Path 1]
B -->|Option 2| D[Path 2]

```

These options give you the flexibility to create diagrams that not only look great but are also arranged to best suit your data’s structure and flow.

| Lo que quieres | Cómo se controla |

| Relleno, borde y texto de **todos** los nodos | `config.themeVariables`: `primaryColor`, `primaryBorderColor`, `primaryTextColor` |
| Color de las líneas | `themeVariables.lineColor` |
| **Líneas rectas** en un flowchart | `config.flowchart.curve: linear` — y `stepBefore`/`stepAfter` para ángulos rectos |
| La curva de **una sola** arista | `A e1@--> B` más `e1@{ curve: linear }` (v11.10.0+) |
| Un **nodo** concreto | `style nodeId fill:#f9f,stroke:#333,color:#fff` |
| Un estilo reutilizable | `classDef nombre …` + `A:::nombre` |
| Aspecto dibujado a mano | `config.look: handDrawn` |

Lo construyo: un panel que **lee y escribe el frontmatter**, no un ajuste aparte.

/**
 * The styling options a user can change, and where each one lives in mermaid's config.
 *
 * Sourced from upstream:
 * - curve options — `docs/syntax/flowchart.md:1177-1184`
 * - `look` — `docs/intro/syntax-reference.md:100-124`
 * - `layout` — `docs/intro/syntax-reference.md:126-152`
 * - theme variables — `docs/config/theming.md:94-119`
 *
 * Every option is expressed as a config path so the style panel writes into the document's
 * frontmatter, never into a side channel. See `frontmatter.ts`.
 */

export interface StyleOption<T extends string = string> {
  /** Dotted config path under `config:` in the frontmatter. */
  readonly path: string
  readonly label: string
  readonly help: string
  readonly choices: ReadonlyArray<{ value: T; label: string; help?: string }>
  /** Diagram type ids this applies to. Empty means every type. */
  readonly appliesTo: readonly string[]
}

/**
 * Edge shape.
 *
 * `linear` is the answer to "make the lines straight". `stepBefore` and `stepAfter` give
 * right-angled routing, which is what people usually mean by "straight" in a top-down
 * flowchart. Diagram-level here; a single edge can be overridden with an edge id and
 * `e1@{ curve: linear }` (v11.10.0+).
 */
export const CURVE_OPTION: StyleOption = {
  path: 'flowchart.curve',
  label: 'Line shape',
  help: 'How edges are drawn between nodes.',
  appliesTo: ['flowchart', 'swimlanes', 'block'],
  choices: [
    { value: 'basis', label: 'Curved (default)' },
    { value: 'linear', label: 'Straight', help: 'Direct lines, no curvature' },
    { value: 'stepBefore', label: 'Right angles, turn first' },
    { value: 'stepAfter', label: 'Right angles, turn last' },
    { value: 'step', label: 'Right angles, centred' },
    { value: 'natural', label: 'Natural' },
    { value: 'cardinal', label: 'Cardinal' },
    { value: 'catmullRom', label: 'Catmull–Rom' },
    { value: 'monotoneX', label: 'Monotone X' },
    { value: 'monotoneY', label: 'Monotone Y' },
    { value: 'bumpX', label: 'Bump X' },
    { value: 'bumpY', label: 'Bump Y' },
  ],
}

export const LOOK_OPTION: StyleOption = {
  path: 'look',
  label: 'Look',
  help: 'The overall drawing style.',
  appliesTo: [],
  choices: [
    { value: 'classic', label: 'Classic' },
    { value: 'handDrawn', label: 'Hand-drawn', help: 'Not supported by Wardley or Railroad' },
  ],
}

export const DIRECTION_OPTION: StyleOption = {
  path: 'flowchart.defaultRenderer',
  label: 'Layout engine',
  help: 'Dagre is the default. ELK arranges large or dense diagrams better.',
  appliesTo: ['flowchart'],
  choices: [
    { value: 'dagre', label: 'Dagre (default)' },
    { value: 'elk', label: 'ELK', help: 'Better for large diagrams' },
  ],
}

export const STYLE_OPTIONS: readonly StyleOption[] = [CURVE_OPTION, LOOK_OPTION, DIRECTION_OPTION]

/**
 * The four colours worth exposing directly.
 *
 * Mermaid derives most variables from these, so changing `primaryColor` moves the border
 * and text shades with it unless they are also set. Deliberately a short list: a panel of
 * a hundred theme variables is not a feature, it is a maze.
 */
export interface StyleColor {
  readonly path: string
  readonly label: string
  readonly help: string
}

export const STYLE_COLORS: readonly StyleColor[] = [
  {
    path: 'themeVariables.primaryColor',
    label: 'Fill',
    help: 'Node background. Borders and text shades derive from it unless set below.',
  },
  {
    path: 'themeVariables.primaryBorderColor',
    label: 'Border',
    help: 'Node outline.',
  },
  {
    path: 'themeVariables.primaryTextColor',
    label: 'Text',
    help: 'Label text inside nodes.',
  },
  {
    path: 'themeVariables.lineColor',
    label: 'Lines',
    help: 'Edges between nodes.',
  },
]

export function optionsFor(typeId: string | null): readonly StyleOption[] {
  return STYLE_OPTIONS.filter(
    (option) => option.appliesTo.length === 0 || (typeId !== null && option.appliesTo.includes(typeId)),
  )
}

/**
 * Merges a document's own `themeVariables` overrides over the token-derived ones.
 *
 * Mermaid applies frontmatter for most config — `look` and `flowchart.curve` arrive
 * correctly — but `themeVariables` passed to `initialize` wins over the frontmatter, so a
 * document that sets `primaryColor` renders in our colour anyway. Rather than depend on
 * mermaid's internal precedence, the host merges: one place decides, and it is this one.
 *
 * @param overrides flattened dotted paths from the document, e.g. `themeVariables.primaryColor`.
 */
export function withDocumentOverrides(
  variables: ThemeVariables,
  overrides: Readonly<Record<string, string>>,
): ThemeVariables {
  const merged: ThemeVariables = { ...variables }
  for (const [path, value] of Object.entries(overrides)) {
    if (!path.startsWith('themeVariables.')) continue
    const parts = path.slice('themeVariables.'.length).split('.')
    if (parts.length === 1) {
      merged[parts[0] as string] = value
    } else if (parts.length === 2) {
      const [namespace, key] = parts as [string, string]
      const existing = merged[namespace]
      merged[namespace] = {
        ...(typeof existing === 'object' ? existing : {}),
        [key]: value,
      }
    }
  }
  return merged
}
'''

Colours, line shape and look, chosen in a panel and written into the

content.text:
Hecho. Botón **Style** en la barra. `bun run verify`: 238 unit + 41 e2e, verde.

**Lo que puedes cambiar ahora mismo:**

- **Relleno, borde, texto y líneas** — selectores de color.
- **Forma de línea** — `Straight` es lo que pedías. También tienes ángulos rectos en tres variantes (`stepBefore` gira al principio, `stepAfter` al final, `step` en el medio), más las siete curvas de d3.
- **Look** — clásico o dibujado a mano.
- **Motor de layout** — dagre o ELK.

Cada control se muestra solo donde aplica: la forma de línea sale en flowchart, swimlanes y block; el look en todos.

**La decisión de diseño que importa:** todo se escribe en el **frontmatter YAML del propio documento**, no en un ajuste aparte.

```yaml
---
config:
  flowchart:
    curve: linear
  look: handDrawn
  themeVariables:
    primaryColor: "#2a78d6"
---
flowchart TD
    ...
```

Así el diagrama **se exporta con su estilo** y se pega en cualquier otro editor de Mermaid igual. Es la regla del proyecto: si no vuelve a texto, no existe.
